stories.title: Southern Ontario braces for heavy rainfall, muggy weather amid special weather statement
stories.summary: Although meteorological fall begins Tuesday, Atchison said summer-like warmth is not ready to leave Ontario just yet.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Much of southern Ontario remains under a special weather statement Monday, with warnings of additional rainfall, heavy downpours and continued muggy conditions through the afternoon and evening. CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison said scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to continue developing through the late afternoon, with some areas at risk of significant rainfall.

“We could see up to 30 millimetres of rain if communities find themselves under one of the heavier thunderstorms,” Atchison said Monday. The unsettled weather is being fuelled by an extremely humid air mass lingering across the region.

Temperatures were hovering between 21 C and 26 C Monday afternoon, with warmer conditions reported toward Essex County. Atchison noted that Windsor-Essex is also facing increasing heat concerns, with a heat warning expected to remain a factor in the coming days as temperatures continue to climb.

“Heat and humidity are really going to play a role over the next several days,” she said. While forecasters expect a brief lull in storm activity during the evening, the threat of additional showers and thunderstorms is expected to return Tuesday afternoon.

Tuesday’s forecast calls for a mix of sun and cloud, along with another chance of showers and thunderstorms as daytime heating combines with the humid air mass. Overnight temperatures are expected to remain unusually warm for late August and early September.

London is forecast to drop only to about 21 C overnight, while communities across Midwestern Ontario are expected to see lows ranging from 19 C to 22 C. The heat is forecast to continue through midweek, with daytime highs between 29 C and 31 C over the next several days.

Atchison said actual temperatures could vary depending on the amount of cloud cover that develops across the region. “The one constant is that the heat and humidity will stay with us for the next few days,” she said. Looking ahead, conditions are expected to gradually become more seasonable heading into the Labour Day weekend.

Thursday is forecast to be mainly cloudy, while Friday will see a mix of sun and cloud. Similar conditions are expected through the holiday weekend, with a mix of sun and cloud forecast for Saturday, Sunday and Labour Day Monday.

Daytime highs are expected to settle closer to seasonal norms, ranging between 24 C and 25 C. Although meteorological fall begins Tuesday, Atchison said summer-like warmth is not ready to leave Ontario just yet. “We welcome meteorological fall tomorrow, but the summer air is holding on,” she said.

CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison said scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to continue developing through the late afternoon, with some areas at risk of significant rainfall.

“We could see up to 30 millimetres of rain if communities find themselves under one of the heavier thunderstorms,” Atchison said Monday. The unsettled weather is being fuelled by an extremely humid air mass lingering across the region.

Temperatures were hovering between 21 C and 26 C Monday afternoon, with warmer conditions reported toward Essex County. Atchison noted that Windsor-Essex is also facing increasing heat concerns, with a heat warning expected to remain a factor in the coming days as temperatures continue to climb.

“Heat and humidity are really going to play a role over the next several days,” she said. While forecasters expect a brief lull in storm activity during the evening, the threat of additional showers and thunderstorms is expected to return Tuesday afternoon.

Tuesday’s forecast calls for a mix of sun and cloud, along with another chance of showers and thunderstorms as daytime heating combines with the humid air mass. Overnight temperatures are expected to remain unusually warm for late August and early September.

London is forecast to drop only to about 21 C overnight, while communities across Midwestern Ontario are expected to see lows ranging from 19 C to 22 C. The heat is forecast to continue through midweek, with daytime highs between 29 C and 31 C over the next several days.

Thursday is forecast to be mainly cloudy, while Friday will see a mix of sun and cloud. Similar conditions are expected through the holiday weekend, with a mix of sun and cloud forecast for Saturday, Sunday and Labour Day Monday.

stories.title: Animal tranquilizer, sedatives found in Winnipeg fentanyl supply, warns expert
stories.summary: Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply.
stories.author: Kayla Rosen
stories.content: Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply. Nurse practitioner Heidi Pharand-Joven, who works for Siloam Mission’s opioid addictions program, said her clinic is continuing to see fentanyl-related issues. She explained one of the problems is that the synthetic opioid is often mixed with benzodiazepines or animal tranquilizers, which makes it less effective against opioid antagonists. “Naloxone, Narcan is not as effective because it doesn’t have any effect on the animal tranquilizers or the benzodiazepines,” she explained in an interview with Your Morning Winnipeg on Monday. “(Opioid antagonists are) still the best way. It’s still really important to educate people on how to use Naloxone and make sure that people who are using substances or who are with people who are using substances have Narcan kits available on them.” Pharand-Joven’s warning comes on International Overdose Awareness Day — a day created to raise awareness and take action against overdoses. According to numbers from the Manitoba government, more than 350 Manitobans died from substance-related deaths between January and November 2025. Beyond the overdoses, Pharand-Joven said injection drug use is also contributing to the province’s high rate of HIV infection. “When I’m working with clients at Siloam, that is definitely something that we talk about: infectious disease … You can’t treat one without the other,” she said “We can’t have these continued siloed approaches for treating addiction and substance-use disorders. We have to consider all the other risk factors.” In May 2026, the Manitoba government declared a public health emergency to fight the spread of HIV. The province reported that HIV rates had been steadily increasing to a high of 328 new cases in 2025. With files from CTV’s Rachel Lagacé

stories.title: 3-alarm blaze at commercial building in Scarborough sparks structural concerns
stories.summary: Toronto fire said it was called to the area of McLevin Avenue and Tapscott Road just before 2 a.m. to try and suppress the flames at a commercial building.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
paragraphs: Firefighters were met with heavy and flames early on Monday morning when they rushed to the scene of a three-alarm blaze in Scarborough.
Toronto fire said it was called to the area of McLevin Avenue and Tapscott Road just before 2 a.m. to try and suppress the flames at a commercial building.
Facing a fierce fire, crews were quickly forced to transition to defensive firefighting, worrying about the deteriorating structural conditions of the building.
Toronto fire said its crews were worried about the condition of the building’s walls and roof.
As the city woke up on Monday, roads were still closed and crews were at the scene.
Officials said there were no longer visible flames, but there were still worries about the smoke emanating from the structure.
“Fire crews still remain on scene applying water to building,” Toronto fire wrote in a statement.

stories.title: TAP Air Portugal flies into red before privatization
stories.summary: TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content: TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon. The company recorded a net loss of 59.3 million euros (US$68.8 million) in the three months to the end of June, compared to a profit of 38.3 million euros in the same period last year. While TAP carried a record 8.2 million passengers and took in record revenue of just over two billion euros over the first half of the year, higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East had a negative impact of 99.2 million euros, the company said. Thanks to the “solidity of demand across our entire network”, the airline was “able to mitigate the significant impact of the sharp increase in fuel prices”, chief executive Luis Rodrigues said in a statement. TAP, which was renationalized in 2020 to stem losses from the COVID-19 pandemic, is in the final stages of being reprivatized. Both Air France-KLM and Lufthansa said in July they had submitted bids to acquire a controlling stake in the airline, with the government expected to announce the result in the coming days

stories.title: London man formally charged with murder in fatal home stabbing
stories.summary: The 40-year-old accused appeared by video Monday as the new charge was read in a London courtroom.
stories.author: Jane Sims
paragraphs: Monday morning, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of no fixed address, appeared in a London courtroom by video link for five minutes from the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre as the new charge was read to him.

Cornejo is charged in the death of Lillian Leonard, 73, who died in hospital last week from stab wounds she received during a break-in at her Raywood Avenue home, north of the intersection of Wellington and Base Line roads.
A publication ban regarding evidence and reasons at a potential bail hearing was put in place by justice of the peace Kristine Diaz during Monday’s court appearance.
Cornejo appeared on the video link in a jail-issued orange T-shirt. His hair is long and he has a beard.
He told Diaz that he has contacted London defence lawyer Nicola Circelli. His case was put over to Sept. 10 to allow time for a legal aid application and to confirm retaining counsel.
Any potential bail hearing would be heard in the Superior Court of Justice, Diaz noted, because the charge is murder.

Police said last week that Leonard and Cornejo were not known to each other. She was stabbed after she heard a noise inside her home shortly after 6 a.m. on Aug. 22, which was a Saturday. She was able to call 911 after she was assaulted, police said.
Officers raced to the address, where London police said a man was found throwing glass at them at the home. An officer received minor injuries, police said.
Cornejo is also charged with aggravated assault, break and and enter with intent, assaulting a police officer with a weapon and obstructing a police officer.
A member of Leonard’s family declined comment when contacted by The Free Press on Monday.
With files from Ryan Goodison, The London Free Press

stories.title: Trump shares Christian group's proposal allowing Canadian Jews facing antisemitism to flee to the U.S.
stories.summary: Donald Trump has shared a report on a potential plan to create a legal pathway into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians facing antisemitism.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
As he finds new ways to poke Canada amid an ugly trade war, U.S. President Donald Trump has amplified a Christian group’s proposal to create a legal pathway into the United States for Canadian Jews facing antisemitism.

He shared on social media a news report about a letter penned by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers (Nacl), which urges Trump to establish an expedited method of entry into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians “who are experiencing persecution or who credibly fear for their safety because they are Jewish.”

It points to “an alarming climate of harassment, intimidation, vandalism, threats, and violence” that Jewish Canadian families have faced since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, adding that “advocates working directly with these families report that more than 2,000 Jewish Canadians have expressed interest in relocating because of growing concerns for their safety.”

The letter continues: “Accordingly, we respectfully ask that you direct the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to identify and implement lawful, secure, and appropriately expedited pathways for eligible Jewish Canadian nationals and their immediate family members who face persecution.”

Nacl founder and president Jason Rapert signed the letter, alongside state representatives and religious leaders, and it was sent to the U.S. president, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and several U.S. senators and representatives on Thursday.

The letter said that any potential program should maintain national security safeguards such as identity, criminal history, medical and security screening, and protect family unity. It also called for the Trump administration to work with states, local governments, Jewish organizations, churches, nonprofits and employers who are willing to assist arriving families.

The letter comes a month after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year. While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.

Jewish schools, synagogues and other institutions have been shot at, firebombed and targeted by hateful graffiti in Canada since Hamas’ October 7 attacks on Israel.

Meanwhile, in the U.S., the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) reported earlier this month that anti-Jewish hate crimes accounted for 63 per cent of all reported religion-based hate crimes last year, according to FBI data. It marked the third-highest year on record of anti-Jewish hate crimes in the U.S.

The letter states that an expedited pathway for Jewish Canadians would be consistent with “America’s historic commitment to stand against religious persecution,” adding, “We believe this moment presents another opportunity for America to demonstrate those principles.”

Elsewhere, the Nacl letter references Jewish and Christian leaders in Tulsa who have already offered to help receive Canadian Jewish families, and points out that Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt previously told Trump his state would welcome Jewish families who legally enter the United States .

In a July 22 letter, Gov. Stitt wrote that “Oklahoma would proudly welcome those who choose to make our state their home,” should Jewish families lawfully move to the U.S. in search of safety.

The Nacl letter concludes: “For generations, America has served as a refuge for people fleeing religious persecution. We urge you to ensure that, consistent with federal law and the security interests of the United States, that door remains open to our Jewish brothers and sisters in Canada who need it today.”

stories.title: London resident dies after head-on crash in Thames Centre
stories.summary: Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: A London resident died in hospital after a head-on crash between an SUV and a transport truck in Thames Centre last week.
Middlesex County OPP and emergency crews responded shortly before 1 p.m. Aug. 26 to the collision on Dundas Street near Fairview Road.
The driver of the transport truck was taken to hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening, police said in a Monday release.
The SUV driver, a 40-year-old from London, was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died.
Members of the OPP Traffic Incident Management Enforcement team attended the scene to assist with the investigation.
Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
Anyone with information is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (Tips).
Provincial police are investigating after people posing as Dorchester Fall Fair representatives collected money and information from prospective vendors for phony permits.
Middlesex County OPP responded to a fraud complaint on Hamilton Road in Thames Centre about 1:40 p.m. on Aug. 27.

The North Dorchester Agricultural Society, which manages the fair, learned potential vendors had provided information and paid an undisclosed amount of money to people posing as fair representatives to secure vendor permits, police said.
The fraudulent messages appeared on social media and in unsolicited emails, police said.
The suspects are unknown, and police believe there May be additional victims.
Anyone who believes they were victimized is asked to contact Middlesex County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (Tips).
For more information about fraud, contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.

stories.title: 'People's festival' no more? Tiff fans grapple with ticket price hikes
stories.summary: When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama “The Woman King” for about $50 each.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: Toronto — When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama “The Woman King” for about $50 each. This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106. “That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on Tiff galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices. While Tiff fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark. Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” justice system thriller “Prima Facie” and the Ryan Gosling-produced “Love of Your Life” going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98. Tiff did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing. The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during Tiff’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access. “It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year. Like many Tiff fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less. “I love Tiff. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said. While Tiff typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at. Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106. In the lead-up to the festival, Tiff advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began. Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said Tiff is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to. Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance. “If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said. But there’s more than demand at play. Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. Tiff is likely no exception. “Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said. On top of inflation, Tiff is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival. In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, Tiff lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995. The federal government offered $23 million to help Tiff launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027. The latest financial information Tiff published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1 million and more than $41.9 million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses. Its revenue was $39.6 million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2 million in expenses, its annual reports show. Tiff’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances. “There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in Tiff’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.” Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of Tiff’s stature — this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows — but she’s still disappointed in the prices. After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket. Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable. But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out. “I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?” Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film — German historical drama “Silent Friend” — and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a Tiff diehard. “I see it as the tail end,” she said. This year, she hopes to see at least one movie — a Midnight Madness film — with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did. “It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.” That’s a problem, said Keil, because Tiff has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year. In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping Tiff lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals. “The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said. “If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026. Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

On top of inflation, Tiff is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival. The federal government offered $23 million to help Tiff launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses. Its revenue was $39.6 million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2 million in expenses, its annual reports show. Tiff’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances. “There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in Tiff’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.” Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of Tiff’s stature — this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows — but she’s still disappointed in the prices. After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket. Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable. But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out. “I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?” Simply put, she didn’t. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.” That’s a problem, said Keil, because Tiff has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year. stories.title: Homicide charge upgraded in fatal south London home invasion; accused remanded in custody
stories.summary: Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, appeared briefly by video from Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre in London court Monday morning.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A new charge of second-degree murder has officially been laid against a man accused in a south London home invasion after the victim died from her injuries. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, appeared briefly by video from Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre in London court Monday morning.

During the approximately three-minute appearance, the second-degree murder charge was read into the record. Cornejo was remanded into custody and is scheduled to return to court Sept. 10. The new charge follows the death of a 73-year-old woman who was seriously injured during an alleged break-in at her home near Wellington Road and Base Line Road East on Aug.

22. London police previously said the woman was sleeping when she was awakened by a loud noise at about 6:10 a.m. Investigators allege an unknown man entered the residence, assaulted and stabbed her before she was able to call 911.

The woman was taken to hospital with serious injuries that were initially believed to be non-life threatening. Police confirmed on Aug. 28 that she died in hospital, and the case is now being investigated as a homicide. Cornejo was originally charged with aggravated assault, break and enter, assaulting a peace officer and obstructing a peace officer.

He now also faces a charge of second-degree murder. The allegations against Cornejo have not been proven in court. With files from CTV News London’s Nick Paparella

stories.title: Thinking of leaving your desk job and entering the trades? Here's your guide
stories.summary: For many Canadians, skilled trades have started to become more attractive as a career option, partly as various levels of government invest heavily in these professions while a boom in artificial intelligence creates fear over the future of many desk jobs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: More than 25 years into his job as a business administrator, Simon Hardcastle felt there was nothing left for him to learn. He didn’t hate his job, but it wasn’t thrilling either, Hardcastle recalled. Then, one day at work, he signed up to drive a skid steer to plow snow, and he knew it was time for a shakeup. “I moved snow, and about two hours later I thought, ‘Wow, this is really good fun! What else can I do?” the 49-year-old Ancaster, Ont., resident said. “So, I spoke to my wife and I was like, ‘I’m thinking of changing careers.’” He knew going from a desk job to a skilled trade wasn’t going to be easy. It meant giving up a stable paycheque for a while, and temporarily transitioning to a single-income household while also raising two kids. But he was sure that’s what he wanted to do. For many Canadians, skilled trades have started to become more attractive as a career option, partly as various levels of government invest heavily in these professions while a boom in artificial intelligence creates fear over the future of many desk jobs. Some career counsellors say they’re seeing more interest among mid-career workers to make a switch. However, not knowing where to begin often delays the process. Start by understanding the different trade opportunities, said Rachel Buesink, general manager at Express Employment Professionals in Hamilton, Ont. Online assessment tools can help you figure out where your strengths lie — whether that’s building things, mathematics and problem-solving, or even general handyman work, she said. But just having an interest isn’t enough. Buesink said a lot of times, people come to her with misconceptions. “So many people come in and say: ‘I’ve hung pictures, I can build anything from Ikea, I want to be a carpenter,’” she said. But many don’t realize how lengthy and demanding the journey is, she said. It can take four years of school and several exams. You also need an employer who can document your progress and is willing to hire you as an apprentice. Shelley Gray, chief executive officer of SkilledTradesBC, says exposure to your desired job or industry can help cement that decision. Gray said several institutions offer sampler or pre-apprenticeship programs to try out various trades. That could also be a help in getting into a full-time program or finding an employer, she said. Buesink said switching careers is about “looking at understanding what each skilled trade opportunity is, trying to best match it with your strengths and interest, and then trying to keep up with the ever-changing economic demands for that trade. “It is a bit of a balancing act.” Keeping up with bills and supporting a family during the transition can also be a challenge. “The biggest thing is the wage cut until you’re trained and able to add value to the company,” Buesink said. She said workers in transition can get employment insurance or make some money from apprenticeships. But overall, it takes time to get to a well-paid job. For Hardcastle, switching to operating heavy equipment was a calculated financial risk. He and his wife saved up for a couple of months before he could finally quit his day job, and he took out a loan for his certification. Getting certified is crucial to landing a well-paying job. But that could take time, depending on the program you choose. For example, it can take about four months to become a truck driver, a year to become a welder and five years to become a qualified electrician. Gray said many skilled trades offer a level of flexibility to apprentices to learn at their own pace. But she said it’s crucial to find an employer who can sponsor you. “Eighty per cent of apprenticeship happens in the workplace.” College programs with co-ops can help with placements in most cases, Buesink said. But if there aren’t enough spots, she said this is where your previous desk job could help boost your resumé and show your eagerness to work. “If you have a strong resume, if you have a good background and a willingness (that shows): ‘Hey, I’m in school, this is what I want to do,’ — that makes you more attractive to the potential employer,” she said. While it can take a while to get trained, Gray said she often hears from people about high levels of job satisfaction alongside good pay. That’s true in Hardcastle’s case. He didn’t have to take a pay cut and now gets to do something that excites him. “Right now, it’s like a kid in a sandbox,” he said. “I’m playing with these big machines and I’m moving material. “Every day is different. It’s so much fun, like, I can’t even explain.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026. Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Seventh B.C. Conservative quits caucus, says she’s lost confidence in Findlay
stories.summary: The Indigenous MLA and former House leader cited the cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called for Monday in light of a "reasonable cause for concern."
stories.author: Chuck Chiang
paragraphs: B.C. Conservative MLA A’a:liya Warbus, one of the Opposition’s most prominent legislators, has joined the exodus from the party’s caucus, saying she has lost confidence in it under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
Warbus said in a statement on Monday morning she would sit as an Independent, becoming the seventh Conservative MLA to quit the caucus this month, including five last week.
The Indigenous MLA and former House leader cited the cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called for Monday in light of a “reasonable cause for concern” about last week’s “implosion.”
“The decision to postpone today’s caucus meeting for a month reflects the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions,” she said in her statement.
“It is one thing to ask for people’s trust, and quite another to blindfold someone and expect faith alone to substitute for transparency and accountability.”
The Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA also said she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Reann Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Findlay, who was narrowly elected party leader on May 30 but does not have a seat in the legislature, had said last week that suggestions a leaked audio recording showed she illegally offered jobs to MLAs, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection, were “preposterous.”
2:45 Byelection called for Abbotsford-Mission riding after Reann Gasper resignation

Gasper has taken a paid position as Findlay’s deputy chief of staff. RCMP said they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators, but “does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who May be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid.”

The party has been in a state of upheaval over the ideological direction and strategies of the party under Findlay since Peter Milobar quit on Aug. 14, saying they had a lack of “ideological alignment.”

stories.title: Canadian Nato intern facing espionage charges to remain in custody, Belgian prosecutor says
stories.summary: Prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that ‘a Canadian national of Chinese origin’ had been arrested on accusations of espionage
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says a Canadian facing espionage charges will remain in custody.

After a hearing today of the woman’s appeal of a July decision to keep her in detention, Belgium’s Chamber of Indictments decided to extend her pretrial custody by one month.

The prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that “a Canadian national of Chinese origin” had been arrested on accusations of espionage and participation in a criminal organization.

The suspect, who has not been named by the prosecutor’s office, worked as an intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe in Mons, Belgium.

The office said she came to the attention of the organization’s security services, who reported the matter to Belgium’s military intelligence agency.

A federal source not authorized to speak publicly about the issue said officials in Canada were proceeding on the basis the suspect is Biwei Zhang – also known as Claire Zhang – who was previously employed by Canadian government agencies.

stories.title: Ontario was warned of ‘suspicious’ Osap activity at a few career colleges: documents
stories.summary: Career Colleges Ontario also asked the government to refer certain related concerns to police, though the details of those concerns are not clear.
stories.author: Allison Jones
paragraphs: The association representing career colleges in Ontario began warning the government about possible “suspicious” student financial aid activity at a few campuses three years ago, documents show.

Career Colleges Ontario also asked the government to refer certain related concerns to police, though the details of those concerns and whether they apply to any particular institutions are not clear.

Two letters from Career Colleges Ontario to the Ministry of Colleges and Universities were filed as part of a court challenge to a government decision to block students at five career college campuses from accessing Osap loans for this school year.

Correspondence from Career Colleges Ontario this February says it started raising concerns about “indicators consistent with suspicious activity” in Osap applications in January 2023 and held four meetings with the ministry about it through that year.

The following year at another meeting between the organization and the ministry, Career Colleges Ontario “requested that related concerns be referred to law enforcement,” the letter says, though the subject of those concerns is redacted in the court record.

“We were advised that the ministry did make contact with police, and that police indicated they would need to conduct their own investigation in order to proceed,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.
It is not clear what happened with police beyond that. Neither Career Colleges Ontario nor the ministry would provide further details to The Canadian Press.

It is also not clear why the letter was redacted when filed in court. As a result of the redaction, the particular concern or concerns that were referred to police, including whether they applied to any particular institution, are unknown.

Career Colleges Ontario, which processes Osap applications for career colleges, told the ministry in a January 2025 letter that it had analyzed data from 2022 to 2024 and found that 10 schools had anomalous increases of an average 855 per cent over the two years.
One school went from 107 applications in 2022 to 2,992 in 2024, an increase of nearly 2,700 per cent, while most schools had flat numbers year over year, Bartz wrote.
“These data points, paired with reports from Financial Aid Officers, suggest a pattern inconsistent with typical enrolment trends,” she wrote.

“Some applicants have shared information that raises red flags regarding eligibility misrepresentation and misuse of Osap funds. These were promptly reported to (the ministry’s Osap inspection and compliance unit).”

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that the total of provincial grants sent to students at just seven career colleges in 2024-25 was about $385 million.

While tuition at career colleges tends to be higher than at publicly funded colleges, that total equals the amount of provincial grants given to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges that year — and more than all Ontario university students.
That is in addition to $137 million in federal grants to those seven schools in 2024-25.

About 18 months after Career Colleges Ontario sent the ministry its data, the government made five schools ineligible for Osap, citing concerns around “compromised participation” in asynchronous online programs, in which students complete coursework on their own schedule.

Critics say it is a failure of oversight that the provincial government allowed a small number of career colleges to increase Ontario Student Assistance Program usage by hundreds of per cent in a short time.
They also accuse the government of using that growth to then declare the entire financial aid program “unsustainable” and reduce grant access for all post-secondary students.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced sweeping changes earlier this year to Osap, including barring career college students from accessing grants and sharply reducing the amount of grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive.
Quinn’s office said oversight of the sector is robust, and that further action will be taken.
“We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system,” spokesperson Dayna Smockum wrote in a statement.

“When serious concerns are identified, we do not hesitate to cut off an institution from Osap entirely, as we have already done in some cases. … This fall, we will introduce additional legislative measures to curb out-of-control growth, strengthen accountability and ensure every public dollar is used responsibly and in the best interests of students.”
NDP Leader Marit Stiles said all post-secondary students who need financial assistance are now paying the price for the government’s not acting quickly enough.
“Unfortunately this really does all come down to the government punishing all students for the failures of this government,” she said.
Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said it looks as though the government has a double standard when it comes to oversight.

“They watch our universities and colleges so closely,” he said. “Now they’ve got this thing where you have 700 per cent growth (at one career college) … That’s incredible. If that happened at a college or university, the government would be all over it.”
Three Academy of Learning career college campuses, which operate as franchises, have launched a court challenge of Quinn’s decision to block their Osap eligibility for the coming year.
They argue not only that the minister did not have the authority to make the decision, but also that the schools complied with inspections and corrective action plans every step of the way.

Career Colleges Ontario had said in February that it would pause processing Osap applications for 14 campuses it had concerns with, but after lawyers for three Academy of Learning schools got involved, Career Colleges Ontario did not go through with the pause.

The Academy of Learning says in a statement that it has received no further communication from Career Colleges Ontario since then and is not aware that it has any outstanding concerns about Academy operations.
“We are committed to the highest ethical standards in the administration of Osap,” the Academy wrote in the statement.
“As the court materials show, we have implemented dozens of new controls over the past year in response to the Ministry’s inspection reports, and the Ministry has acknowledged those steps.”

The school also says in its statement that it is worth noting that Career Colleges Ontario’s board is made up of owners and managers of other private career colleges, “many of them our direct competitors.”
The Academy of Learning also said in a previous statement that as Ontario’s population grew, their schools’ enrolment grew with it.
Court documents show the ministry’s concerns with the five schools it blocked from Osap eligibility were around “compromised participation” in asynchronous learning programs.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the province temporarily extended Osap eligibility to students in online and/or asynchronous programs, then later made it permanent.

stories.content:
The association representing career colleges in Ontario began warning the government about possible “suspicious” student financial aid activity at a few campuses three years ago, documents show.

Career Colleges Ontario also asked the government to refer certain related concerns to police, though the details of those concerns and whether they apply to any particular institutions are not clear.

Two letters from Career Colleges Ontario to the Ministry of Colleges and Universities were filed as part of a court challenge to a government decision to block students at five career college campuses from accessing Osap loans for this school year.

Correspondence from Career Colleges Ontario this February says it started raising concerns about “indicators consistent with suspicious activity” in Osap applications in January 2023 and held four meetings with the ministry about it through that year.

The following year at another meeting between the organization and the ministry, Career Colleges Ontario “requested that related concerns be referred to law enforcement,” the letter says, though the subject of those concerns is redacted in the court record.

“We were advised that the ministry did make contact with police, and that police indicated they would need to conduct their own investigation in order to proceed,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.

It is not clear what happened with police beyond that. Neither Career Colleges Ontario nor the ministry would provide further details to The Canadian Press.

It is also not clear why the letter was redacted when filed in court. As a result of the redaction, the particular concern or concerns that were referred to police, including whether they applied to any particular institution, are unknown.

Career Colleges Ontario, which processes Osap applications for career colleges, told the ministry in a January 2025 letter that it had analyzed data from 2022 to 2024 and found that 10 schools had anomalous increases of an average 855 per cent over the two years.

One school went from 107 applications in 2022 to 2,992 in 2024, an increase of nearly 2,700 per cent, while most schools had flat numbers year over year, Bartz wrote.

“These data points, paired with reports from Financial Aid Officers, suggest a pattern inconsistent with typical enrolment trends,” she wrote.

“Some applicants have shared information that raises red flags regarding eligibility misrepresentation and misuse of Osap funds. These were promptly reported to (the ministry’s Osap inspection and compliance unit).”

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that the total of provincial grants sent to students at just seven career colleges in 2024-25 was about $385 million.

While tuition at career colleges tends to be higher than at publicly funded colleges, that total equals the amount of provincial grants given to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges that year — and more than all Ontario university students.

That is in addition to $137 million in federal grants to those seven schools in 2024-25.

About 18 months after Career Colleges Ontario sent the ministry its data, the government made five schools ineligible for Osap, citing concerns around “compromised participation” in asynchronous online programs, in which students complete coursework on their own schedule.

Critics say it is a failure of oversight that the provincial government allowed a small number of career colleges to increase Ontario Student Assistance Program usage by hundreds of per cent in a short time.

They also accuse the government of using that growth to then declare the entire financial aid program “unsustainable” and reduce grant access for all post-secondary students.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced sweeping changes earlier this year to Osap, including barring career college students from accessing grants and sharply reducing the amount of grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive.

Quinn’s office said oversight of the sector is robust, and that further action will be taken.

“We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system,” spokesperson Dayna Smockum wrote in a statement.

“When serious concerns are identified, we do not hesitate to cut off an institution from Osap entirely, as we have already done in some cases. … This fall, we will introduce additional legislative measures to curb out-of-control growth, strengthen accountability and ensure every public dollar is used responsibly and in the best interests of students.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said all post-secondary students who need financial assistance are now paying the price for the government’s not acting quickly enough.

“Unfortunately this really does all come down to the government punishing all students for the failures of this government,” she said.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said it looks as though the government has a double standard when it comes to oversight.

“They watch our universities and colleges so closely,” he said. “Now they’ve got this thing where you have 700 per cent growth (at one career college) … That’s incredible. If that happened at a college or university, the government would be all over it.”

Three Academy of Learning career college campuses, which operate as franchises, have launched a court challenge of Quinn’s decision to block their Osap eligibility for the coming year.

They argue not only that the minister did not have the authority to make the decision, but also that the schools complied with inspections and corrective action plans every step of the way.

Career Colleges Ontario had said in February that it would pause processing Osap applications for 14 campuses it had concerns with, but after lawyers for three Academy of Learning schools got involved, Career Colleges Ontario did not go through with the pause.

The Academy of Learning says in a statement that it has received no further communication from Career Colleges Ontario since then and is not aware that it has any outstanding concerns about Academy operations.

“We are committed to the highest ethical standards in the administration of Osap,” the Academy wrote in the statement.

“As the court materials show, we have implemented dozens of new controls over the past year in response to the Ministry’s inspection reports, and the Ministry has acknowledged those steps.”

The school also says in its statement that it is worth noting that Career Colleges Ontario’s board is made up of owners and managers of other private career colleges, “many of them our direct competitors.”

The Academy of Learning also said in a previous statement that as Ontario’s population grew, their schools’ enrolment grew with it.

Court documents show the ministry’s concerns with the five schools it blocked from Osap eligibility were around “compromised participation” in asynchronous learning programs.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the province temporarily extended Osap eligibility to students in online and/or asynchronous programs, then later made it permanent.

stories.title: Tiff fans grapple with ticket price hikes
stories.summary: The hike they noticed this year marks the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama The Woman King for about $50 each.

This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106.

“That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on Tiff galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices.

While Tiff fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark.

Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner Fjord , justice system thriller Prima Facie and the Ryan Gosling-produced Love of Your Life going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98.

Tiff did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing.

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during Tiff’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many Tiff fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.

“I love Tiff. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.

While Tiff typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, Tiff advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.

Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said Tiff is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.

“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.

But there’s more than demand at play.

Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. Tiff is likely no exception.

“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.

On top of inflation, Tiff is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.

In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, Tiff lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.

The federal government offered $23-million to help Tiff launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information Tiff published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1-million and more than $41.9-million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.

Its revenue was $39.6-million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2-million in expenses, its annual reports show.

Tiff’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in Tiff’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”

Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of Tiff’s stature – this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows – but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.

Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.

But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”

Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film – German historical drama “Silent Friend” – and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a Tiff diehard.

“I see it as the tail end,” she said.

This year, she hopes to see at least one movie – a Midnight Madness film – with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”

That’s a problem, said Keil, because Tiff has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping Tiff lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.

“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.

“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”

stories.title: Cami plant to remain open, hope for potential armoured vehicle production
stories.summary: Employees at the Cami Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ont. were surprised to learn of a few details in their new three-year agreement with General Motors.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Employees at the Cami Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ont. were surprised to learn of a few details in their new three-year agreement with General Motors. At the ratification vote Saturday in Woodstock, Ont. members of Unifor Local 88 learned of the company’s intent to keep the Cami plant open during the duration of the deal and also the potential for a new vehicle.

“It’s a three-year deal with General Motors and I think it’s an important agreement,” said Mark Gee, the plant chairperson. There was also wage increases, extended benefits for those whose were about to expire and productivity and quality bonuses for laid-off employees.

“In my opinion, it is a best case scenario,” said employee Peggy Falkingham. After Canadian auto assembly plants were hit with 25 per cent tariffs last year, auto workers were laid off. Months later, General Motors ended production of the Brightdrop vehicle in Ingersoll.

It’s been a difficult stretch since then for employees to make ends meet. “I come from a family that is dual income from General Motors,” said Falkingham. “My husband also works at Cami as well, so it is difficult. It’s a whole new family structure that we have to work around.

And still the uncertainty of our future is definitely there.” Gee says it’s been tough for members going all the way back to the beginning of the pandemic. As they attended the meeting Saturday, Unifor members were worried they were about to hear about a plant closure.

Instead, they learned of a potential future. “I’m surprised about the future opportunity for a new vehicle,” said Todd Sleeper, a Cami employee. “If there’s a military contract, then Cami gets first crack at building that that military vehicle.

That sounds positive.” In the letter from General Motors to the union, it states that if the Government of Canada approves a Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) contact, the company will discuss with Unifor the potential allocation of GM Defence work to Cami Assembly.

If the CAF contract is awarded, Cami will be first consideration. “It’s the carrot dangling in front of us,” said Falkingham. “We’ll take it, because right now that’s what we have to take. If that is a possibility in the future, I’m sure everyone would jump on it to be able to get back in the plant.” While employees don’t have all the answers, the do know they have a shot at returning to work and finishing out their pension.

“There is hope for a future,” added Falkingham. “They’re not closing the doors. That is that is a big thing right there.” Statement from GM Canada Today marks an important moment for GM Canada. With the ratification of new three-year collective agreements with Unifor, we have reached an outcome that supports our employees, strengthens our manufacturing operations and provides a solid foundation for GM’s future in Canada.

Reaching an agreement requires collaboration and a shared focus on the future. Recognizing the Contributions of Our People The new agreements include meaningful improvements to wages, benefits and job security, and recognize the valuable contributions of our represented employees while helping sustain good-paying jobs that have long been a cornerstone of Canada’s automotive industry.

Our represented employees play a critical role in GM Canada’s success. Their skill, dedication and commitment to quality help ensure the vehicles we build continue to earn the trust of customers across North America. Building on Our Commitment to North American Manufacturing Today, we are also announcing significant new and reaffirmed investments that further strengthen GM’s manufacturing footprint in Canada.

Together, planned investments in Oshawa and St. Catharines total approximately C$1.4 billion over the next three years, reinforcing the important role Canadian operations will continue to play in GM’s North American manufacturing network.

At Oshawa Assembly, an additional C$144 million investment will bring next-generation GMC Sierra Heavy-Duty production to the plant, building on the previously announced C$343 million investment in next-generation truck production and manufacturing enhancements.

Together, these investments bring total planned investment in Oshawa to nearly C$500 million. This is an important addition for Oshawa, for GM Canada and for our customers. It means Oshawa will now build both of GM’s next-generation heavy-duty trucks, the GMC Sierra HD and the Chevrolet Silverado HD, strengthening the plant’s role in one of the company’s most important vehicle segments while building more of the trucks Canadians rely on every day.

At St. Catharines Propulsion, a new C$215 million investment establishes the plant as the sole source for an important next-generation transmission. Combined with the previously announced C$691 million for sixth-generation V8 engine production, total investment in St.

GM’s Presence Across Canada While today’s announcement includes important investments in manufacturing, GM Canada’s presence is built on a broad ecosystem that spans vehicle engineering, software development, sales and customer care, parts distribution, and corporate operations.

That includes our Canadian Technical Centre, where more than 1,000 engineers, developers and technical experts are helping advance the next generation of vehicle technology, software and testing. As Canada’s vehicle sales leader, our success is powered by approximately 450 Chevrolet, Buick, GMC and Cadillac dealerships employing over 20,000 Canadians and serving customers in communities across the country.

Together, our people, dealers and operations contribute to local economies, support communities and advance innovation. Their contributions help strengthen GM’s North American business and underscore the important role Canada continues to play in our shared success.

Looking Ahead The strength of GM Canada has always been our people. Their expertise, dedication and commitment will continue to shape our future and the role we play in Canada’s automotive industry. I am optimistic about the future and confident in what we can achieve together.

Jack Uppal President and Managing Director GM Canada

stories.title: ‘We’re not at war with Canada,’ U.S. treasury secretary says
stories.summary: Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs, a new poll suggests.
stories.author: Uday Rana
paragraphs: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that he would meet with his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, ON the sidelines of a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors, adding that the U.S. was not in a war with Canada .
“I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match. I mean, we’re not at war with Canada,” Bessent told Cnbc in an interview.
He added that Carney was “not doing what’s best for Canada.”
In his interview, Bessent also called out Canada’s retaliatory tariffs.
“I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” he said.
1:46 Canadians weigh in on Carney government’s response to U.S. tariffs

Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs, a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

The poll found that 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of older boomers supported both of those positions.
— with files from Reuters and Global’s Sean Boynton

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that he would meet with his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, ON the sidelines of a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors, adding that the U.S. was not in a war with Canada .

“I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match. I mean, we’re not at war with Canada,” Bessent told Cnbc in an interview.

He added that Carney was “not doing what’s best for Canada.”

In his interview, Bessent also called out Canada’s retaliatory tariffs.

“I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” he said.

1:46 Canadians weigh in on Carney government’s response to U.S. tariffs

Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs, a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

The poll found that 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of older boomers supported both of those positions.

— with files from Reuters and Global’s Sean Boynton

stories.title: London driver identified as victim in head-on crash with transport truck
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to Dundas Street near Fairview Road at about 12:56 p.m. on Aug. 26 after reports of a serious collision involving the two vehicles.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London resident has been identified as the victim of a head-on collision involving an SUV and a transport truck in Thames Centre, according to police. Emergency crews were called to Dundas Street near Fairview Road at about 12:56 p.m. on Aug.

26 after reports of a serious collision involving the two vehicles. The driver of the transport truck was taken to hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The driver of the SUV, a 40-year-old from London, was transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, police said.

On the day of the crash, Dundas Street was closed for several hours between Fairview Road and Shaw Road while investigators examined the scene. The cause of the collision remains under investigation. There is no word on how the crash happened or if any charges will be laid.

stories.title: France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy
stories.summary: France will from Tuesday impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost 20 euros per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content: France will from Tuesday impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost 20 euros per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein. The levy follows legislation passed by the French parliament in June to regulate so-called “ultra-fast fashion” companies, known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices. It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years. “The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Friday as details of the measure were published. Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price. The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards. In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to two euros for T-shirts, nine euros for jeans and 12 euros for a jacket. The levy could reach up to 19.50 euros (US$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price. A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies’ own declarations, is under development, Lefevre’s office said. Shein -- which on Monday was valued at US$26.3 billion in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering -- declined to comment when contacted by AFP. Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect. In July, Lefevre’s office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies. French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion. The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre’s office said those concerns had been “dispelled” and the measure was not expected to be blocked. China meanwhile warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as “discriminatory” and in violation of trade principles. Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 to 40 per cent since a separate three-euro EU levy on such shipments came into force on July 1, according to the French government.

stories.title: B.C. Conservative MLA Warbus leaves caucus
stories.summary: Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA cites her loss of confidence in the party under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay
stories.content:
B.C. Conservative MLA A’a:liya Warbus has announced she is leaving the party’s legislative caucus, joining an exodus under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Warbus says in a statement she will sit as an Independent, citing her loss of confidence in the party under Findlay.

She is the seventh Conservative MLA to quit the party this month, including five last week.

Warbus, who was one of the most prominent figures in the party as an Indigenous MLA and former House leader, also cites the cancellation of a caucus meeting she says had been called for Monday in light of the “implosion” of events last week.

She says the cancellation reflects a “lack of value” being placed in caucus members’ opinions.

The Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA also says she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Reann Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: Toronto — Canada’s main stock index was down more than 350 points in late-morning trading, weighed down by losses in the industrial, technology and base metal sectors, while U.S. stock markets also fell. The S&P/TSX composite index was down 373.20 points at 36,180.72. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 347.87 points at 53,212.12. The S&P 500 index was down 34.23 points at 7,677.53, while the Nasdaq composite was down 89.63 points at 26,312.79. The Canadian dollar traded for 72.11 cents US compared with 72.00 cents US on Friday. The October crude oil contract was up US$1.76 at US$85.16 per barrel. The December gold contract was down US$45.30 at US$4,484.60 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: On-duty OPP officer driving drunk 3x legal limit pleads guilty, fined $3,000
stories.summary: A veteran provincial police officer charged with with driving drunk on the job pleads guilty.
stories.author: Mike Arsalides
stories.content: A veteran provincial police officer charged with driving drunk on the job earlier this year in Midland, Ont., has taken a plea deal. Suspended with pay since January, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) officer Christopher Prout has pleaded guilty to driving with more than three times the legal limit of alcohol in his system while on duty in a police cruiser with a gun on his hip. The court heard, as part of an Agreed Statement of Facts read by the Crown, Prout had been drinking at home and drove to work in his police cruiser for a performance review at the Southern Georgian Bay OPP detachment, when officers in the meeting room smelled alcohol on him. Prout failed a breath test and provided two samples that produced readings of nearly 260 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. The defence noted Prout did not show signs of impairment, saying he was shocked by the readings, and that he felt “essentially sober” that day. His lawyer told the court Prout, 40, who has been a police officer in Midland for 17 years, was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (Ptsd) and substance-use disorder. According to the defence, his Ptsd was the result of years of dedicated service while experiencing trauma as a police officer. The defence noted Prout hit “rock bottom” while dealing with mental health struggles and a family history of alcoholism as issues in his personal life affected his performance at work. The defence said Prout had not sought help for his issues before being charged Jan. 15 and has since taken accountability through counselling and two months at the Homewood medically supervised addiction treatment centre as he continues to receive outpatient care and counselling while maintaining his sobriety. Prout addressed the court, saying he was embarrassed and that he hurt his platoon and hates and regrets what he did. He vowed “it will never happen again.” “Alcohol is not an issue anymore,” Prout told the court, adding he is working hard to move forward. Following a joint submission by the defence and a Crown attorney brought in from Newmarket to handle the case, the judge handed Prout a $3,000 fine and two-year driving ban. Justice Edward Prutschi told Prout it was sheer dumb luck and divine intervention that his actions didn’t result in a crash that killed himself or others out on the road. The OPP did not provide a response to Prout’s guilty plea. Along with being placed on probation for two years, Prout could now face further discipline under the Police Services Act.
