Dr. Sheena Belisle, Paediatric Emergency Medicine Physician at LHSC.

E-scooters have become a common sight zooming around neighbourhoods and city roads. For many riders, they offer a fun and convenient way to get around, but over the course of the spring and summer months, emergency physicians at Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) have noted an alarming increase in the number of patients seeking care for injuries related to unsafe riding.

Between April and June of 2025, Children's Hospital treated approximately 22 injuries related to incidents involving e-scooters. During the same time period in 2026, that number has increased to 58, a 164 per cent increase. Physicians believe that trend has continued through the summer months.

Dr. Sheena Belisle, Paediatric Emergency Medicine Physician and Assistant Professor for the Department of Paediatrics at Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry at Western University, says she and her colleagues are growing more concerned as the number and severity of injuries continues to climb, with many of them preventable.

"We've definitely seen an increase in the number of children and teens coming to the emergency department with e-scooter-related injuries," says Belisle. "While some injuries are relatively minor, we're also seeing patients with broken bones, significant cuts, facial injuries and concussions. What's particularly concerning is that many of these injuries involve children who are younger than the legal riding age. When we see a child seriously injured on an e-scooter, it often means the crash should never have had the opportunity to happen in the first place.”

Some patients are lucky with their tumbles only leading to cuts and bruises that heal relatively quickly. However, other injuries are so severe that they require surgery and lead to recoveries that stretch for weeks or even months, putting a significant damper on summer fun.

"The injuries that concern me the most are head injuries. My main concern is the potential for intercranial bleeds which can be life threatening or life altering," Belisle explains. "Even concussions can have long term consequences as they are more at risk for future concussions and it can take them longer to return to regular activities and routines."

Dr. Belisle hopes that by sharing the impact these injuries can have on children and families, more people will understand the importance of following safety rules and taking steps to prevent serious injuries.

"Many of the injuries we see share common factors. Riders May not be wearing helmets, there May have been more than one person on the scooter, or they are riding distracted."

Belisle also comments that families are often surprised that some of the most serious injuries occur during short, routine rides close to home.

"The length of the ride isn't what determines the risk. What matters is whether a child has the physical coordination, judgement and awareness needed to safely operate the scooter and respond to what's happening around them," says Belisle also noting the importance of following provincial regulations which prohibit children under the age of 16 from riding the devices. To help address the growing number of injuries, LHSC has partnered with community organizations including London Police Service , the City of London , the Middlesex-London Health Unit and Western University to raise awareness about e-scooter safety and local bylaws.

Throughout the summer, medical students from Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry engaged with community members to better understand what residents know about e-scooter safety and regulations. Their findings helped inform the safety messages being shared by Belisle and her colleagues.

Belisle encourages families to have ongoing conversations about road safety and responsible e-scooter use, particularly around the importance of wearing a helmet and following local regulations. More importantly, she wants families to know that if an injury does occur, they should never hesitate to seek medical care.

"We would always rather someone come in to get checked if they're worried about an injury," says Belisle.

For Belisle, the message is ultimately a simple one. "E-scooters are not toys. Our goal isn't to take the fun away from riding them, but to help children and families stay safe. If sharing what we're seeing in the emergency department helps prevent even one serious injury, then these conversations are worth having."

stories.title: Federal government assures farmers of support amid trade war concerns
stories.summary: Federal government representatives are conducting outreach across the country, hosting events designed to reassure Canadians about the impacts of the ongoing trade war.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Federal government representatives are conducting outreach across the country, hosting events designed to reassure Canadians about the impacts of the ongoing trade war. A recent stop brought MP Wayne Long to Forbesvue Farm in St.

Clair Township, east of Sarnia, to emphasize the government’s commitment to financial support for farmers. The Forbes family, who have operated their dairy farm for three generations, manage approximately 350 head of cattle, including 200 milking cows.

While they have witnessed numerous U.S. administrations target the Canadian supply management system, Kevin Forbes stated their focus remains firmly on the domestic market. “We’re not really looking to export. We’re not trying to get into that game,” Forbes said.

“Our primary focus is strictly Canadian consumers and a fair and equitable quality product for them.” During the visit, Long, the Secretary of State responsible for the Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions, stressed the federal government’s dedication to providing funding to help farmers navigate economic challenges.

“Canada is taking action for defense workers, businesses and communities,” Long stated. Earlier this week, the federal government announced an additional $7.5 billion in funding for tariff impact relief. This package aims to help farmers offset increased costs, particularly on equipment purchases.

Long highlighted the government’s commitment to rapid deployment of these resources. “There’s a sense of urgency here. We’re going to make sure the regional development agencies, obviously, the Business Development Bank of Canada, are funded.

So these programs will go out literally within weeks.” The Secretary of State explained that working with regional development agencies (RDA) like FedDev Ontario and the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) is key to the effective distribution of funds.

“The RDAs are going to actually manage the funding, especially through the rapid response initiative,” he noted. “So applications are actually actively going in there now. They’re being evaluated. We’re going to turn those around really, really quickly.” Forbes expressed his continued dedication to running the farm and supporting local businesses, adding a message of confidence in the government’s broader strategy.

“I think you have to filter out the noise a certain amount and have faith in our government that they’re going to continue to do what’s right for Canadians,” he said. “And not just the dairy farms, but negotiating trade deals that are mutually beneficial for all Canadians, Canadian families, consumers and businesses.”

stories.title: Resale housing market, already sluggish, could take hit from Trump tariffs
stories.summary: "If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while . . . that can certainly slow things down."
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Ontario’s sluggish resale housing market could face some headwinds from renewed trade tensions between Canada and the U.S., but the impact is unlikely to completely derail its ongoing recovery – at least in the short term, industry watchers say.

Uncertainty and low consumer confidence resulting from the trade war, which entered a new chapter after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, have been some of the driving factors behind slower-than-expected home sales in the province in 2026.

Last month, for example, 16,276 homes were sold in Ontario, a 1.3 per cent decline from July 2025, while year-to-date sales also remain below 2025 levels, according to the latest figures from the Canadian Real Estate Association (Crea).

However, ON a month-to-month basis, July also marked the fourth straight month of gains in home resale activity at the national level, with upticks also seen in recent months in provincial markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London and Ottawa.

“This latest round of the trade war with the U.S. puts at risk the confidence gains we’ve seen in recent months,” said Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada.

“It certainly raises the risk of being derailed once again. But still, our base case is that the recovery will remain on track. It’s going to be gradual. It’s going to be uneven, and it’s probably going to be bumpy but, overall, it’s still likely to be sustained going forward.”

After talks collapsed last Friday, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian products on Aug. 22, with Ottawa announcing on Tuesday a dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff response, slated to come into effect starting Sept. 8.

Hogue, however, said that while the latest tariffs will hit certain sectors and businesses hard, from a larger perspective, “this is unlikely, in our view, to push Canada’s economy into a recession.”

He said that despite the uncertainty of recent months, the Canadian economy has shown signs of resiliency. Canada’s jobless rate, for example, went down to 6.4 per cent in July, its lowest level over the past year. Interest rates have also remained steady after peaking in 2024.

And while sales have been far from spectacular, Hogue also said there’s a lot of pent-up demand in the market from people who would’ve otherwise already purchased a home.

“So, we’re not quite at the point of saying the housing market is about to fall off again,” he said. “We think there’s a bit of momentum there.”

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Place Centre economic think-tank at the University of Ottawa, said the impact on the housing market will depend on how long the U.S. tariffs remain in place.

“If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while, and we start seeing job layoffs, particularly in the manufacturing sector, that can certainly slow things down,” he said. “But I think, overall, we’ve just had this uncertainty for so long that I think we’ve grown kind of numb to it.”

“The housing market, over the last five to 10 years, has had to adjust to so many big changes, whether it be population growth or COVID-related migration, big swings in interest rates, and I think we’re dealing with the effect of that right now, where a lot of the market is just locked up.”

Kevin Barry, owner and broker at Thrive Realty Group in London, said it’s still too early to gauge whether the latest trade-war developments are having an impact on buyers, given August is traditionally a slow month for sales.

“Whenever anything big like this shifts, changes, or moves, there’s a moment of pause in the market, which I think we are seeing right now,” he said.

“But people are also focused on going back to school, getting back into routine, getting the kids ready for the fall, so we normally see a bit of a lull in the market right now, so it’s tough to measure it against the reality of what’s happening south of the border.”

Barry, however, acknowledged worries about the economy have been an issue for many buyers over the past several months, keeping some on the sidelines of the market.

“The big conversation is need versus want,” he said. “If you need to move, you’re still going to do it. If you want to move, you’re going to pause and maybe be a little bit more considerate, a little bit more deliberate with your decision-making process.”

Uncertainty and low consumer confidence resulting from the trade war, which entered a new chapter after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, have been some of the driving factors behind slower-than-expected home sales in the province in 2026.

Last month, for example, 16,276 homes were sold in Ontario, a 1.3 per cent decline from July 2025, while year-to-date sales also remain below 2025 levels, according to the latest figures from the Canadian Real Estate Association (Crea).

However, ON a month-to-month basis, July also marked the fourth straight month of gains in home resale activity at the national level, with upticks also seen in recent months in provincial markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London and Ottawa.
“This latest round of the trade war with the U.S. puts at risk the confidence gains we’ve seen in recent months,” said Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada.

“It certainly raises the risk of being derailed once again. But still, our base case is that the recovery will remain on track. It’s going to be gradual. It’s going to be uneven, and it’s probably going to be bumpy but, overall, it’s still likely to be sustained going forward.”

After talks collapsed last Friday, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian products on Aug. 22, with Ottawa announcing on Tuesday a dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff response, slated to come into effect starting Sept. 8.
Hogue, however, said that while the latest tariffs will hit certain sectors and businesses hard, from a larger perspective, “this is unlikely, in our view, to push Canada’s economy into a recession.”

He said that despite the uncertainty of recent months, the Canadian economy has shown signs of resiliency. Canada’s jobless rate, for example, went down to 6.4 per cent in July, its lowest level over the past year. Interest rates have also remained steady after peaking in 2024.
And while sales have been far from spectacular, Hogue also said there’s a lot of pent-up demand in the market from people who would’ve otherwise already purchased a home.
“So, we’re not quite at the point of saying the housing market is about to fall off again,” he said. “We think there’s a bit of momentum there.”
Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Place Centre economic think-tank at the University of Ottawa, said the impact on the housing market will depend on how long the U.S. tariffs remain in place.

“If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while, and we start seeing job layoffs, particularly in the manufacturing sector, that can certainly slow things down,” he said. “But I think, overall, we’ve just had this uncertainty for so long that I think we’ve grown kind of numb to it.”

“The housing market, over the last five to 10 years, has had to adjust to so many big changes, whether it be population growth or COVID-related migration, big swings in interest rates, and I think we’re dealing with the effect of that right now, where a lot of the market is just locked up.”

Kevin Barry, owner and broker at Thrive Realty Group in London, said it’s still too early to gauge whether the latest trade-war developments are having an impact on buyers, given August is traditionally a slow month for sales.
“Whenever anything big like this shifts, changes, or moves, there’s a moment of pause in the market, which I think we are seeing right now,” he said.

“But people are also focused on going back to school, getting back into routine, getting the kids ready for the fall, so we normally see a bit of a lull in the market right now, so it’s tough to measure it against the reality of what’s happening south of the border.”
Barry, however, acknowledged worries about the economy have been an issue for many buyers over the past several months, keeping some on the sidelines of the market.

“The big conversation is need versus want,” he said. “If you need to move, you’re still going to do it. If you want to move, you’re going to pause and maybe be a little bit more considerate, a little bit more deliberate with your decision-making process.”

stories.title: Multilingual volunteers help patients navigate St. Joseph’s Health Care London
stories.summary: St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital. Multilingual volunteers are now wearing buttons identifying the languages they speak, making it easier for patients to find someone who can communicate with them in their preferred language.

In the first two weeks of the initiative, volunteers have helped more than 25 people communicate in another language. There are currently 14 languages represented, including Arabic, Mandarin, French, and Hindi, with more expected to be added as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

Monica Naskret-Reyes, a volunteer who speaks Spanish, said seeing someone who speaks their language can provide relief for patients who are already dealing with the stress and uncertainty of being in hospital. “When people come to the hospital, the concern they have about their health, the uncertainty, what is going on and not speaking the language is a lot of pressure,” said Naskret-Reyes.

“But when they see someone speaking their own language it’s like, ‘oh my God’, what a relief. At least I can communicate a little bit with this person.” According to Statistics Canada, more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021.

About 22 per cent of Londoners identify as immigrants. Tracy Drenth, manager of Volunteer Services at St. Joseph’s, said the program reflects the diversity of the community. “Patient population is becoming a lot more diverse much like the community.

So, we have had several patients come into the hospital who have limited English proficiency. So, we want to provide the best customer service as possible as patients enter our buildings,” she said. The initiative also supports people who communicate using sign language.

Melissa Fowler, a sign language volunteer, said she has helped patients communicate where they need to go within the hospital. “I’ve had quite a few people come in that don’t know how to speak to somebody, so I’ve let them know that I know sign language and then able to finger spell to me where they need to go and then can take them there,” said Fowler.

For languages that aren’t represented by an on-site volunteer, trained volunteers can use an iPad equipped with an interpretation service that provides access to an additional 200 languages. The live interpretation service is intended for general information, such as finding a department, getting directions or locating the cafeteria.

It is not intended for clinical information. St. Joseph’s says more languages could be represented at hospital entrances as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

stories.title: International Overdose Day marks 25 years in Oxford County
stories.summary: International Overdose Awareness Day was recognized this week in Oxford County, with a series of events to mark 25 years of remembering those lost to addictions.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
International Overdose Awareness Day was recognized this week in Oxford County, with a series of events to mark 25 years of remembering those lost to addictions. In Tillsonburg, resident Gary Graham was on hand to check out an awareness campaign by the Oxford Mental Health and Addictions Action Coalition (Omhaac) Thursday.

He pulled no punches when describing the situation in the downtown. “Every day there’s ambulances out here looking after overdosed people,” Graham said. He said the addiction crisis is also contributing to homelessness in the community.

“They’re pretty much all in the underground, or they’re spread all over the place. The town should be doing something about it,” he remarked. Members of Omhaac had a display set up in front of the Tillsonburg mall in the heart of downtown.

They were spreading awareness of the ongoing crisis, handing out naloxone kits, and even training people how to use them to save lives. Omhaac member Patti Monaghan says street drugs appear to be getting stronger. “We are noticing that one naloxone kit isn’t enough.

We need to do multiple, sometimes up to like five or six kits of administering naloxone, because the substances that are out there are a lot more serious than prior years,” she explained. According to Ohmaac, the rate of opioid-related incidents resulting in ER visits in Oxford County peaked in 2021 during the pandemic.

While it declined through 2024 (44.2 per 100,000 population), it remained more than five times higher than 10 years earlier in 2014 (7.2 per 100,000 population). Opioid-related deaths also peaked in 2021, before declining by 2024 (15.5 per 100,000 population).

But the rate was still more than one and a half times higher than in 2018, pre-pandemic (9.3 per 100,000 population). Joanne Beresford, Administrator at the Tillsonburg BIA, says the ongoing opioid crisis shows little signs of waning, and is being felt most in the downtown.

“This is where the hub is. Unfortunately, things happen at night-time and sometimes during the day as well. It’s a sad state apparently when they come in sometimes in the morning and everything’s turned upside down and graffitied on and whatever,” she said.

Ohmaac hosted awareness events this week in Woodstock as well. Patti Monaghan asked that people have compassion. “Nobody wants to live this life. Nobody wants to be stuck in these cycles of addiction,” she said.

stories.title: Missing swimmer found dead at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Beachgoers found the missing 28-year-old's body on Thursday, police said
Provincial Police in Lambton County say they have recovered the body of a missing swimmer who was last seen at a Pinery Provincial Park beach on Wednesday afternoon.

Police say visitors to the beach located the body of the individual on Thursday. They did not share any details of the person's identity, other than specifying the deceased as a 28-year-old from Scarborough.
OPP say the search began when police were called at 1 p.m. on Aug. 26, about the missing swimmer who was last seen at a beach in the park.

Two OPP boats, as well as the underwater search and recovery unit, and OPP aviation services, were helping with the search. Anishnabek Police Service, which operates a detachment at Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, also helped.
It's unclear why it took almost 24 hours for OPP to notify the public about the missing swimmer.

stories.title: ‘Dream come true’: New Muslim community centre opening in London
stories.summary: Fourteen years in the making, Noor Gardens brings worship, education and recreation under one roof in the city’s southwest.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
A 14-year effort to build a new home for London’s Muslim community will culminate Friday with the opening of Noor Gardens in the city’s southwest.

The mosque and community centre at 457 Southdale Rd. W. combines worship, education and recreation under one roof. It features a prayer hall, gymnasium, youth lounge and classrooms for educational and social programs.

“This is truly a dream come true,” said Dr. Nabil Sultan, chair of the Noor Gardens centre committee and a physician with London Health Sciences Centre.

The Muslim Association of Canada bought the 13-acre property near Wonderland and Southdale roads in 2012, Sultan said. The organization placed the total project cost at $14.3 million in a fundraising update last year, up from the $12-million estimate reported when plans were presented to the city in 2017.

Sultan said the project was funded by London’s Muslim community throughout the years from donations ranging from $5 and $10 to much larger amounts.

“There’s probably thousands of individual donations that have been made to this project by the community here in London,” he said.

The centre arrives as existing mosques face growing pressure for space, particularly during Friday prayers and Ramadan. About 35,000 Londoners identified as Muslim in the 2021 census , representing 8.4 per cent of the city’s population.

London’s Muslim roots stretch back generations. Families began raising money for a mosque in the 1950s and bought a house at 151 Oxford St. W. in 1956. After fire destroyed that building in 1961, the current London Muslim Mosque opened in 1964. It is recognized as Ontario’s first mosque and Canada’s second.

Sultan, who has lived in London since 1989, recalled growing up with cramped worship spaces and few of the recreational and educational services Noor Gardens will offer.

Its name means “gardens of light” in Arabic, a theme carried through the large windows, lighting and traditional Islamic architectural details inside the building. The property was once home to Wally World, a water park remembered by many longtime Londoners.

“As the community grew, the needs and the aspirations and what we wanted to achieve started to grow with the numbers of people,” said Dr. Munir El-Kassem, Imam of the Islamic Centre of Southwest Ontario.

El-Kassem, marking his 50th year in London, said Noor Gardens marks the community’s evolution from modest beginnings to a new generation of Muslims in London.

He believes the centre will be a place of reflection, peace and dialogue for people of all backgrounds.

A ribbon-cutting ceremony for the public is scheduled for Friday at 11 a.m., followed by tours of the facility.

Organizers also envision Noor Gardens hosting open houses, interfaith events and conversations intended to connect Muslim and non-Muslim Londoners.

“Our doors are wide open for any visitors to come,” Sultan said.

stories.title: Kincardine wants more municipal input on potential data centres
stories.summary: The Municipality of Kincardine believes municipalities should have to give formal support to a data centre before it can be built in their community.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The Municipality of Kincardine believes municipalities should have to give formal support to a data centre before it can be built in their community. That’s just one of several recommendations Kincardine is making to the Ontario government as they put together Ontario’s plan on how to deal with prospective projects.

The large projects have been divisive across the country and world as they use large amounts of electricity and water. Kincardine says closed loop water systems and clear standards for electricity usage should be laid out before any data centre project can proceed.

Council directed town staff to submit their recommendations to the province advocating that stronger municipal involvement, cost recovery, environmental protections, community benefits, transparency, and emergency planning are needed for responsible investment, while ensuring host communities share in the long-term benefits of potential growth.

The public has until Sept. 12 to share their comments with the provincial government about data centre development.

stories.title: Bruce County warns of “fraudulent emails” that appear to come from them
stories.summary: Bruce County officials are warning residents of fraudulent emails that appear to originate from Bruce County email accounts.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Bruce County officials warn residents of fraudulent emails that appear to originate from Bruce County email accounts. They say they are actively investigating where the emails originated from, and asking residents to share any suspicious emails that look like they’re from Bruce County with them.

In one instance, a fraudulent e-mail was seeking an e-transfer payment. Bruce County say they do not use e-transfers as payments. Officials say some of the fraudulent e-mails contained invoices, County logos and branding to appear legitimate.

If you suspect you’ve received a fraudulent email from Bruce County, officials ask you to send it to them at https://www.brucecounty.on.CA/whats-news/contact

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as Ontario company shifts away from U.S. suppliers
stories.summary: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's London Morning on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"We knew there will be opportunities for customers who are currently buying in the U.S. to look for local manufacturing and we approached Chapman's to discuss if they would be interested to buy locally," said president Steeve Tremblay.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.
The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”
Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream ditching U.S. ingredients as trade war escalates
stories.summary: The Southwestern Ontario company is replacing U.S. ingredients and vowing no price hikes until March 2028.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A Southwestern Ontario ice-cream maker whose products are sold across Canada is ditching U.S. ingredients as the Canada-U.S. trade war escalates.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is replacing American ingredients with Canadian and other non-U.S. alternatives, while pledging not to raise prices until March 2028.

The family-owned company began exploring other suppliers in March 2025 to avoid “future headaches,” CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“In March last year, we released a statement saying we would not raise our prices due to the aggravation from the tariffs, and that’s kind of what started us on this journey,” Chapman said.

By mid- to late 2027, the company expects to have replaced 70 per cent of its American-sourced ingredients with Canadian or other non-U.S. alternatives, he said.

“This is a perfect story of Canadian companies cooperating,” Chapman said. “… No interest in using any American dairy or any American products that we can source other places.”

Chapman’s has signed a five-year deal with Original Foods, near Hamilton, to supply sugar cones, with the switch expected to be completed by the end of the year, Chapman said.

“And we will be the only ice cream company in the country that has 100 per cent Canadian ice cream cones,” he said.

While Chapman’s will continue using 100 per cent Canadian dairy, producing entirely Canadian ice cream is “impossible” because Canada does not produce cocoa, sugar cane and other key ingredients, Chapman said.

But “the reliability of the United States is in question, to say the least,” he added.

“That’s what we want for our business. We want able trading partners that are not emotional, and whenever there’s a dispute, we can just sit down and have an adult conversation and get to the end,” Chapman said.

“With the Trump administration interfering in the business world worldwide, it really has changed our view and a lot of other companies’ views on who we should be making long-term deals with.”

New supply deals include almonds from Australia by mid-2027 and cherries from Chile.

“Shockingly, they’re slightly less expensive than the American almonds, even when you factor in the transportation,” Chapman said. “There are some companies out there that really want to deal with Canadians and really want to ship their product here, and when you get to the economies of scale that we have, it just works out.”

Chapman said the company is also working internally to improve systems, cut costs and find suppliers that can provide high-quality products at lower prices.

“It’s a really nice time (for Canadian companies), shockingly, considering the trade war, because we’re finding new partners that we can rely on,” he said. “This is a time to think outside of the box and set us up for success in the future.”

“And we will be the only ice cream company in the country that has 100 per cent Canadian ice cream cones,” he said.

While Chapman’s will continue using 100 per cent Canadian dairy, producing entirely Canadian ice cream is “impossible” because Canada does not produce cocoa, sugar cane and other key ingredients, Chapman said.
But “the reliability of the United States is in question, to say the least,” he added.

“That’s what we want for our business. We want able trading partners that are not emotional, and whenever there’s a dispute, we can just sit down and have an adult conversation and get to the end,” Chapman said.
“With the Trump administration interfering in the business world worldwide, it really has changed our view and a lot of other companies’ views on who we should be making long-term deals with.”
New supply deals include almonds from Australia by mid-2027 and cherries from Chile.

“Shockingly, they’re slightly less expensive than the American almonds, even when you factor in the transportation,” Chapman said. “There are some companies out there that really want to deal with Canadians and really want to ship their product here, and when you get to the economies of scale that we have, it just works out.”
Chapman said the company is also working internally to improve systems, cut costs and find suppliers that can provide high-quality products at lower prices.

“It’s a really nice time (for Canadian companies), shockingly, considering the trade war, because we’re finding new partners that we can rely on,” he said. “This is a time to think outside of the box and set us up for success in the future.”

stories.title: Clouds, cooler air move into southwestern Ontario, but fair weather ahead
stories.summary: Mainly cloudy skies are expected today as temperatures rise into the afternoon, despite a cold front moving through the region.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A cold front moving through southwestern Ontario is bringing cooler temperatures and increased cloud cover Thursday, but a stretch of pleasant late-summer weather is on the way. According to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison, the front ushered in cooler air from Lake Huron, leading to mainly cloudy skies with occasional breaks of sunshine across the region.

“We have had a cold front come through the area and that is generating a bit of cloud cover with the cool air coming in off Lake Huron,” Atchison said. Temperatures varied considerably across southwestern Ontario Thursday afternoon, with cooler conditions closer to the lake. Atchison said temperatures near the Bruce Peninsula remained between 16 C and 18 C, while London reached about 23 C and Windsor climbed to 26 C.

A few lingering showers were also possible, particularly north of London. Light rainfall was reported in parts of northern Huron County, while London faced only a slight chance of precipitation through the late afternoon. “The probability through the late afternoon is just a 30 per cent chance,” Atchison said.

Overnight temperatures are expected to fall to about 14 C in London as a weak backdoor cold front moves through the region. Atchison said the system will usher in cooler, drier air ahead of the weekend. “High pressure is forecast to build into southwestern Ontario overnight, clearing skies and setting up what forecasters describe as an extended period of comfortable weather.”

Conditions on Friday are expected to be mainly sunny, with only a few fair-weather clouds and a daytime high near 23 C. The favourable pattern is expected to continue through the weekend, with sunny skies and temperatures around 26 C on Saturday. Sunday is forecast to bring a mix of sun and cloud, with temperatures remaining in the mid-20s.

Atchison said there is a 40 per cent chance of showers Sunday night, although any rainfall is expected to hold off until after sunset. “The next few days are looking good with lots of sunshine in the forecast and some comfortable conditions,” said Atchison. stories.title: London hospital tackles language barriers with volunteers, interpretation iPads
stories.summary: The measures offer language support in 14 volunteer-spoken languages and more than 200 through interpretation software.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
St. Joseph’s Health Care has introduced two measures to reduce language barriers at the hospital as London’s population becomes more diverse.

In June, St. Joseph’s launched an initiative in which volunteers wear buttons identifying additional languages they speak, said Tracy Drenth, manager of volunteer services. Fourteen languages – including Spanish, French, Arabic and Hindi – are represented, with more expected as additional volunteers join.

Drenth said the initiative grew out of an increase in patients and visitors whose first language is not English.

“We wanted to be able to make our entrances more welcoming and inclusive,” Drenth said.

“We had volunteers already doing similar things without the buttons, but then when we sent out a survey, we recognized that so many of our volunteers speak a second language. So that’s why we started offering and showing people transparency and showing that people do speak a second language and are able to help them.”

The second measure, introduced earlier this month, is the installation of “interpretation iPads” equipped with language interpretation software covering more than 200 languages, Drenth said.

The devices are available at information desks at three St. Joseph’s Hospital entrances and the Parkwood Institute Main Building entrance. They can assist patients and visitors when a volunteer who speaks their language is unavailable.

Volunteers are only permitted to assist patients and visitors with navigation, wayfinding and greetings, not medical interpretation, Drenth said.

The measures come as London’s population becomes increasingly diverse.

Census data indicates more than 56,000 people speak a language other than English or French at home, according to a St. Joseph’s news release. The release also noted more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021, with 22 per cent of Londoners identifying as immigrants.

Patients and visitors have been “extremely receptive” to the measures, Drenth said.

One of the volunteers is Monica Naskret-Reyes, who wears a button that says “Hablo español,” identifying her as a Spanish-speaking volunteer.

Stationed at St. Joseph’s Hospital’s Cheapside entrance on Thursday, Naskret-Reyes said she has already noticed greater comfort among people whose first language is Spanish – the language with the most interactions since the initiative launched.

A seven-year hospital volunteer, Naskret-Reyes said the relief she sees in people she is able to help in Spanish “means a lot to” her.

“It’s been a great impact in our patients,” Naskret-Reyes said. “When they see someone wearing (a button), and they feel like there is no barrier, they feel more confident despite of all their worries (or) their concerns about their health.”

Drenth said there are plans to expand the initiative into more “patient-facing areas” as St. Joseph’s anticipates the program will grow.

“It serves our mission here at the hospital, and the volunteers are fantastic people who just are here to help,” she added.

stories.title: Western recruits renowned severe storm risk and resilience expert as Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair
stories.summary: Seth Guikema joins Western as the Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair of Canada in Climate Risk and Resilience Analytics, receiving $8 million in federal funding.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
paragraphs: As severe weather becomes more frequent and costly, Western University has recruited a global leader in risk, resilience and disaster analytics to help build the next generation of tools that measure the impacts of storms, wildfires and other natural hazards.

Seth Guikema , an internationally recognized civil and environmental engineer, is joining Western as the Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair of Canada in Climate Risk and Resilience Analytics, receiving $8 million in federal funding. Guikema, who held previous appointments at Texas A&M University and Johns Hopkins University, comes to Western Engineering from the University of Michigan.

“Western is home to an extraordinary group of researchers focused on helping the world prepare for and respond to devastating natural events. We think of it as future-proofing our planet. As our first Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair, Seth Guikema brings global expertise and new approaches to better manage risk and help protect the most vulnerable,” said Western President Alan Shepard. “Western is thrilled to support his work, which will have an impact on communities around the world.”

The new research chairs program is designed to recruit world-leading experts, whose work addresses critical national and global challenges, to Canadian post-secondary institutions. The initiative emphasizes both research excellence and tangible impact in Canada’s strategic priority areas, including advanced digital technologies, climate resilience and the Arctic, defence and dual-use applications and community resilience.

“The Eddie Goldenberg Research Chairs of Canada represent a significant investment in university research and innovation, which help drive Canada’s economic growth,” said Shepard. “We’re grateful for the federal government’s support to recruit leading scientists like Seth Guikema to advance solutions for Canada and the world.”

Guikema’s arrival strengthens Western’s growing international leadership in natural hazards research, adding a new dimension to the work already underway through the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory (Cssl) and its research programs focused on tornadoes, hail, severe weather observation and climate resilience. He develops data-driven solutions and practical tools to help communities prepare and respond to severe weather.

“The hope is always to provide actionable information to decision makers – from the federal government to individual households – about the potential impacts of severe storms,” said Guikema. “That knowledge can help drive better decisions about reducing risk from the hazards faced today, while also preparing for changes in future hazard risk induced by climate change.”
Western was an ideal setting for Guikema to advance his research, which connects engineering, risk analysis, artificial intelligence (AI), data science and community resilience.

“I knew Western would be the perfect place due to the incredible expertise in the Faculty of Engineering and the Canadian Severe Storms Lab that complements what I do,” said Guikema, who previously served as president of the Society for Risk Analysis.

With a focus on social inequity and strengths in severe weather, engineering, meteorology and natural hazards research, Western provides an environment where Guikema can collaborate with researchers across disciplines.

“There aren’t many places in the world that have Western’s depth and breadth of expertise in severe weather research,” said Guikema. “I can’t wait to join the excellent team of engineers and scientists who have spent years building some of the world’s most detailed observations of severe weather. Together, the goal is to move beyond understanding hazards to helping communities prepare for what comes next.”

Western engineering dean Ken Coley, Western’s new Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair of Canada in Climate Risk and Resilience Analytics Seth Guikema and ImpactWX Chair in Severe Storms Engineering Greg Kopp visit the Boundary Layer Wind Tunnel Laboratory. (Steve Anderson / Western Communications)
Guikema’s focus on impact, and preparing for it, distinguishes his work.

A typical project could involve working with a utility company to develop models that predict how severe weather May affect the electrical grid. Using historical data, weather information and machine learning, Guikema and his team can estimate where outages are likely to occur, how extensive they might be and what resources May be needed to restore power. Other projects focus on community resilience, using data and modelling to understand how changing hazards May affect access to critical resources and help communities and governments make better decisions about adaptation.
The goal is to strengthen human expertise by providing better information sooner.
“Humans still have to make these decisions, but AI can provide them with more detailed information, faster,” said Guikema.
That philosophy guides his approach to AI. The most effective decisions combine AI-driven insights with human judgment, experience and an understanding of local communities, Guikema said.

“It’s about more than AI being ‘right’. No AI system is always right,” said Guikema. “Humans bring deep expertise, and communities bring valuable lived experience. The goal of trustworthy AI is to help communities better understand and adapt to the hazards they face by providing useful information that complements human knowledge and respects local experience.”
For Guikema, resilience is not only about infrastructure. It’s also about people.

Two communities can experience the same storm and recover very differently. One neighbourhood May regain power quickly and return to normal. Another May face longer disruptions because of reduced access to transportation, health care, childcare, food and other essential services. Understanding those differences requires looking beyond engineering.

“My approach is to work closely with social scientists, urban planners and policy experts, particularly those studying inequalities, well-being and population health. The goal is to find common understanding and build solutions to complex societal problems,” said Guikema.

That interdisciplinary lens aligns closely with the research environment at Western, where scientists and engineers are examining severe weather across multiple perspectives – from observing storms in the field to understanding their impacts on society.

“We are thrilled to be welcoming Seth to our faculty. His research is transforming the ways in which we understand and manage risk and resilience, and offers real-world solutions that strengthen communities, improve critical infrastructure and benefit millions of people,” said Western Engineering dean Ken Coley. “Seth’s appointment is particularly exciting because of the way it dovetails with Western’s world-class research in severe storms to drive even greater impact on society.”

Through Cssl, Western Engineering researchers have built one of the most detailed pictures of severe weather in Canada. The Northern Tornadoes Project, Northern Hail Project and Northern Mesonet Project are collecting critical observations across a vast and changing landscape.

“One of the biggest limitations facing severe storm science is the lack of detailed historical data. We have observations covering large areas, but relatively little information about how storms behave at the local scale where people live, work and build,” said Guikema.

“Western’s leadership in collecting high-quality field observations through its severe storm research programs creates an extraordinary foundation for applying risk analysis, simulation, AI and other methods to improve our understanding of storm risk and community resilience.”

That combination – detailed observations of hazards and advanced models of their impacts – creates new opportunities to better understand risk and build resilience. Using these integrated tactics is becoming increasingly important as climate change affects how communities experience hazards. Many engineering standards and risk calculations have historically relied on the assumption that past conditions provide a reliable guide for the future. But that assumption is becoming more complicated.

“The historical data isn’t fully representative of the future,” said Guikema. “Any time we’re dealing with a severe weather event, we have to think about climate change. Otherwise, we’re likely to underestimate the risk.”
Guikema said resilience-based strategies must begin long before disaster strikes. Proper risk analysis, fortified by public investment, helps communities withstand and recover from future events.
“We should leverage disruptions to try to increase the resilience of the system, rather than rebuild what we had before,” said Guikema.

The Eddie Goldenberg Research Chairs of Canada provide up to $1 billion over 12 years to support Canadian post-secondary institutions in recruiting exceptional international researchers and expatriate Canadian researchers leading transformational research projects.

These chairs will help ensure that the next generation of researchers, innovators and leaders have the opportunity to build their futures in Canada and contribute to discoveries that will benefit people across the country and around the world.

stories.title: Police seize $32,000 in drugs, arrest six people after multi-month investigation
stories.summary: St. Thomas police say a multi-month drug trafficking investigation has resulted in six arrests, dozens of charges and the seizure of drugs
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
St. Thomas police say a multi-month drug trafficking investigation has resulted in six arrests, dozens of charges and the seizure of fentanyl, cocaine and other controlled substances with an estimated street value exceeding $32,000.

Police announced the conclusion of Project Apex on Thursday, saying it began in March 2026 after investigators identified individuals suspected of trafficking fentanyl and other drugs to people considered at heightened risk of exploitation and drug-related harm.

“Fentanyl continues to pose a serious threat to individual and community safety,” police said in a release. “Its presence creates a significant risk of overdose and death, particularly for people experiencing vulnerability.” Between the launch of the investigation and August 2026, officers arrested six people and laid a combined 64 criminal charges.

Police did not immediately release the identities of those charged. The case remains before the courts.

stories.title: OPP search for missing swimmer at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Beachgoers found the missing 28-year-old's body on Thursday, police said
Provincial Police in Lambton County say they have recovered the body of a missing swimmer who was last seen at a Pinery Provincial Park beach on Wednesday afternoon.

Police say visitors to the beach located the body of the individual on Thursday. They did not share any details of the person's identity, other than specifying the deceased as a 28-year-old from Scarborough.
OPP say the search began when police were called at 1 p.m. on Aug. 26, about the missing swimmer who was last seen at a beach in the park.

Two OPP boats, as well as the underwater search and recovery unit, and OPP aviation services, were helping with the search. Anishnabek Police Service, which operates a detachment at Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, also helped.
It's unclear why it took almost 24 hours for OPP to notify the public about the missing swimmer.

stories.title: Damage from electrical fire at new London high-rise triggers city safety order
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 27
Power, AC systems impacted at South Street building that opened last year

The City of London has issued a make-safe order at a newly-opened residential high-rise on the former South Street hospital grounds, after a fire last week resulted in damage the city says compromised the “structural integrity and fire separations" of its electrical room.

City officials handed out the order to Toronto-based Medallion Corporation on Monday, giving it until Sept. 24 to submit a report detailing planned repairs at 375 South St., a 588-unit dual-tower complex which opened last year under the name SoHoSQ.

Medallion is required to retain a professional, licensed engineer to review the damage, and submit a report on the condition and the remedial steps that will be taken, according to the order, a copy of which could be seen taped to the building’s entrance.

“Failure to correct this unsafe condition by the time specified in this Order May result in the issuance of a further Order prohibiting the use or occupancy of the building,” and/or legal action and steep fines, the document reads.

Large temporary generators have been powering the building since the fire, which occurred on Aug. 20 in the building’s electrical room. Crews were called to the complex around 3:30 a.m. and arrived to find a large electrical panel fire, according to dispatch audio reviewed by CBC News.

No one from the London Fire Department was available to comment on the initial incident, and a department official said any information would have to come through a formal freedom of information request.
In a statement sent after publication, Medallion Corporation said it was working closely with contractors, engineers and London Hydro to investigate the incident.

"We restored temporary power to the whole building within the same day and are working to restore full power as quickly and as safely as possible," said George Espinola, director of residential property management at Medallion.
In an update to tenants on Tuesday, Medallion said a professional engineer had been onsite to determine next steps and the scope of repairs that May be required.

“We understand that residents have questions about how long temporary power will be required and when all building systems will return to normal. At this stage, we cannot provide timelines until the necessary assessments have been completed and we have reliable information to share,” the update reads.
Damian Cowan, a fire suppression installer who worked on the building, was at the property after the fact and saw the damage first-hand.

“I honestly don’t know how else I would want to describe that, other than it looked like a small-scale bomb went off, as blunt as that is,” he said, noting a large crack could be seen in a cinder block wall.
He believes the longest delay getting the problem resolved will be various agencies needing to come in to determine what caused the incident.
“The sooner that investigation gets its foot past the door, the sooner that they can get everything fixed.”

In his statement, Espinola said Medallion understood how the situation has been disruptive to residents, including noise from the generators, and said, "We are looking at an alternative solution that will eliminate the need for generators."
"We will be communicating updates to residents as soon as we have them," he said.
The generators sit just outside the apartment window of Bri Watson and their partner, who live on the building's second floor, and can be heard with the doors and windows closed.

"It's louder at night, and the windows rattle. We have three cats, they can't sleep at all. Two apartments down from us, they have two young kids. You can hear the generators kick in extra loud at night, and you just hear the crying start."
Watson has lived in the building for one year, and says it all adds to existing problems they’ve experienced with their $2,700 per month unit.
“Mid-June, we just lost air conditioning,” they said. Each unit has individually-controlled heat and air conditioning, according to
the building's website . “It took several weeks for them to arrive at a conclusion of when they constructed the building, they didn’t install several vents correctly.”

“Ours is right in the corner of the building, and the corners of the building are all big glass windows. It’s basically turned into a greenhouse in there. When the AC does work … it does cool it off pretty well.”
The fire knocked out air conditioning to the entire building, according to the email Medallion sent to tenants on Tuesday. Technicians were expected to visit the building on Friday.
Hot water was also impacted, but was restored on Friday along with power, according to other messages from Medallion. Watson says the water temperature has not returned to normal.

Watson estimates the building has also seen more than two dozen unplanned fire alarm activations over the past year, something which affects their partner’s epilepsy. They note work is still active on upper floor units.
A fire alarm activation occurred Tuesday because of the ongoing repairs, and tenants have been told to expect a power interruption on Thursday as the generators are refuelled.
It’s unclear how long it will take for power to return to normal, but Watson says they won’t be there when it does as the two are moving into a larger, cheaper apartment downtown on Sept. 1.

“I am baffled that we’ve been paying that much,” they said of their current unit. “It’s stressful as hell to move, but it’s not worth staying in this building given what we’ve seen over the past year.”

stories.title: Ilderton, Ont. vocal coach helps Rush’s Geddy Lee through ‘Fifty Something’ tour
stories.summary: He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice. “I found out, and it was a shock that I was his first vocal coach,” exclaimed Ilderton, Ont. based vocal coach Mitch Seekins.

“He never studied voice before. So, everything that he’s done has been completely natural up to that point, which is incredibly rare.” A vocal coach for more than 35 years, Seekins was contacted in spring 2025 to help Lee prepare for Rush’s Fifty Something Tour.

With Lee now in his 70s, Seekins knew the work would be demanding. “The Rush repertoire in my mind has got to be the most difficult rock gig to sing because it’s so high, and it stays so high, the whole show. He rarely gets a break.

So, does he have that in him anymore? What has the aging process done,” wondered the long-time voice expert. Seekins worked with Lee nearly every day for four months, helping to build his voice to withstand the rigors of touring.

The rock icon proved to be a highly disciplined student,” said Seekins. “And he started to see the progress starting to happen, and things were coming back. And it was a lot of work. But thank goodness he’s focused, very focused,” he explained.

While Geddy Lee is his most notable, a who’s who of great talents can be found among Seekins’ roster of students, including Luke Bentham of Canadian rock band, The Dirty Nil. “My imagination is kind of pushed to its limits kind of imagining what the rebuilding process would be like after taking such a sustained break as Geddy has.

And it makes it all the more impressive when I watch the footage of them playing this tour that they’re on,” Bentham said. Seekins has also taken on Rush guitarist Alex Lifeson as a student. Lifeson’s vocal role in Rush performances has historically been relatively minimal, but he wanted to expand his involvement for the current tour.

stories.title: 6 people charged with 64 offences in St. Thomas fentanyl investigation
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 3:01 PM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 3:01 PM | Last Updated: August 28
Police say drugs seized during Project Apex had an estimated street value of $32,185

The St. Thomas Police Service (Stps) says six people have been charged with a total of 64 criminal offences following a months-long investigation into the alleged trafficking of fentanyl and other controlled substances.
Police say Project Apex began in March, with the six accused arrested between March and August.
During the investigation, officers executed search warrants at several locations in St. Thomas and seized fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, prescription drugs, cash and weapons.
Police estimate the total street value of the drugs seized at $32,185.

194.3 grams of fentanyl – estimated street value of $19,430 54.4 grams of cocaine – estimated street value of $5,440 22.6 grams of methamphetamine – estimated street value of $2,260 16.8 grams of crack cocaine – estimated street value of $1,680 487 prescription tablets, including Oxycodone, Dilaudid, Morphine and other suspected controlled substances – estimated street value of $3,375
Police also seized $4,016.28 in Canadian currency, a conducted energy weapon, a crossbow and ammunition.
"Fentanyl continues to have devastating consequences for individuals, families and our broader community," said Chief Marc Roskamp.

"Addressing this threat requires a balanced approach, focused on enforcement against those who traffic these substances, while supporting collaborative health, social service, housing and recovery pathways for people affected by addiction."
Stps Insp. Matt Lobsinger called the operation a significant success for the police service.

"No single investigation is going to entirely eliminate the illicit supply of fentanyl, but what an investigation like this can do is disrupt it from coming into our community and remove the dangerous drugs from circulation," said Lobsinger.
"Any investigation of this magnitude ... is going to be successful. Every one of these arrests and all these investigations are significant."
Lobsinger couldn't share specifics on the ages or identities of the accused, but said a majority of them lived in the St. Thomas area.
"We're going to hold those people accountable, [and] provide deterrent for people thinking about getting into it, while gathering information for future investigations," Lobsinger said.
The investigation remains ongoing, police said.
The allegations have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Four Western researchers awarded fellowships in the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences
stories.summary: Cahs Fellows from Western University in 2026 are Daniel Ansari, Mansour Haeryfar, Nicole Redvers and Victor Yang, honoured for leadership in health research
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
paragraphs: Four Western University researchers have been elected Fellows of the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences (Cahs), one of Canada’s highest honours in health sciences research and leadership.

Daniel Ansari, Mansour Haeryfar, Nicole Redvers and Victor Yang were nominated and elected Cahs Fellows by their peers in recognition of their leadership, research productivity and demonstrated commitment to advancing public health outcomes, among other criteria. The Western researchers now join a distinguished national network of health scientists, clinicians and scholars whose expertise informs health policy, research and health-system improvements across Canada.

The Western scholars are four of the 59 new Fellows announced Aug. 25 . Drawn from Canadian universities, health-care and research institutes, Cahs Fellows support the academy in generating evidence-informed guidance and leadership to address urgent health concerns facing Canadians.
Daniel Ansari, Faculties of Education and Social Science
Canada Research Chair in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience and Learning , Daniel Ansari , is a world leader in the examination of children’s development of math and numeracy skills.

Ansari is the principal investigator in the Numerical Cognition Lab at Western. His research is opening new avenues to identify children who struggle with math and address these difficulties before they become lifelong barriers to success. His substantial body of published research informs how researchers in Canada and beyond understand children’s mathematical development and how to teach mathematical thinking.
Mansour Haeryfar, Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry
Immunology professor Mansour Haeryfar ‘s research has transformed our understanding of immune responses in health, infectious diseases and cancer.

An advocate for immunization against vaccine-preventable diseases, he has pioneered novel vaccination strategies against respiratory viruses and led a team that invented the application of a bacterial molecule to make vaccines more effective . Haeryfar has also developed effective experimental immunotherapies for sepsis and cancer. He engages global media to make research accessible. As president of the Canadian Society for Immunology , his leadership advanced Canada’s scientific standing around the world.
Nicole Redvers, Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry
Western research chair Nicole Redvers , a member of the Deninu K’ue First Nation (NWT), is the director of Indigenous Planetary Health at the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

Her research examines the links between climate change, ecological health and Indigenous health promotion. Redvers also serves as vice-president of research for the Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada . She advises several World Health Organization technical groups and co-leads the health and wellbeing section of the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report .
Dr. Victor Yang, Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry
Neurosurgery and medical biophysics professor , Dr. Victor Yang , is an internationally recognized neurosurgeon, clinician- scientist and engineering innovator .

Yang’s research has advanced cutting-edge machine-vision surgical robotics and smart material implants for neurovascular diseases and spinal injuries. stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as it shifts away from U.S. suppliers
stories.summary: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's London Morning on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"We knew there will be opportunities for customers who are currently buying in the U.S. to look for local manufacturing and we approached Chapman's to discuss if they would be interested to buy locally," said president Steeve Tremblay.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.
The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”
Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.

stories.title: Six arrested, 64 charges laid after months-long drug probe: Police
stories.summary: "Fentanyl continues to have devastating consequences for individuals, families and our broader community"
stories.author: Free Press staff
paragraphs: St. Thomas police say a months-long investigation into drug trafficking has led to six arrests, 64 criminal charges and more than $30,000 in drugs seized.

With help from the Criminal Intelligence Service Ontario, which a partnership between local law enforcement as well as the provincial and federal government, St. Thomas police on Thursday announced the conclusion of its so-called “Project Apex” investigation.

In a news release, police said the investigation began in March after officers identified individuals “suspected of trafficking fentanyl and other controlled substances to people at heightened risk of drug-related harm” in the community.

“Project Apex demonstrates our commitment to holding accountable those who profit from trafficking dangerous substances and exploiting people who May be particularly vulnerable to drug-related harm,” St. Thomas police Chief Marc Roskamp said in a statement.

“Fentanyl continues to have devastating consequences for individuals, families and our broader community. Addressing this threat requires a balanced approach, focused on enforcement against those who traffic these substances, while supporting collaborative health, social service, housing and recovery pathways for people affected by addiction.”
Between March and August, six people were arrested and collectively charged with 64 offences, police said. No details were shared about who was arrested.
During the investigation, officers conducted search warrants “at several locations in St. Thomas,” and seized an estimated $32,185 worth of drugs, police said. The items seized include:

stories.title: Juno-winning band to headline Western Fair's packed music lineup
stories.summary: The Western Fair is bringing Juno award-winning band the Strumbellas, longtime band Wide Mouth Mason and a long list of other acts to this year's festival.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
paragraphs: The Western Fair is bringing Juno award-winning band the Strumbellas, longtime rockers Wide Mouth Mason and a long list of other acts to this year’s festival.
The fair runs from Sept. 11 to 20, with concerts at the Bud Light Music Gardens every night.

The Strumbellas, whose hits include I’ll Wait, will headline opening night on Friday Sept. 11. The Lindsay folk-rock band will be playing at the fair for the first time this year, said Angela Hawkins, a Western Fair spokesperson.
“I think that’s going to be such a good day,” Hawkins said. “I love the Strumbellas. That was personally the one that I was very excited to announce.”
Opening weekend continues with blues-rock band Wide Mouth Mason, who first started recording hit songs in the late 1990s, ON Saturday, Sept. 12, and London-based band Texas King on Sunday, Sept. 13.
This year’s performances will span rock, blues, pop and country – a mix Hawkins says is key to bringing people out.
“Every year we try to get new concerts that would appeal to a range of concertgoers,” she said. “So it’s something that, hopefully, everybody can find something that they like.”

For country music fans, the fair’s final night will feature Canadian artists Tyler Lorette, Carson Janik and Sully Burrows. Lorette recently was named the 2026 Country Music Association of Ontario breakthrough artist of the year, while Burrows won the same award the year before.

A new addition this year is a Latin music day on Sept. 19, featuring music and cultural performances throughout the day, including the Ana Mexico Latin Power Band and Los Grandes Del Norte. Hawkins says the event is a way to bring in London’s Latin community, especially after seeing the success of Latin street festivals throughout the summer.
“I think it’s just one of those things that the community would love to see, love to try, and we really love to have different cultures represented at the fair,” she said.
All performances are free with general admission to the fair. A single-day ticket costs $15 when bought in advance until Sept. 10, or $20 at the gate.

stories.title: Fire destroys golf course clubhouse in Huron County
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 11:54 AM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 11:54 AM | Last Updated: August 27
The Bluewater Golf Course is closed until further notice
The province's fire marshal is investigating after a golf course clubhouse northwest of London was burnt to the ground Wednesday night.
Just after 8 p.m., crews responded to a structure fire near the intersection of Bluewater Highway and Bayfield Road in Central Huron, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).
Fire crews successfully extinguished the fire, OPP said, but a golf course clubhouse at the location was destroyed.
The Bluewater Golf Course and Campground
posted on its social media Wednesday night that the course is "closed until future notice."

"Thank you to our staff for their hard work and quick response. We would also like to extend our sincere thanks and appreciation to all of the first responders who attended the fire so quickly," the post said.
Nobody was injured in the fire, police said.
Ontario's Office of the Fire Marshall is expected to visit the location and investigate the cause of the fire, OPP said.
Bluewater Highway and Bayfield Road were closed for several hours as crews responded to the fire, but have since reopened.
