stories.title: Loss of Strathroy hospital's obstetrics unit forces pregnant moms to travel long distances
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:48 AM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:48 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Hospital closed unit in 2024 following low birth volumes, and to refocus on other aspects of women's health
More than two years after Strathroy
closed down its obstetrics unit, some mothers are describing the challenges they've faced travelling out of town to London or St. Thomas to give birth.

For Melbourne, Ont., resident Tamia Chicas, Smgh is only 20 minutes away, but the lack of an obstetrics unit meant she had to travel twice that distance to London several times throughout her pregnancy for her prenatal appointments, ultrasounds and delivery.

"It was stressful," said Chicas, who had her son in 2024. "When you're pregnant and you know you need to go that far, sometimes you wonder to yourself, if there are any complications ... driving that far is really scary."
The hospital announced in March 2024 that it would

transition obstetrical deliveries to its regional partner hospitals, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital, as it re-envisions women's health care. Its last delivery was
Julie McBrien, president and CEO of Middlesex Hospital Alliance, which includes Smgh and Four Counties Health Services, said the decision followed record low births at the hospital.
"In our last year of providing obstetrical services, we did 59 deliveries so when you factor that over a year, that's just a little over one each week and that's challenging," she said.

"I think what it told us when we did our review of the situation was moms were choosing to deliver in London or St. Thomas anyway. Hence why we had lower volumes because we were a low-risk birthing centre."

However, for some new and expectant mothers, the trip away from their home community has been a logistical challenge. Chicas worries this can have a negative impact on women's health care outside of larger urban centres.

Chicas said she had a miscarriage before she got pregnant with her now two-year-old son and that made her worry about any possible complications and how difficult it would be to travel all the way to London for medical attention.

"I was just scared the entire time during my pregnancy. If something went wrong, we would have to go so far out of the way. Even if they had an ambulance or something come out here, it would still be quite the drive going all the way to London," she said.

Veronica Marchuk gave birth to her older daughter at Smgh, which was walking distance from her parents house. However, for her now seven-month old daughter, she had also had to travel to London, which made for a lengthy and tiring experience.

"With the first, I was able to labour on the couch and we basically just went [to Smgh] to deliver her and it was amazing. It was such a good experience because I was able to let my body do what it needed to. But with the second, we had to go into London for an actual induction and I had to do the whole labour in the hospital rather than being in the comfort of my own home," she said.
Transportation is also not readily accessible for many families in rural communities, so driving a long distance for the hospital can be a major inconvenience, added Marchuk.
"It makes it harder with the prices of gas too. A lot of people in Strathroy would have to take the bus, schedule an Uber or find somebody to drive them."

McBrien said Smgh has instead focused its efforts on other aspects of women's health care, such as advancing its breast health program through mammograms, breast ultrasounds, a new MRI service at the hospital, and breast cancer and reconstruction surgeries. These initiatives resulted from community feedback, she added.

"Those are things that now women don't have to travel to London for, they can get that care close to home. So we are focusing on the areas where we feel that we can excel, provide high quality care, that we can do lots of activity and really be an area of excellence in," said McBrien.

However, both Chicas and Marchuk believe that with Strathroy's population rapidly growing, an obstetrics department close to home would benefit the entire community and provide more incentive for young couples and families to live in the municipality.

stories.title: Old South neighbours fed up with traffic, trucks cutting through residential streets
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Residents say commercial trucks have ripped down internet and cable wires and tree branches

Residents living on one street in London’s Old South neighbourhood say they are frustrated with the number of cars and large commercial trucks using the area as a shortcut while construction continues on Wellington Road.

Several residents on High Street, located between Commissioners Road East and Grand Avenue, say there has been increased traffic since phase two of the Wellington Gateway bus rapid transit project started in May.
Construction has caused lane closures and slowdowns at Commissioners and Wellington roads — one of London’s busiest intersections — that are expected to last into 2028.

“The trucks come over, and they shake my entire house,” said High Street resident Margaret Dow. “They’ve taken down internet lines and cable lines. Speed is also an issue because it’s just been very noisy to the point where I can’t even have my windows open on nice days.”
Dow has lived on High for 20 years, and said she’s never seen as much cut-through traffic as this summer.
Despite three signs on Commissioners indicating that no heavy trucks are permitted down High, Dow said she has seen transport trucks, cement mixers and dump trucks travelling down the street daily.

“I recognize that with the construction, we’re going to have increased traffic … It is annoying that it takes me about 5 minutes to get out of the driveway in the morning, but that’s the cost you pay to have additional infrastructure in the city,” Dow said. “So cars are not the issue. It’s the trucks.”
Two doors down, Narek Papian said he is fed up with traffic on High, especially because he and his two young children like to bike in the area.

“There’s just too many cars. You don’t leave your house around 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. because you know you’re going to get stuck behind everything,” he said. “So, you wait for your errands or you just make sure you go around the block.”
Papian said he’s also noticed a “speeding culture” on the street, with people driving at what he thinks is about 50 km/h.
The speed limit on High Street is 40 km/h, with yellow 30 km/h advisory signs near speed cushions.
“I don’t understand why they would do that. It’s just so fast, and there’s kids,” Papian said.
Both Papian and Dow said they think the solution is a mix of increased truck traffic enforcement and general calming measures.
“People won’t drive better. You can’t teach people, so you have to create obstacles so they have to slow down,” Papian said.
Doug MacRae, the city’s director of transportation and mobility, said the city considers setting up temporary calming measures before major construction projects even begin.

“We identify early during planning any potential routes that we anticipate will be subject to increased traffic. Then, throughout the construction season as conditions change, we adjust and redeploy measures as necessary and based on neighbourhood feedback,” MacRae explained.
However, MacRae said the strip of High between Base Line Road and Commissioners – where Papian and Dow live – already has permanent speed cushions, so no additional obstacles were installed.
“That section was deemed already traffic calmed,” he said, adding that the city is continuing to analyze resident feedback.
North of Base Line Road, there are several temporary traffic-calming measures on High Street, including speed bumps, posts and hazard signs.
Patrick Clancy, who lives on that side of High, said despite the obstacles, large commercial trucks continue to barrel down the street and have torn branches off the tree in his front yard.

“They put in some calming measures, but it’s not enough to solve the whole problem,” he said. “I’ve yet to see anyone set up on the side of the road to control any speeding or any trucks or anything like that, so it’s a lot of words, not a lot of action.”
MacRae said the city has requested London police enforcement of trucks on non-truck routes and there are plans to install additional no truck signage.
Clancy, Dow and Papian all said they reached out to the city about traffic issues, while the former two also reached out to Ward 11 Coun. Skylar Franke and London police.
"The Road Safety Section has reviewed the issue and conducted targeted enforcement in the area," said London Police Const. Gavin Dell.
"Drivers who fail to comply May be subject to enforcement under applicable traffic legislation. The London Police Service will continue to monitor the area and address violations as appropriate.”
Franke did not respond to CBC News before publication.
Not satisfied with the response so far, neighbours along High Street have been sharing their woes with one another through front lawn conversations and Facebook posts.
Papian said that inspired him to start collecting signatures from neighbours who want to see change.
MacRae said the best way for residents to share their traffic concerns is through the city’s online Service London portal.
He said residents can also use the portal to request a front lawn sign that reminds other drivers to “respect the limit.”

“I recognize that with the construction, we’re going to have increased traffic … It is annoying that it takes me about 5 minutes to get out of the driveway in the morning, but that’s the cost you pay to have additional infrastructure in the city,” Dow said. “So cars are not the issue. It’s the trucks.”
Two doors down, Narek Papian said he is fed up with traffic on High, especially because he and his two young children like to bike in the area.

“There’s just too many cars. You don’t leave your house around 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. because you know you’re going to get stuck behind everything,” he said. “So, you wait for your errands or you just make sure you go around the block.”
Papian said he’s also noticed a “speeding culture” on the street, with people driving at what he thinks is about 50 km/h.
The speed limit on High Street is 40 km/h, with yellow 30 km/h advisory signs near speed cushions.
“I don’t understand why they would do that. It’s just so fast, and there’s kids,” Papian said.
Both Papian and Dow said they think the solution is a mix of increased truck traffic enforcement and general calming measures.
“People won’t drive better. You can’t teach people, so you have to create obstacles so they have to slow down,” Papian said.
Doug MacRae, the city’s director of transportation and mobility, said the city considers setting up temporary calming measures before major construction projects even begin.

“We identify early during planning any potential routes that we anticipate will be subject to increased traffic. Then, throughout the construction season as conditions change, we adjust and redeploy measures as necessary and based on neighbourhood feedback,” MacRae explained.
However, MacRae said the strip of High between Base Line Road and Commissioners – where Papian and Dow live – already has permanent speed cushions, so no additional obstacles were installed.
“That section was deemed already traffic calmed,” he said, adding that the city is continuing to analyze resident feedback.
North of Base Line Road, there are several temporary traffic-calming measures on High Street, including speed bumps, posts and hazard signs.
Patrick Clancy, who lives on that side of High, said despite the obstacles, large commercial trucks continue to barrel down the street and have torn branches off the tree in his front yard.

“They put in some calming measures, but it’s not enough to solve the whole problem,” he said. “I’ve yet to see anyone set up on the side of the road to control any speeding or any trucks or anything like that, so it’s a lot of words, not a lot of action.”
MacRae said the city has requested London police enforcement of trucks on non-truck routes and there are plans to install additional no truck signage.
Clancy, Dow and Papian all said they reached out to the city about traffic issues, while the former two also reached out to Ward 11 Coun. Skylar Franke and London police.
"The Road Safety Section has reviewed the issue and conducted targeted enforcement in the area," said London Police Const. Gavin Dell.
"Drivers who fail to comply May be subject to enforcement under applicable traffic legislation. The London Police Service will continue to monitor the area and address violations as appropriate.”
Franke did not respond to CBC News before publication.
Not satisfied with the response so far, neighbours along High Street have been sharing their woes with one another through front lawn conversations and Facebook posts.
Papian said that inspired him to start collecting signatures from neighbours who want to see change.
MacRae said the best way for residents to share their traffic concerns is through the city’s online Service London portal.
He said residents can also use the portal to request a front lawn sign that reminds other drivers to “respect the limit.”

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: August 26, 2026
stories.summary: Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.

Working in business for many years, I have never seen a person submit a budget request like the police department did and get everything they wanted. We need someone to stand up for the taxpayer and challenge budgets like it was their own money.

Maybe in another four years people will see the light.

Gary Rogers, London

I drive on Dundas Street at least once a week. It appears that the vagrancy situation and all its ills is not being addressed. Sorry, but a person lying face down on the sidewalk is not acceptable.

With the London election coming up on Oct. 26, 2026, I would challenge all candidates to state their position on homelessness and what they promise to do if elected.

I can’t think of a more important issue facing Londoners at this time, so let’s demand that candidates address it.

Dogs frequently ingest corn cobs whole or in pieces, resulting in a bowel obstruction. Please, keep corn cobs out of reach.

Paul Francis, Thorndale

stories.title: Victoria Park enhancements to brighten visitor experience year-round
stories.summary: Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features, enhancing community e
paragraphs: Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features , enhancing community events and everyday park use throughout the year. Improvements include new multi-colored LED lighting surrounding the concrete pad and the interior of the bandshell, along with a portable raised seating area that will feature railings and a wheelchair-accessible ramp.

The improvements are made possible through a $165,000 donation from Canada Life, recognizing the company's deep roots in London as it celebrates 100 years at its downtown location. Coinciding with the City's Bicentennial, the investment will enhance one of London's most cherished public spaces while improving accessibility and the visitor experience.

The upgraded lighting will help create a more vibrant atmosphere for festivals, community gatherings and public skating, while the new accessible viewing area will allow more Londoners to comfortably experience performances and events.

"Victoria Park has been bringing Londoners together for generations, and these improvements will ensure even more people can enjoy everything this important community space has to offer," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "We're grateful for Canada Life's generous donation, which will create a vibrant and accessible destination for residents and visitors alike."

"Having spent nearly 40 years working in downtown London, I know firsthand how Victoria Park has long been at the heart of community life in London, bringing people together to celebrate, connect and create lasting memories," says Jeff Van Hoeve, Senior Vice-President, Business Integration, Canada Life. “As Canada Life marks 100 years in downtown London, we're proud to support improvements that will help make this treasured public space more accessible and enjoyable for residents and visitors for years to come."
The improvements support Victoria Park's role as one of London's premier gathering spaces, creating a more accessible and welcoming destination for residents and visitors for years to come.

stories.title: ICE UNIT INVESTIGATION 25-107385
stories.summary: Update - London, ON (August 26, 2026) – A London man is facing additional charges after members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit (ICE) located additional evidence on seized electronic devices.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
UPDATE - LONDON, ON (August 26, 2026) – A London man is facing additional charges after members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit (ICE) located additional evidence on seized electronic devices.

On August 21, 2026, the accused, who was out on bail, was arrested on the additional charges.

As a result of the investigation, Isaac Higgs, 23, of London, has been additionally charged with the following offences:

Possession of child pornography;

Print/publish/possess to publish child pornography;

Import/sell/distribute, etc. child sexual abuse material;

Luring a person under 16 years of age by means of telecommunication;

Making available sexually explicit material to a person under or believed to be under 18 years of age; and

Obtaining sexual services for consideration.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on September 1, 2026, in relation to the charges.

ORIGINAL - LONDON, ON (May 21, 2026) – A London man was arrested last week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to possession of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (CSAEM).

In October of 2025, members of the London Police Service commenced an investigation after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) made them aware of information involving a London man.

On Friday, May 15, 2026, a search warrant was executed at a residence near Elias Street and Adelaide Street North.

A male suspect was arrested, and electronic devices were seized. Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (CSAEM) were located.

As a result of the investigation, Isaac Higgs, 23, of London, has been charged with one count of possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

The accused is scheduled to appear in London court on June 11, 2026, in relation to the charges.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to Protect Children from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation on the Internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Uncertainty about temporary winter homeless shelter’s location sparks debate about clustering in core business districts
stories.summary: City Council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
City council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.

The updated plan will see homeless shelters open a total of 235 overnight spaces every night between Dec. 1, 2026, and March 31, 2027, plus an additional 29 overnight spaces when temperatures drop below -15C or -20 windchill.

Most of the spaces will be within existing shelters, but Ark Aid Street Mission is looking to secure a yet-to-be-determined location for 40 spaces that would operate nightly from 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. Concerned about the clustering of frontline agencies in the Old East Village (OEV) BIA, Coun.

Susan Stevenson proposed requiring council approval of the location before it receives municipal funding. “To say that there are no other locations [but the main street of core area BIAs] is counter to our whole objective of 12 to 15 [homeless] hubs around the city,” she asserted.

Coun. Hadleigh McAlister expressed similar concern about the Hamilton Road BIA in his ward, “We need to recognize that we have repeatedly asked two areas of the city to shoulder the responsibility and that is grossly unfair.” Downtown London Coun.

David Ferreira acknowledged, “I understand the capacity that we have is really within these [core] areas, however, I also see that there is a reality that we do have service providers within a small area.” Stevenson pressed staff about a previous council decision not to fund shelter spaces on the main streets of BIAs, but council supported a “not withstanding” amendment essentially exempting this decision from the previous restriction.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis rejected the notion that council continues to cluster frontline services for homeless Londoners in OEV, Downtown London, and along Hamilton Road. “The core is not the only location where we have homelessness services,” Lewis stated.

“On Clarke Road in the east end I have the YOU (Youth Opportunities Unlimited) youth shelter. I also have the Anova Women’s Shelter. South of [Highway] 401 is where we put the micro-modular shelter.” The deputy mayor emphasized that The Ark and Unity Project own their buildings on Dundas Street in the OEV BIA and receive private donations to fund some of their operations.

“So if you want to talk about moving them, then you better talk about a multi-year budget business plan for property acquisition, to then do land swaps with them, because that is what you’re talking about,” he added.

content_blocks.text: City council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.

The updated plan will see homeless shelters open a total of 235 overnight spaces every night between Dec. 1, 2026, and March 31, 2027, plus an additional 29 overnight spaces when temperatures drop below -15C or -20 windchill.

Most of the spaces will be within existing shelters, but Ark Aid Street Mission is looking to secure a yet-to-be-determined location for 40 spaces that would operate nightly from 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. Concerned about the clustering of frontline agencies in the Old East Village (OEV) BIA, Coun.

Susan Stevenson proposed requiring council approval of the location before it receives municipal funding. “To say that there are no other locations [but the main street of core area BIAs] is counter to our whole objective of 12 to 15 [homeless] hubs around the city,” she asserted.

stories.title: Trade war escalation: New U.S. tariffs spark economic fears, could hit London SMEs hard
stories.summary: Escalating trade tensions with the U.S. have landed a significant blow to the London region’s economy, with new, steep tariffs threatening to disproportionately impact the city’s numerous small and medium-sized businesses.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Escalating trade tensions with the U.S. have landed a significant blow to the London region’s economy, with new, steep tariffs threatening to disproportionately impact the city’s numerous small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs). The recent tit-for-tat tariff announcements are adding considerable pressure to an economy already grappling with one of Canada’s highest unemployment rates for large urban centres.

New U.S. tariffs, reportedly at 50 per cent on nearly $20 billion worth of Canadian exports, were announced Saturday, targeting a selective list of products that include key sectors for London. Graham Henderson, CEO of the London Chamber of Commerce, warned that this isn’t just an issue for large manufacturers.

“This isn’t a problem that is just facing big car manufacturers and steel manufacturers,” Henderson stated. “This is an issue that’s going to impact probably disproportionately small and medium sized businesses, of which there are 14,000, I think, in London.” The impact is already being felt by local companies.

For businesses like Vaughn Hockey, which manufactures specialized goalie equipment including now-tariffed sticks, or Black Fly Beverages, a local producer of alcoholic drinks, the tariffs present immediate challenges. “If you’re making alcoholic beverages here in London and your market is in the U.S., you’re going to wake up with a 50 per cent headache,” Henderson explained.

“And if your business model is based around selling into the U.S., that’s a problem.” The Chamber of Commerce’s own Op-Ed further illustrated this, noting that a 50 per cent tariff can make a product dramatically more expensive than competitors, forcing customers to reconsider purchases, turning a competitive business on Friday into one facing a “completely different commercial calculation on Monday.”

This new economic challenge comes at a time when London’s unemployment rate is already among the highest for large urban centres in Canada. Graham Henderson likens the current trade conflict to the struggles faced during the 2008 recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Historically, London has shown resilience; Henderson recalled that the city “sort of went into the recession last and came out first,” a recovery he credits to the city’s “economic diversity” in terms of sectors and export markets.

The concerns extend beyond London. Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley expressed strong support for the federal government’s response, calling it “excellent” and noting that “most Canadians” support the stance. However, he acknowledged the significant challenges ahead for Southern Ontario. “Well, right now the tariffs that are coming forward are going to be on plastic.

And the auto tariffs are really disturbing because everything that goes into the automobile at some point comes through Sarnia, from the plastic, to the carbon black, to the gasoline itself,” Bradley stated, warning this could “devastate not just our local economy, not just southwestern Ontario, but the entire nation’s economy.”

Henderson highlighted that while U.S. tariffs impact about five per cent of Canada’s sales into the U.S. (approximately $20 billion worth of goods), for businesses whose products fall within that five per cent, the problem is much larger. More than 700 London businesses exported roughly $7.8 billion to the U.S. in 2023, many reliant on that market.

Henderson stressed that beyond direct financial costs, an “economic cost that is harder to measure” is uncertainty, making critical business decisions about hiring, investment, and expansion far more difficult when market access can change “dramatically within days.” The consequences ripple outward: If exporters lose orders, their suppliers, transportation companies, and contractors can also suffer, eventually impacting businesses that don’t export at all.

The Chamber of Commerce advocates for continued efforts towards predictable U.S. market access while accelerating trade diversification.

stories.title: London tenant facing homelessness as advocates call for stronger ‘demoviction’ protections
stories.summary: A London tenant facing eviction says he could be homeless within days as tenant advocates call on the city to strengthen protections against what they describe as ‘demovictions.’
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London tenant facing eviction says he could be homeless within days as tenant advocates call on the city to strengthen protections against what they describe as ‘demovictions.’ Darcy Barnes, 63, has lived in a unit at 34 Adelaide Street South for about 10 years.

He says he is on disability, as he awaits a double hip surgery. “Homelessness, basically. I’m debilitated,” Barnes said during a tenant rally outside his home Tuesday. “I have osteoarthritis in both hips. Nerve pain in my leg.

And I can’t get my furniture out of the house. And I have nowhere to bring it.” Barnes says his landlord served him a N13 eviction notice last year, saying the unit needed to be vacated for work involving the building. A N13 notice can be used by landlords when a rental unit is needed for demolition, conversion, or extensive repairs or renovations.

Barnes challenged the eviction at the Landlord and Tenant Board but lost his case in July. “Now I don’t have any options with my health and I’m just begging for help basically,” Barnes said. Barnes says he has been in contact with London’s Coordinated Access program and has an intake appointment scheduled for September.

He says he is concerned that appointment will come too late. Tenant advocacy group Acorn London organized Tuesday’s rally and is calling on the City of London to close what it describes as a loophole in the city’s renoviction protections.

“Darcy is the vulnerable tenant that we’ve been talking about for, you know, for the years that we’ve been organizing here,” said Jordan Smith of Acorn London. “Darcy is the example.” London’s Rental Unit Repair Licence bylaw requires landlords seeking to evict tenants for extensive repairs or renovations to meet additional municipal requirements.

However, the city’s rental unit repair licence does not apply to N13 notices issued for demolition or conversion. Those cases are primarily governed by Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act and the Landlord and Tenant Board.

Acorn says the distinction leaves tenants vulnerable to displacement when a landlord uses a N13 for demolition or conversion. “It leaves him completely stuck,” Smith said. “It leaves him homeless in the next few months, unless one of our councillors steps in and someone, a champion from the city, steps in and puts their money where their mouth is and protects the vulnerable tenants.” Acorn is calling on the city to adopt stronger, enforceable protections against demovictions and to provide immediate housing support for vulnerable tenants facing displacement.

Smith also alleges the work cited in Barnes’ eviction does not match what has happened at the property. “The whole purpose was originally that five units were going to be converted into two, and that’s just not happened,” Smith said.

“In fact, the landlord has gone and rented the units that were vacant.” Those allegations have not been independently verified. CTV News contacted the landlord by phone and email seeking comment on Barnes’ eviction and the allegations raised by Acorn.

He did not respond. The property at 34 Adelaide Street South has previously been the subject of a planning application before the city. In November 2025, London city council approved a zoning amendment for the property that recognized the existing converted dwelling and permitted up to six residential units.

City protections don’t cover demolition N13s. The City of London’s current renoviction rules are intended to provide additional protections for tenants when landlords require vacant possession to carry out extensive repairs or renovations.

However, the municipal Rental Unit Repair Licence does not apply when a N13 is issued for demolition or conversion. The city has previously considered whether to expand its renoviction protections to cover those situations.

Council has so far declined to make that change, while broader tenant protections related to demolition and redevelopment could be considered as part of future municipal policy work. For Barnes, the debate over how London’s rental housing rules should change is now immediate.

He says his health makes finding another home particularly difficult and he fears he will have nowhere to go when he is required to leave.

stories.title: One small business. $2M in exports to the U.S. And now, $1M in tariff costs
stories.summary: Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
paragraphs: The tariff war between Canada and the U.S. has created a million-dollar problem for one concrete business in Stratford.

The U.S. administration recently hit a long list of unique Canadian business sectors with the 50 per cent import tax. Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is among the affected businesses – a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.
The business, which makes concrete products, will have to now pay about $1 million annually on its $2 million in export sales to the U.S., general manager Byron Veldjesgraaf said.
That’s a big hit for a small business.
“This is not ideal, it’s not sustainable,” Veldjesgraaf said.

After tariff and trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last week, the U.S. levied 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of goods shipped from Canada into America. It is also considering increasing tariffs on vehicles and auto parts to 50 per cent in January.
Canada announced Tuesday it will hit the U.S. with a series of counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of goods, starting in September.
Veldjesgraaf is now looking at import codes that apply to products sold into the U.S. to see if he can ship his concrete products south of the border under different codes to avoid tariffs.
“We’re reassuring customers we’ll eat tariffs for now” until the business can use different import codes, he said. “Each product can fall under different codes that aren’t tariffed.”

Exports to the U.S. make up about 10 per cent of his business and if it can’t get tariff relief, they May have to cut costs including staffing reductions. “That could happen, absolutely, if there’s a reduction in our exports. This is bad for the Canadian economy.”
Ed’s makes concrete products, including “architectural” pieces such as benches and large planters. It has supplied Ford Motor Co. headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan.

Jason Bates is director of the London Region Manufacturing Council. He believes the 50 per cent tariffs will have a limited impact in Southwestern Ontario. He’s hearing little about it driving up costs but he’s concerned about the toll on business investment and confidence because tariffs create uncertainty.

“It’s an odd list” of businesses being hit by President Donald Trump’s new tariffs, he said. “It’s mostly small businesses that will feel it. But it adds to the confusion, the frustration and May slow investment as some businesses are taking a wait-and-see attitude” about future growth and investment.
“It’s frustrating.”

While some wood products are hit with the additional export fees, Element5, the fast-growing business in St. Thomas that uses wood in construction and has expanded into the U.S., has dodged the tariff bullet, said its president, Chris Latour.
“We’re not impacted but we’re still concerned,” Latour said. “People in small businesses are adding up costs now and not going ahead with projects they planned. This uncertainty is a challenge.
“Construction companies have to price plywood, toilets and sinks and they don’t know what their costs are. Widespread tariffs of any sort will impact decision-making in every industry.”

content_blocks.text: The tariff war between Canada and the U.S. has created a million-dollar problem for one concrete business in Stratford.
content_blocks.html: The tariff war between Canada and the U.S. has created a million-dollar problem for one concrete business in Stratford.

content_blocks.text: The U.S. administration recently hit a long list of unique Canadian business sectors with the 50 per cent import tax. Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is among the affected businesses – a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.
content_blocks.html: The U.S. administration recently hit a long list of unique Canadian business sectors with the 50 per cent import tax. Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is among the affected businesses – a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.

content_blocks.text: The business, which makes concrete products, will have to now pay about $1 million annually on its $2 million in export sales to the U.S., general manager Byron Veldjesgraaf said.

content_blocks.text: That’s a big hit for a small business.

content_blocks.text: “This is not ideal, it’s not sustainable,” Veldjesgraaf said.

content_blocks.text: After tariff and trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last week, the U.S. levied 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of goods shipped from Canada into America. It is also considering increasing tariffs on vehicles and auto parts to 50 per cent in January.

content_blocks.text: Canada announced Tuesday it will hit the U.S. with a series of counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of goods, starting in September.

stories.title: Local animal rescue cleared to resume adoptions after four-month halt
stories.summary: The rescue is reopening adoptions while an animal-welfare investigation and appeal over a nearly $200,000 bill continue.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
After a nearly four-month halt in finding homes for its animals, a St. Thomas animal rescue has been cleared to resume adoptions.

Saving Animals’ Lives Together (Salt) Rescue Organization received approval to adopt out 10 cats following a visit from Provincial Animal Welfare Services on Friday. The rescue was initially directed to halt all adoptions after an April 30 inspection led to an ongoing animal-welfare investigation.

The inspection resulted in about 60 cats being taken into provincial care, with 17 later euthanized. Salt was also issued a nearly $200,000 bill for veterinary and boarding costs associated with the animals in provincial care.

On Wednesday, Brent Ross of the Ministry of the Solicitor General told The Free Press that Animal Welfare Services removed 81 cats from the property over concerns about their health and Salt has been advised not to adopt out any remaining cats that are in distress.

In an email, he wrote that Animal Welfare Services will continue conducting regular inspections of the rescue to ensure animals are receiving the quality of care mandated by the province.

Salt owner Bonnie Smith said, “It’s been very difficult every day, even now it is. I just want these animals to find their homes.”

The return of adoptions comes as Salt continues to face financial pressure. Smith said the rescue is trying to raise money through a GoFundMe campaign to help pay the $198,165.28 statement of account while also covering ongoing veterinary bills and other operating costs.

Tuesday was the deadline to settle the statement of account, but Smith said payment has been paused while Salt goes through the appeal process.

Smith said donations have declined amid criticism of herself and the rescue. Since it began Aug. 16, the GoFundMe campaign has raised $2,335, less than two per cent of its goal.

“We just don’t have the money because many people aren’t donating. I think it’s because of all the negativity out there, which is unfortunate because the cats are the ones that are going to suffer,” Smith said.

After halting adoptions for months, the rescue will not be taking in new animals. Smith said she wants the animals already at Salt to find homes rather than spend more time in cages.

She also said the number of animals at the rescue was one factor that contributed to it becoming overwhelmed.

“This has been a nightmare and we do not want to have this reoccurring, so we are going to be not taking a lot of animals right now, maybe even in the future. We can’t get into this situation ever again,” Smith said.

stories.title: Kirsten Krose promises traffic plan, city hall dashboard in mayoral platform
stories.summary: The mayoral candidate says her plan is built around the issues she hears about most from Londoners.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
The first to register and the first to release a platform, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose has unveiled her campaign promises, including a plan for her first 100 days in office.

Released early this week, Krose’s platform focuses on four main pillars: public safety, better city services, better traffic management and restrained taxpayer spending – all linked by a fifth campaign element: housing.

“After talking extensively at the door to different organizations, to different groups, different people, businesses, everything, there were a lot of recurring themes. Traffic was a really big one. Homelessness, feeling safe downtown, safe in other areas, safe on the roads, public transit,” she told The Free Press Tuesday.

“These all kind of just kept coming up, and if the taxpayers . . . are the ones complaining about it, that’s really where we need to be focusing – because clearly they’re not satisfied.”

On public safety, Krose promises elements of both policing and city-building measures, including preventing homelessness through rent and eviction supports and faster navigation of the housing system. On policing, she calls for a greater focus on crime while improving co-ordinated responses to mental health, addictions and homelessness-related calls.

On transportation, one of her first 100-day pledges is to create a “traffic bottleneck program” to evaluate London’s most congested intersections and corridors, as well as school zones for risk.

Boosting transit reliability and frequency is another element, along with evaluating the results of bus rapid transit once it fully launches.

On spending and city services, the platform includes a housing report card, modernizing development approvals, a review of all city departments and, most crucially to Krose, a public city hall performance dashboard.

“What decisions did we make, where is that decision in a process, how much will it cost,” Krose said. “If there’s any changes that are needed – do we know what those changes are, and what do those look like, and have we enacted them? Have we gone forward with them?

“Then also, once a program is running or a change has been made, let’s look at the results of that, and let’s measure that and see at the end what did it cost, what result did it produce, and if we need to do something different, what would that look like?”

Krose said that while she has not held elected office and is an outsider in that regard, she has a broad base of political experience as a bureaucrat, political staffer and public affairs consultant that gives her a different perspective from other candidates.

“Other than the fact that I’m an actual outsider, I did not serve on council. I’ve never served on any council. I have a different perspective as someone that really comes from the business community and as a ratepayer,” she said. “I can represent multiple different areas, and I can see things a little bit differently.”

paragraphs: The first to register and the first to release a platform, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose has unveiled her campaign promises, including a plan for her first 100 days in office.

Released early this week, Krose’s platform focuses on four main pillars: public safety, better city services, better traffic management and restrained taxpayer spending – all linked by a fifth campaign element: housing.

“After talking extensively at the door to different organizations, to different groups, different people, businesses, everything, there were a lot of recurring themes. Traffic was a really big one. Homelessness, feeling safe downtown, safe in other areas, safe on the roads, public transit,” she told The Free Press Tuesday.
“These all kind of just kept coming up, and if the taxpayers . . . are the ones complaining about it, that’s really where we need to be focusing – because clearly they’re not satisfied.”

On public safety, Krose promises elements of both policing and city-building measures, including preventing homelessness through rent and eviction supports and faster navigation of the housing system. On policing, she calls for a greater focus on crime while improving co-ordinated responses to mental health, addictions and homelessness-related calls.
On transportation, one of her first 100-day pledges is to create a “traffic bottleneck program” to evaluate London’s most congested intersections and corridors, as well as school zones for risk.
Boosting transit reliability and frequency is another element, along with evaluating the results of bus rapid transit once it fully launches.

On spending and city services, the platform includes a housing report card, modernizing development approvals, a review of all city departments and, most crucially to Krose, a public city hall performance dashboard.

“What decisions did we make, where is that decision in a process, how much will it cost,” Krose said. “If there’s any changes that are needed – do we know what those changes are, and what do those look like, and have we enacted them? Have we gone forward with them?

“Then also, once a program is running or a change has been made, let’s look at the results of that, and let’s measure that and see at the end what did it cost, what result did it produce, and if we need to do something different, what would that look like?”

Krose said that while she has not held elected office and is an outsider in that regard, she has a broad base of political experience as a bureaucrat, political staffer and public affairs consultant that gives her a different perspective from other candidates.

“Other than the fact that I’m an actual outsider, I did not serve on council. I’ve never served on any council. I have a different perspective as someone that really comes from the business community and as a ratepayer,” she said. “I can represent multiple different areas, and I can see things a little bit differently.”

stories.title: St. Thomas considers tougher approach to vacant downtown storefronts
stories.summary: The city is weighing monthly fire inspections and other measures to encourage landlords to fill vacant properties.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
St. Thomas is exploring ways to entice landlords of empty downtown storefronts and buildings to fill vacancies in the growing community, Mayor Joe Preston says.

Although there May be the “fewest (number) of vacant stores” downtown since Preston moved to St. Thomas roughly 35 years ago, he said there are still “some investors who believe that just the asset growth in their property is enough,” and the city is looking at ways to address those vacancies.

“We’ve been looking at a number of different ways and looking at some other communities that have been trying to address vacant storefronts or vacant buildings in their own right,” Preston said, pointing to Oakville, which has a bylaw requiring inspections of vacant buildings.

One option St. Thomas is considering is more frequent fire inspections.

“We’re working on a plan that makes our fire inspection team inspect the buildings once a month and at a little cost to the landlord, which May inspire them to actually make them not vacant buildings and not make them vacant storefronts,” he said.

Preston pointed to a “couple of major fires” in recent years, including a July 2025 arson fire downtown that destroyed a 144-year-old building and caused $1 million in damage. He said the close proximity of buildings in the core can create dangerous conditions during a fire.

There have been discussions among city council and the fire department about potentially implementing a bylaw to enforce fire inspections, Preston said.

“(The) fire inspection team and the chief have been talking about how to best write the bylaw because it really would take a certain bylaw (to enforce),” he said.

Preston also said any tax breaks once available for vacant storefronts were removed during his tenure as mayor, meaning landlords pay the same tax bill whether a building is occupied or not.

“We want to make sure, first of all, from a safety point of view, and from an incentive of a landlord who’s sitting with an empty storefront to do something else with it,” Preston said.

“There is way more activity right now among landlords to really renovate and move forward anyway, but if we can offer some incentive for them not to leave the storefronts empty, then we’ll move as fast as we can on it.”

Downtown storefronts have been gradually filling over the past several years, Preston said, crediting in part the city’s introduction of special constables to the core.

“(It makes) downtown safe for people to be there and welcoming, and that’s really made quite a difference,” he said. “Almost once a week there’s another new business opening up somewhere.”

Commercial growth is also visible elsewhere.

Preston said downtown “becomes the next place to be” after businesses have flocked to the “absolutely full and growing” SmartCentres outdoor shopping centre and the Elgin Centre mall.

The city’s commercial growth comes amid an industrial boom, with Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo’s $7-billion EV battery plant expected to open in 2027 and eventually employ 3,000 people, along with nearby Vianode’s planned factory.

“I would say, in my whole 35 years in St. Thomas, this is as vibrant a downtown as we’ve had to this point,” Preston said.

“There’s no stopping us now. There’s still vacancy. There’s still people who need a place to do commercial activity in our community.”

stories.title: Satan’s Choice president rips anti-patch law targeting Hells Angels
stories.summary: The debate follows recent sightings of patch-wearing Hells Angels members at London restaurants.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The head of Canada’s fastest-growing outlaw motorcycle club is blasting a recent decision to ban public displays promoting the Hells Angels logo in Quebec.

The Quebec crackdown follows a series of sightings of Hells Angels members wearing their patches at London restaurants, a move one organized crime expert says is meant to intimidate rival bikers in Southwestern Ontario.

In April, Quebec passed Bill 13, known as the anti-patch law, to reinforce public safety by barring the public display of names and images associated with an “entity with a criminal purpose.” The law allows Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière to declare certain organizations criminal groups and bars those groups from displaying symbols to promote themselves.

Lafrenière signed a decree last week saying the Hells Angels will be the first criminal group targeted by the law.

“When three Hells Angels walk into a restaurant wearing their jackets, it’s not usually just to go eat . . . it’s to intimidate people and often to collect money,” said Maxime Tardif, a spokesperson for Lafrenière’s office.

The law, which takes effect Sept. 2, applies to the Hells Angels name, the club’s Death Head logo and other symbols and acronyms such as 81, representing H and A in the alphabet, and Affa, or Angels Forever, Forever Angels.

Police can demand individuals wearing clothing promoting the Hells Angels remove it or risk being fined or having the items seized.

News that the world’s largest outlaw motorcycle club will be the first targeted by the anti-patch law drew criticism from many in the one-per-cent biker community, including Satan’s Choice national president Harley Guindon.

“It’s a sad thing that’s happening to our country. Our freedoms being stripped . . . this is getting ridiculous,” Guindon wrote on social media. “Just spend more taxpayers money for something that won’t stop anything.”

Guindon, former vice-president of the Brooklin, Ont., chapter of the Hells Angels, revived the club his father helped launch decades ago. Since relaunching Satan’s Choice last year, the club has opened 50 chapters across Canada, including three in Southwestern Ontario.

Guindon said he hopes his former club mounts a legal challenge against the anti-patch law “for everyone.”

Lawyers representing the Hells Angels have previously vowed to challenge the law, according to a report from The Globe and Mail.

The Hells Angels have a long and bloody history in Quebec. The club, founded in Fontana, Calif., in 1948, opened its first Canadian chapter in Montreal in 1977. Over the decades, the Hells Angels have fought turf battles with rival motorcycle clubs, street gangs and mafia groups in Quebec.

The debate over whether outlaw bikers should be able to wear their patches in public was recently reignited in London after a group of Hells Angels were spotted at a south-end steakhouse and another member on the patio of an Old South restaurant.

Ontario doesn’t have any laws prohibiting public displays promoting outlaw biker clubs, but police in several cities have launched programs barring individuals from wearing biker- and gang-affiliated clothing inside businesses.

Police in participating cities provide signs with the words “No Gang Colours, No Gang Clothing” to local businesses and say the policy is enforced through the Trespass to Property Act. Businesses are instructed to call police to remove patrons violating the rule.

With files from The Montreal Gazette

stories.title: London Knights training camp: Blue line a clear strength as OHL season nears
stories.summary: London Knights, Maksim Sokolovskii, Henry Brzustewicz, Easton Cowan, OHL, junior hockey, CHL
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Maksim Sokolovskii got a lot of social media mileage out of flipping a 1,000-pound tire during his summer workouts.

But being nearly 6-foot-8 and 240 pounds won’t shield the big defenceman from the expected playful jabs about it in the early days at London Knights training camp.

“I told him the real workers work in silence,” Henry Brzustewicz, the L.A. Kings first-rounder, joked. “They don’t need to film themselves and stuff like that.”

Was that impressive TikTok video a sign that the gregarious Russian has grown too big for his britches in his second year with the famous OHL franchise?

“Maybe,” Brzustewicz said.

Sokolovskii thought carefully, then mustered up his most threatening glance.

“I’ll say (to him), ‘See you on the ice,’” the Flyers first-rounder warned before breaking into laughter.

The obvious strength of the Knights this season is the blue line. The biggest questions right now are how much has Sokolovskii improved and will Brzustewicz ever play another regular-season game in London?

“So busy summer,” the 18-year-old man mountain said. “Back-to-back Russia to North America around four times. I was in Philly (development) camp. Really enjoyed it. I was with (Denver Barkey and Oliver Bonk) and we had a very good time together.”

His confidence in speaking English and playing at an elevated level has grown immensely since he arrived in London.

“So much better,” he said. “Of course, it helped me so much (being with the Knights) last year. It’s like a mini-NHL team here.”

To a man, the returning players see last year’s first-round playoff loss to Sault Ste. Marie as an unfortunate blip.

“Memorial Cup, that’s the goal,” Sokolovskii said. “We have a really good team and will work to win games.”

It’s hard to argue with a guy who can flip a 1,000-pound tire.

SO Long?: The Knights are understandably bracing themselves for losing Brzustewicz to the pro ranks this fall.

A new and controversial rule will allow NHL first-rounders to stay in the American Hockey League even if they have major junior eligibility remaining. The 19-year-old Michigander is already one of Los Angeles’s prize prospects and will use this time with the Knights as a springboard to a successful Kings training camp.

“Being able to play in scrimmages here and get into game shape with some preseason should be good for getting my game going,” he said. “(Being in London) helps you a lot. It’s the most pro guys there are and (the Hunters) know what they’re doing.

“We went to a good situation here and you want to show you’re ready for the next step. When I go (to L.A.), I just want to play my game, show what I’ve got, play with confidence and do what I can to give myself the best chance for that opportunity.”

For now, he plans to be an example.

“I hope I can,” he said. “You want the Knights to do well every year even if you’re not playing there. You just want to be a good role model and leader to the younger guys. There are some high-calibre leadership guys here (already).”

Around THE Rink: Knights grad Easton Cowan was at Canada Life Place Monday filming a commercial. He is expected to go on the ice here ahead of Maple Leafs training camp, as will back-to-back Memorial Cup champions Sam O’Reilly (Lightning) and Jared Woolley (Kings) after their successful run with Kitchener. “It’s awesome,” London associate GM Rob Simpson said. “It gives our new players and younger guys a real understanding of, this is how you have to compete, this is how you practice and these are the details you need in your game if you’re going to be a first-round NHL pick or legitimate prospect beyond our league. We love when those guys come out because it’s a good learning experience for everybody else.” . . . Will Swedish import forward Marcus Nordmark play in London this season? That question won’t be answered until after the Anaheim first-rounder attends Ducks training camp. The 18-year-old is currently skating with the Swedish national team until the end of the week . . . As always, there are deep hockey roots at Knights camp. London’s 2026 first-rounder Ryan Beaulieu, of course, is the son of 2005 Memorial Cup champ Josh Beaulieu, Ewan Sim is the 16-year-old brother of 2025 Memorial Cup champ and 2026 Calder Cup champ Landon Sim, Jaxon Welychka’s cousin Brett played for the Knights from 2010-15 and Anthony Thomas-Maroon’s dad Pat was here in 2007-08 before a long NHL career. Even more recently, Dylan Wilmott is the younger brother of Ben Wilmott, who was a top scorer for London last season before being dealt to the Barrie Colts and drafted by Vegas in the third round. . . . It doesn’t stop there. Recently signed forward Kane Barch’s father Krys is a former Knight who will do some development work with London after coaching the Niagara IceDogs last year. Ryker Kesler is the son of former NHLer Ryan Kesler and Bradley Marchant’s dad Todd was a long-time Edmonton Oiler and Anaheim Duck. . . . Import forward Luca Santala, who represented Finland at the Hlinka Gretzky Cup, grew up with father Tommi playing pro hockey in Europe and a couple of NHL stints with Atlanta and Vancouver. Santala was at his playmaking best in some of the early Knights scrimmages . . . Up-and-coming defenceman Cooper McAslan, a London Nationals star last year, will miss some early camp time with a lower-body injury. He won gold with Canada at the Hlinka Gretzky Cup with an 8-1 victory over the United States in the final . . . The Knights’ annual Green-Gold game will be played Wednesday, 4 p.m. at Canada Life Place.

stories.title: Extortion trial dates set for former London city councillor
stories.summary: Mariam Hamou, a former Ward 6 politician, was charged in November with extortion and harassing communications.
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
A former London city councillor is heading to trial next year on extortion and harassment charges.

Mariam Hamou, 51, was charged in November with extortion and harassing communications after an investigation headed up by the St. Thomas police.

A court-ordered publication ban protects the identity of the complainant.

Hamou’s defence lawyer, Laura Ellis, made a quick video court appearance before justice of the peace Chantal Bertrand in a London courtroom Tuesday where she confirmed that Hamou is scheduled to have a two-day Ontario Court of Justice trial on Feb. 26 and March 2.

Hamou was not in court for the brief appearance and was not required to attend.

Hamou represented Ward 6 for about a year after former city councillor Phil Squire stepped away from city hall politics. She was appointed in November 2021, but narrowly lost her seat the following year in the civic election to Coun. Sam Trosow.

Following the charges, Hamou resigned from the London Health Sciences Centre’s community advisory committee, saying publicly that “I don’t want to bring any negativity or anything toward LHSC while I am under investigation.”

Hamou served on several boards and committees before her appointment to council.

The St. Thomas police were called in to investigate the London-based complaint to ensure no conflict of interest, as required by the Community Safety and Policing Act.

No other details about the investigation were released by the police at the time of the charges.

Hamou’s case was brought before the Ontario Court several times over the past months for case management before the trial dates were set on Tuesday.

stories.title: ‘Game on’ for AdaptAbilty network, co-founded by Western researchers
stories.summary: A new platform, AdaptAbility, provides information on local opportunities for sport and exercise for people with disabilities.
stories.author: Special
paragraphs: When her feet hit the water for her first coached swim, eight-year-old Hannah Burns thought, “this must be what flying feels like.”
“Swimming to me means freedom. No special equipment, no barriers. Just me and the water and how fast I can go,” she said.

Today, as a high-performance athlete and a swim coach, Burns wants to make sure other kids and families don’t have to rely on word-of-mouth, as she did, to find parasports opportunities that bring them joy.

“A lot of opportunities are out there but they need to be widely available and visible. Sport is so important for everyone’s developmental path whether you’re born with a disability or acquire one later in life. Sport challenges you and gives you a community in a deeper way.”

Burns is among several sports enthusiasts who – with St. Joseph’s Health Care London (St. Joseph’s) and Western University as catalysts and sustainers – have created a unique-in-Canada network of London-based groups and advocates involved in parasports and physical activity.
AdaptAbility London aims to build local support, connection and community through sport and exercise for people with a disability.
Its website, AdaptabilityLondon.CA , provides contact information for specific sports; is searchable by season, sport, venue and time; and is also a portal for volunteering and other resources.

Site visitors could learn, for example, that boccia takes place on Wednesdays, adaptive climbing monthly at The Junction, wheelchair basketball Thursday evenings, goalball on Fridays and fitness activities for people with physical and/or intellectual disabilities most weekdays at Hutton House.
Until now, that was information you might find – if you found it at all – by scouring the internet, scrolling through social media pages or by word-of-mouth.
“This is a one-stop shop in the London area,” said Stephanie Marrocco, research coordinator at St. Joseph’s Parkwood Institute.
Marrocco says the network is new but gaining momentum.
“Everyone is very passionate about what they do, so everyone wants to see their program succeed and grow.”

Network participants include athletes and adaptive sports organizations, along with co-founders Marrocco, Western kinesiology professor Laura Misener, Lawson Research Institute scientist Dalton Wolfe and Western psychology professor Dr. Blair Evans.

“Many of these groups don’t have any other way of getting connected so getting them together was the first big task. And then, because it’s their network and not ours, the next question we asked was, ‘what are your needs?’” said Misener, who is also Western’s Dr. Frank J. Hayden Endowed Research Chair in Sport and Social Impact.
We’re facilitators of the network, but we co-create the solutions with athletes, organizations and participants. It’s shared expertise, shared leadership,” added Wolfe.

For sport organizers, needs often include: resources to train, retain and sustain volunteer engagement; advertising and awareness; collective advocacy; finding fully accessible sports venues; and brainstorming sustainable funding models.
Participant needs include building social connections with peers and finding information on sports specific to their interests, preferred schedules and seasons.

Adam Purdy, a Canadian Paralympic swimmer, coach and Canadian Paralympic Committee member whose PhD studies focus on participation in accessible sports, says the network benefits everyone, from participants to high-performing competitors to the people who support them.
“Sport is what nourishes a culture. We need it for healthy communities and it should be accessible to all. Every body deserves to experience it.” – Adam Purdy, PhD candidate in kinesiology
There isn’t another network like this in Canada.

Calgary Adapted Hub powered by Jumpstart is similar to AdaptAbility London but is aimed at children and youth, not adults. ParaSport Ontario provides information about more than 30 sports accessible to people with disabilities but doesn’t sort by calendar or include sports specific to people with intellectual disabilities.
“We all have common needs, including the need for connection,” Misener said. “I sometimes think there’s a false dichotomy between high performance and participation.”
Misener believes in the importance of valuing self-determined physical activity and creating pathways for all these opportunities across the lifespan.
“If you want to do yoga twice a week, that’s great. And if you want to pursue a high-performance route, we need to make sure these opportunities are also available.”

stories.title: London library hunting for 125 missing high school yearbooks
stories.summary: The library is asking Londoners to donate yearbooks to help fill gaps in a collection dating back more than a century.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
If you have an old high school yearbook lying around, chances are the London Public Library might want it.

A new campaign from the library is asking Londoners to donate their high school yearbooks for its collection at the Ivey Family London Room, the London-specific archive at Central Library, 251 Dundas St.

David Caloren, the library’s coordinator of central adult services and supervisor of the London Room, says the campaign is a way to fill gaps in the collection.

“Yearbooks are not something you can just buy from a vendor, you have to be connected to the school in some way to get them,” he said. “We’ve relied on people giving them to us because we can’t really seek them out that way.”

Caloren says the library has been building its yearbook collection for decades, starting in the 1960s, and has volumes from 34 different high schools in London and the surrounding area – some of which have since closed.

He estimates there are more than 750 unique yearbooks stored at the London Public Library, all donated by Londoners over the years.

“We’ve never had a program of actively collecting them, they come to us sort of haphazardly,” Caloren said.

Caloren says yearbooks are especially valuable to researchers and Londoners because of their hyperlocal subject matter, often showing what was happening in a community and trends in fashion, music and clubs.

“They tell a lot about what was important for that particular community at that particular time,” he said.

They are also a good source for finding old photos of famous Londoners from when they were younger, he joked.

Caloren says the oldest official yearbook in the collection is from London Central Secondary School in 1922.

But the library also has documents dating back to 1903 that he describes as “yearbook-adjacent” – small, student-produced booklets that were never formally issued as yearbooks.

The library is currently looking for around 125 yearbooks to fill gaps in the collection, he says, but most of what it needs is fairly recent.

“I’m really hoping those Gen Z kids have a look. We’re missing a lot of the 2010 yearbooks and that would be a great score for us if we could fill in our gaps for this century,” Caloren said.

Some of the oldest material the library needs is from De La Salle High School, which closed in the 1950s. The collection has only one yearbook from the school.

Londoners looking to donate their high school yearbooks can contact the London Room by email at research.request@lpl.CA or by phone at 519-661-5100 ext. 2410.

stories.title: Ingersoll Driver Charged in Thames Centre
stories.summary: The 23-year-old is facing impaired driving charges.
stories.content:
The 23-year-old is facing impaired driving charges.

Thames Centre - Someone from Ingersoll is facing charges in Thames Centre.

Middlesex OPP officers responded to reports of a suspicious vehicle at business on Hamilton Road shortly before 5:00 a.m. on Friday.

They pulled the vehicle over and charged the 23-year-old driver with operation while impaired and operation while impaired with a blood alcohol concentration over 80. He has a court date in London next month.

If you spot a drive that you believe could be impaired, the OPP say you should call police immediately.

stories.title: London's small, medium-sized businesses will be hit harder by new U.S. tariffs, warns expert
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 25, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 25
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 25, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 25
Some 700 London businesses exported $8B worth of goods to the U.S. in 2023: Ledc

New, steep tariffs imposed by the U.S. over the weekend will hit small and medium-sized businesses in the London area harder than previous levies, and the region’s economic picture will likely “get a whole lot worse” before it gets better, one economic expert says.

While previous tariffs announced by Donald Trump's administration were broad targeting sectors including auto, steel and aluminum, the 50 per cent levies that took effect Saturday affect billions of dollars worth of Canadian products from a range of industries, including alcohol, honey, hockey sticks and jewelry.

“All of those things involve small and medium-sized enterprises, or small and medium-sized enterprises who rely on some of the other producers,” said Mahmood Nanji, a policy fellow at Ivey Business School and former Ontario associate deputy finance minister.

“I think this will exacerbate London's, sort of, weaker economy. London has had one of the highest unemployment rates in Canada for the last six to nine months, and I think you're likely to see more layoffs. The uncertainty means that these businesses will not invest if they're going to expand their operations.”
For the London area, which has been dependent on the manufacturing sector, the tariffs have “had the impact, (and) it’s likely to get a whole lot worse,” he added.

Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the U.S. on Friday, accusing them of trying to introduce last-minute measures which could have restricted Canada’s ability to do deals with other countries and protect its culture.

As a result, new 50 per cent tariffs took effect Saturday on roughly $28 billion Cdn ($20 billion US) worth of Canadian goods, layering on top of existing sanctions. Carney has promised dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs by Sept. 8.
Trump has since threatened a 50 per cent tariff on vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada effective Jan. 1, and on social media, threatened Canadian energy flowing through the United States.
"When the Americans go to the negotiation table first, with the right attitude toward our industries and a true partnership, of course we'll come to the negotiating table," Carney said Monday.
WATCH | Political scientist on Premier Ford's 'emotional' response to Trump:

According to the London Economic Development Corporation, some 700 businesses in London exported around $8 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2023, said Graham Henderson, CEO of the London Chamber of Commerce. Roughly 450 manufacturers employ about 20,000 people, he said.

“People hear tariffs and they tend to think of auto plants, but there’s businesses in London that manufacture here, they’ve built a market in the U.S., and suddenly there’s a 50 per cent tariff aimed directly at their product category,” Henderson said.

“This is not a blanket 50 per cent tariff on everything London exports. It covers $20 billion US of Canadian exports, and that is roughly five per cent of our annual exports to the United States,” he said.
While five per cent of Canadian exports sounds manageable, a London manufacturer whose product is inside that five per cent, "woke up Saturday with a 50 per cent problem,” Henderson added.
It’s a reality being faced by Melanie Pierce, owner of Seven Sisters Ritual Apothecary on Dundas Place.

The downtown business, which Pierce describes as a “house of authentic witchcraft and magic,” makes and sells several products that fall under the tariffs, including candles, essential oils, toilet waters and botanical herbs.

“I would say just over 80 per cent of our online clientele are American, so this is greatly going to affect our online sales, which are already greatly impacted, probably bringing them down to hardly anything at all,” Pierce said.
Like other local merchants selling south of the border, Seven Sisters has already had to contend with shifting regulations when it comes to shipping, including last year's
de minimis exemption which allowed goods under $800 to enter the U.S. duty-free.

“We have recently had to fill out a whole slew of extra paperwork to even be able to ship into the U.S., and it was such a headache I honestly couldn't even look at it for a while. I just wrapped my head around what that looked like and got that going again,” Pierce said.

Pierce hasn’t seen a clear drop in U.S. demand yet, but it’s still early days. Already concerned about trade volatility, she says work has been underway to add manufacturing capacity at a sister store in Massachusetts, but notes that's still months from completion.
In the meantime, she says she's looking to boost domestic sales and invest in local advertising away from social media to offset any tariff-related impacts.
