stories.content:
Dr. Timothy Carey and Dr. Patrick Thornley, Paediatric Orthopaedic Surgeons at Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) pictured with a Mazor Robotic System.

Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has achieved a major milestone in surgical innovation, becoming the first hospital in Ontario to use the Medtronic Mazor robotic spine platform for a paediatric scoliosis correction.

Mazor features software that allows surgeons to upload their patients’ imaging in order to plan their procedures ahead of time and then

action them in the operating room (OR). The system has three arms: a robotic arm that assists with the procedure, one that performs CT scans and another that takes X-rays, giving care teams access to the latest imaging right in the OR.

Fourteen-year-old Paige Hillman first started complaining about back pain last summer. Not long after, her mother Melissa spotted the telltale signs of scoliosis, a condition she also has.

“I could see the curve in Paige’s back. It was like her whole body was curving to the spine, even her shoulders,” Melissa says. “You could see it when she was walking and when she was wearing tighter clothes.”

Given her first-hand knowledge of how painful a scoliosis spinal malformation can be, Melissa didn’t want the same fate for her daughter.

“As I get older, I’m in more pain than I used to be with a lot of pain in my lower back and up in my neck area,” Melissa says. “I just didn’t want her to feel like that. I wanted her to grow up and have fun.”

Melissa called their family physician in Windsor, who then referred Paige to Children’s Hospital.

Dr. Patrick Thornley, Paediatric Orthopaedic Surgeon, and his colleagues worked with Paige and her family to come up with a plan to address her scoliosis. Knowing the Hillmans were open to surgical intervention, they asked if they would be interested in having the robotic Mazor platform used during Paige’s procedure. Up until that point, the system had only been used on adults at LHSC.

After conversations with the care team, the Hillmans said yes and in March 2026 Paige became the first paediatric patient in the province to undergo a scoliosis correction using Mazor.

Using images of Paige’s spine taken during low-dose radiation CT scans, Dr. Thornley and the care team used the Mazor planning software to map out Paige’s entire procedure ahead of time and design the surgical plan.

That plan was then uploaded directly onto the robotic platform in the operating room (OR) where they took X-rays to confirm Paige’s positioning, all of which enabled real-time visualization that supported Dr. Thornley through the procedure.

Dr. Thornley opted to use the robot to place the most challenging screws in Paige’s spine, reducing the time it would usually take to accomplish that task from roughly 20 minutes manually down to about three. The actual spinal correction took a little less than four hours to complete, with Paige’s dedicated care team spending about eight hours in total with her in the OR.

The procedure was a success resulting in a near-perfect result with Paige even gaining a couple of inches in height thanks to the spine correction. She was able to go home to Windsor after just a few days in hospital and returned to school after roughly four weeks, instead of the expected six.

Most importantly, her quality of life has greatly improved.

“My back would hurt most of the time before the surgery and even more when I would lie down,” Paige says. “Now it barely hurts. It’s really nice.”

As for how it makes her feel to know her surgery was the first such case in Ontario, Paige doesn’t hold back.

“It feels amazing. Sometimes I like to brag to my friends about it,” she says with a chuckle.

"Performing the corrective surgery now rather than when Paige reached adulthood will greatly reduce her chances of further issues and ensure she’ll have a much healthier spine moving forward,” says Dr. Thornley.

“The risk of progressive deformity has been removed by this surgery,” he says. “It’s everything we could hope for at least in the early stages.”

“I feel proud of Paige as a patient, I think she’s done a great job.”

Paige’s positive experience is a testament to Children’s Hospital’s commitment to innovation and investment in the latest technologies. Both the University Hospital as well as the Victoria Hospital and Children’s Hospital sites now operate their own Mazor robotic platforms, and to date, surgeons across LHSC have performed 10 to 15 procedures using the platform, across a range of patient ages and conditions. The costs associated with both robotic platforms are supported through provincial funding.

Robotic‑assisted surgery is transforming operating rooms worldwide, but uptake across Canada remains varied. LHSC has long been a leader in the field, recognizing the potential for improving patient care.

“The strength of Mazor and other spine robotic platforms, will ultimately be that we're going to see increased accuracy, increased safety, better outcomes, and safer, faster surgeries for kids and adults,” says Dr. Thornley. “That's the whole point of why we want to use it.”

stories.title: Lifelong Friends Donate $2.4 Million to Advance Cancer Care—and Encourage Others to Give Back
stories.summary: August 13, 2026
paragraphs: Craig Combe (left) and Ken MacMaster.

London, Ont. — What began as a friendship has grown into a shared dedication to helping others. Today, that dedication is reflected in an extraordinary $2.4-million gift from the Combe and MacMaster families to expand access to specialized cancer treatment at the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

Their desire to support better cancer care was inspired by seeing how the disease has touched their friends and loved ones. Long-time supporters of London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf), Ken and his wife, Barb, have been giving back to LHSC and the community it serves for more than 20 years. As previous owner and long-time leader of MacMaster Chevrolet Cadillac Buick GMC, a family-owned and operated dealership, Ken has long been committed to supporting the communities his business serves.

"I took it in my heart to help people if I could," says Ken. "If we can eliminate some suffering or grief for families, then it'll be worth it." Together, they saw an opportunity to make a meaningful difference by helping ensure patients have access to the latest cancer treatments in the area.

"I wanted to see this advanced way of treating people brought to London," says Craig. "Our physicians already have the expertise, but this helps ensure they have the tools to match. If we can help give patients even greater peace of mind during one of the most difficult times in their lives, that's worth investing in."

Their gift will support the purchase of LHSC's second Varian Ethos therapy system, an AI-driven linear accelerator and the introduction of the AlignRT radiation therapy and HyperSight imaging system across the hospital's fleet of linear accelerators (LINACs). Donor-funded upgrades to medical technology are crucial to helping LHSC deliver faster, more precise and personalized radiation therapy while expanding capacity to meet the needs of a growing number of patients.

Linear accelerators are used to treat many types of cancer, including prostate, bladder and lung cancers, as well as some blood cancers. Together, these software upgrades will enhance the precision and efficiency of radiation treatment in London, helping clinicians deliver even more accurate, personalized radiation treatment while improving each patient’s experience.

AlignRT allows continuous monitoring of a patient's position throughout treatment, helping clinicians maintain accuracy during radiation delivery. For many patients, it can also eliminate the need for the small permanent tattoos traditionally used to guide treatment—a lasting reminder of one of life's most difficult chapters. Hypersight gives a sharper, faster picture of the patient on the machine for clearer visualization of the tumour and nearby organs.

LHSC provides radiation treatment to approximately 300 patients each day across 9 linear accelerators (LINACs). As patient demand continues to grow, the hospital is working to expand access to new advanced technology, with donor support playing a critical role in completing specialized software upgrades for its linear accelerators (LINACs). Craig and Ken's gift is a significant step toward that goal. They hope it will inspire others to help complete the remaining upgrades so more patients can benefit from this technology. Donations of every size will help bring these innovations to more treatment rooms, improving care for people with cancer across the region.

Thanks to Ken and Craig's generosity, these innovations will help clinicians deliver faster, more personalized radiation treatment by allowing them to adapt treatment plans in real time, improve precision and better protect healthy tissue. The technology is designed to target tumours with exceptional accuracy while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue—similar to treating only the yolk of an egg without affecting the white or shell.

"This remarkable gift will help ensure our patients continue to benefit from some of the most advanced radiation technologies available," says Dr. Michael Ott, department head of oncology at LHSC. "By giving our clinical teams greater precision and flexibility in how we plan and deliver treatment, this investment will enhance the care experience for thousands of patients in the years ahead. We are deeply grateful to the Combe and MacMaster families for helping shape the future of cancer care in our region."

As longtime supporters of London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf), the two friends believe investing in local health care strengthens the entire community. They hope their gift will encourage others to help fund the remaining funding needed to upgrade LHSC's linear accelerators.

"Craig and Ken's generosity is already changing what's possible for cancer patients in our community," says John H. MacFarlane, president and CEO of Lhsf. "Donor support helps make innovations like these possible, ensuring more patients across Southwestern Ontario can benefit from the latest developments in cancer care."

It is estimated that over two in five Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime, a reality the Combes and MacMasters hope will inspire others to give back. While their gift will help shape the future of cancer care, they believe every donation can make a meaningful difference. Together, gifts of every size help bring new advancements to LHSC and ensure more patients can receive the care they need.

stories.title: Middlesex County Council Meeting Highlights – August 11, 2026
stories.summary: Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes.
paragraphs: Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes .
Strategic Plan to Guide Future at Strathmere Lodge

The Committee of the Whole approved a new strategic plan for Strathmere Lodge that will guide the next five years of delivering resident-centred care, strengthening organizational sustainability, and preparing for the future. The new plan is the culmination of an extensive planning process that combined research, operational analysis, jurisdictional comparisons, and broad engagement with residents, families, staff, volunteers, leadership, and other interest holders. An updated organizational logo as well as vision, mission, and value statements will also be implemented with the new strategic plan.
To learn more, read the Strathmere Lodge Strategic Plan – 2026-2031 report .
Economic Development & Tourism- Q2-2026 Performance Report

The Committee of the Whole received the second quarterly performance report under the Economic Development and Tourism Strategic Plan (2026–2030) . Approved by Council in March 2026, the plan focuses on investment attraction, business growth, workforce alignment, site readiness, and tourism development, and marks a shift to outcome-based measurement and reporting.

During Q2 2026, Middlesex County supported more than 1,000 investment inquiries and more than 900 regional investment attraction initiatives with partner organizations such as the Ontario Food Cluster, Ontario Manufacturing Community Alliance, Southwestern Ontario Marketing Alliance, and Invest Ontario. Business retention and expansion initiatives engaged 165 employers, identified six expansion opportunities and connected 22 businesses with provincial, federal, and regional support programs.

Workforce initiatives included the launch of the Workforce Navigator program, which helped six participants secure employment, increased collaboration with regional workforce partners and significant growth in the Work in Middlesex platform, where job seeker registrations surpassed 1,200 people. Tourism promotion expanded through the Find It Here in Middlesex County campaign, generating hundreds of thousands of digital impressions and supporting local tourism operators and events.
For detailed information, read the Economic Development & Tourism – Q2-2026 Performance Report .
Update on Renewed Woodlands Conservation By-Law after 18 months

County staff provided the Committee of the Whole with an update on the implementation of the Woodlands Conservation By-Law revised in January 2025. The by-law regulates the destruction or injuring of trees within woodlands on private property to prevent deforestation and promote good forestry practices. The 2025 changes introduced several administrative updates, including clearer application requirements, modernized forms, simplified fine provisions, and updated terminology. Since 2025, the County received and processed 144 Notices of Intent to harvest woodlands, which is consistent with historic rates.

Today, there are approximately 55,700 hectares (137,700 acres) of woodland within Middlesex County. Each year, about 2,000 acres of woodlands are selectively harvested, with timber valued at over $2 million, supporting both the local economy and long-term forest health.
For more information, read the Woodland Conservation By-Law Implementation Update report .
Five new Community Safety Zones on County Roads

County Council passed amendments to the Community Safety Zones By-Law to establish five new zones on County Roads. Community Safety Zones are typically located near places where people are more likely to be walking, cycling, or crossing the road, including schools, playgrounds, parks, and other community facilities.
All Community Safety Zones in Middlesex County are in effect 24 hours a day, seven days a week, year-round.
New zones include:
For more information, and a complete list of Community Safety Zones on Middlesex County Roads, visit the Community Safety Zones webpage.

Recommendations made by the Committee of the Whole at the August 11, 2026, meeting will be considered by County Council at its next regular meeting on September 8, 2026. The Legislative Services Department maintains the official record for all County government proceedings.
For more information please contact: @email

stories.content:
Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes .

Strategic Plan to Guide Future at Strathmere Lodge

The Committee of the Whole approved a new strategic plan for Strathmere Lodge that will guide the next five years of delivering resident-centred care, strengthening organizational sustainability, and preparing for the future. The new plan is the culmination of an extensive planning process that combined research, operational analysis, jurisdictional comparisons, and broad engagement with residents, families, staff, volunteers, leadership, and other interest holders. An updated organizational logo as well as vision, mission, and value statements will also be implemented with the new strategic plan.

To learn more, read the Strathmere Lodge Strategic Plan – 2026-2031 report .

Economic Development & Tourism- Q2-2026 Performance Report

The Committee of the Whole received the second quarterly performance report under the Economic Development and Tourism Strategic Plan (2026–2030) . Approved by Council in March 2026, the plan focuses on investment attraction, business growth, workforce alignment, site readiness, and tourism development, and marks a shift to outcome-based measurement and reporting.

During Q2 2026, Middlesex County supported more than 1,000 investment inquiries and more than 900 regional investment attraction initiatives with partner organizations such as the Ontario Food Cluster, Ontario Manufacturing Community Alliance, Southwestern Ontario Marketing Alliance, and Invest Ontario. Business retention and expansion initiatives engaged 165 employers, identified six expansion opportunities and connected 22 businesses with provincial, federal, and regional support programs.

Workforce initiatives included the launch of the Workforce Navigator program, which helped six participants secure employment, increased collaboration with regional workforce partners and significant growth in the Work in Middlesex platform, where job seeker registrations surpassed 1,200 people. Tourism promotion expanded through the Find It Here in Middlesex County campaign, generating hundreds of thousands of digital impressions and supporting local tourism operators and events.

For detailed information, read the Economic Development & Tourism – Q2-2026 Performance Report .

Update on Renewed Woodlands Conservation By-Law after 18 months

County staff provided the Committee of the Whole with an update on the implementation of the Woodlands Conservation By-Law revised in January 2025. The by-law regulates the destruction or injuring of trees within woodlands on private property to prevent deforestation and promote good forestry practices. The 2025 changes introduced several administrative updates, including clearer application requirements, modernized forms, simplified fine provisions, and updated terminology. Since 2025, the County received and processed 144 Notices of Intent to harvest woodlands, which is consistent with historic rates.

Today, there are approximately 55,700 hectares (137,700 acres) of woodland within Middlesex County. Each year, about 2,000 acres of woodlands are selectively harvested, with timber valued at over $2 million, supporting both the local economy and long-term forest health.

For more information, read the Woodland Conservation By-Law Implementation Update report .

Five new Community Safety Zones on County Roads

County Council passed amendments to the Community Safety Zones By-Law to establish five new zones on County Roads. Community Safety Zones are typically located near places where people are more likely to be walking, cycling, or crossing the road, including schools, playgrounds, parks, and other community facilities.

All Community Safety Zones in Middlesex County are in effect 24 hours a day, seven days a week, year-round.

stories.title: Registration now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference
stories.summary: Registration is now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference, inviting Londoners to connect, learn and discover resource
stories.content:
Registration is now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference, inviting Londoners to connect, learn and discover resources that support healthy aging in London.

Presented by the Age Friendly London Network, this year’s conference takes place on Wednesday, October 14, at the Best Western Lamplighter Inn. The annual event brings together local organizations, health professionals, community leaders and residents for a full day of learning, conversation and connection focused on building a more age-friendly community.

The conference will once again feature, expert speakers, engaging presentations, interactive sessions and an exhibitor marketplace showcasing programs, services and supports available to older adults across London and Middlesex. Headlining this year's program is keynote speaker Mary Lou Smoke, whose presentation, Medicine and Song, will explore the power of culture, storytelling and healing.

"Creating an age-friendly city means ensuring older adults have access to information, resources and opportunities to stay connected to their community," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "The Age Friendly London Conference brings people together to learn from one another, discover valuable local services and explore practical ways to support healthy aging."

The conference reflects London's ongoing commitment to fostering an inclusive community where people can age well. Since becoming the first Canadian city to join the World Health Organization's Global Network of Age-friendly Cities in 2010, London has continued to work alongside residents and community partners to improve the quality of life for older adults.

For additional conference details, including the full agenda and registration information, visit London.CA/AFLConference .

About Age Friendly London

The Age Friendly London Network is a collaborative group of older adults, caregivers, service providers and community members working together to make London a more age-friendly city. Through partnerships, education and community action, the Network supports initiatives that help older adults remain active, connected and engaged in all aspects of community life. To learn more, visit London.CA/AgeFriendly .

stories.summary: Western Fair ticket holders can ride on London Transit to the fair for free!
paragraphs: Western Fair ticket holders can ride on London Transit to the fair for free!

Fair goers can ride transit to and from the Western Fair from September 11 to 20, 2026 for free two hours before the fair starts until end of service. Given the Fair’s operating hours, attendees on weekdays can ride for free from 1PM to end of service and on weekends from 9AM to end of service. To ride to the fair for free on transit simply show the driver your valid Western Fair ticket, either printed or digital, when you board the bus.
Routes that stop near the fairground are Routes 2, 7, 20 & 94 but riders travel for free on all London Transit routes to connect to the fair. Enjoy the Western Fair !

stories.title: London surpasses Housing Accelerator Fund target ahead of federal deadline
stories.summary: The City of London is pleased to announce that it has surpassed its three-year Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) target of 11,803 new housing un
paragraphs: The City of London is pleased to announce that it has surpassed its three-year Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) target of 11,803 new housing units, reaching 11,966 new units four weeks ahead of the September 7, 2026 federal deadline.

The milestone reflects continued housing growth across London and the collective efforts of City Council and staff, builders, developers, non-profit housing providers and other partners to increase housing supply across the city.

“Surpassing our Housing Accelerator Fund target is a significant achievement for London, and it demonstrates what is possible when we set ambitious goals and have the leadership to deliver on them,” says Mayor Josh Morgan. “This progress didn’t happen by accident. It is the result of deliberate choices, a focused approach to getting housing built, and policies that have removed barriers and accelerated approvals. The federal investment through HAF has been an important partner, but it is the decisions we have made here in London that are turning that investment into real homes and real results. As we look ahead, Londoners should know that the work is not finished, and that staying focused on building more housing, creating affordability and keeping our city moving forward will require steady leadership and a willingness to keep delivering.”

The Housing Accelerator Fund is a federal program delivered through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc) that provides funding to municipalities to accelerate housing construction and support lasting changes that increase housing supply.

“This milestone represents an extraordinary amount of work by people across the Corporation and throughout London’s building and development industry,” says Scott Mathers, Deputy City Manager, Housing and Community Growth. “HAF provided London with an important federal investment that allowed us to move more quickly and try new approaches to supporting housing development. Our staff embraced that challenge, and our builders and developers continued to bring projects forward and turn approvals into new homes. Everyone involved should be proud of what we have accomplished together.”
London has also completed all 11 initiatives included in its HAF action Plan. Together, the initiatives have helped increase housing supply by:

{'text': 'expanding financial incentives for homeowners and builders to create new housing', 'html': 'expanding financial incentives for homeowners and builders to create new housing'}
{'text': 'improving development approval processes and reducing barriers to housing construction', 'html': 'improving development approval processes and reducing barriers to housing construction'}
{'text': 'investing in infrastructure needed to support housing growth in key areas of the city', 'html': 'investing in infrastructure needed to support housing growth in key areas of the city'}

While London has now surpassed its housing supply growth target, approval of the fourth and final Housing Accelerator Fund payment remains subject to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation’s review of London’s third-year HAF report. That review will include confirmation that the requirements of the funding agreement have been met and an assessment of London’s performance against all targets under the agreement.

Reaching the HAF target is an important milestone in London’s broader efforts to respond to continued growth and housing needs. The City will continue working with the building and development industry, housing providers and other partners to increase housing supply and build on the momentum created through HAF.
Learn more at London.CA/morehomes .

stories.title: The Wild Child returns: From Maine museum back to London, Ont.
stories.summary: Car enthusiasts were given a special treat Saturday when an iconic drag racer made its return to its original home.
stories.author: Brent Lale
paragraphs: Car enthusiasts were given a special treat Saturday when an iconic drag racer made its return to its original home. The ‘Wild Child’ was a legendary 1965 Ford Falcon B/FX (Factory Experimental) drag racer campaigned by London’s Rankin Ford dealership.

Current owner Joe Germann brought the car to display at the East London Timing Association car show Saturday. “Ford of Canada decided to build some BFX race cars (in 1965),” said Germann. “They built three B/FX race cars with 289 HiPo (High Performance 89 cubic-inch, small-block V8) in them, nine-inch rear end, Nascar top loader, fiberglass body parts and things of that nature of this date.

One of them is completely gone and the other one is just the shell. So, this is the only car of those that were built up here to be race cars that is alive.” The car was acquired by Rankin Ford in May 1965 and driven by local racers Ev Rowse and John McIntyre at Canadian tracks like Grand Bend, Cayuga, and St.

Thomas, as well as throughout the U.S. It piled up a string of victories in its successful debut in the Nhra’s B/FX class in 1965, running in the 11.50s at about 120 mph. “It was brand new and it was pretty damn exciting,” said Rowse of Dorchester.

“It was a nice ride, and it could go like hell and make a lot of noise.” In 1965, Rankin Ford held a contest in the newspaper to name the vehicle. The winner received $25. “It was a local car that did well on the bigger screen,” said Dave Mathers, one of the few people who have owned the vehicle.

“Some of the national events it went to, and it did well. It won a bunch of races, and it was good advertising for Rankin Ford at the time as well.” Mathers is one of six people who have owned the vehicle since 1965. “At the end of the 1967 season, Rankin decided they’d had enough, so they sold the car to Bob Jezquel from Woodstock,” said Mathers.

“Bob kept it till 1993 when I bought it and I restored back to one of the original colours. A guy came in (to the showroom where Mathers displayed it) and offered me a lot of money for the car, so I sold it to him. He sold it to another guy, and then that guy sold it to Joe.” Germann is from Boston and has kept the car at both his home and in the Owls Head Transportation Museum in Maine.

He had no idea the history of the car, when he bought it in auction in 2003. “I’d been looking for a ‘Cammer’ motor, (Overhead-Cam 427-cu.in. V-8 engine, also known as the Sohc),” said Germann. “I found the car, and I didn’t know the history.

I found out about Ev Rowse, John McIntyre, some years later. I restored the car back to what it was originally. The only difference and a difference in the restoration was in ‘67, they put the stock motor in it and painted the car blue.

I didn’t want the car blue. I wanted it the ‘Wild Child’ red. So, we painted it the (original) ‘Wild Child’ red.” Saturday, Rowse – a Canadian Drag Racing Hall of Famer- was able to see the car again. “I’m pretty proud of Joe,” said Rowse.

“The work he’s done and the way this car looks today, it’s fantastic. It’s just gorgeous.” Germann brings has brought the car back to its original home a few times over the past 23 years. He often takes it out on the track but wasn’t able to this time because of the rain Friday.
“We come back every few years, and it’s nice to come back and see our old friends,” said Germann.

What is a culvert?

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.
Why is this happening now?

Repairs and replacement in the near term are required to ensure structural integrity, address safety hazards, protect infrastructure from damage due to stream water fluctuation and precipitation runoff, prevent upstream flooding, and ensure compliance with environmental standards.
Transportation impacts

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Please follow the detour signage. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

stories.title: Strong interest received for LHSC’s Board renewal: Update to the community
stories.summary: August 6, 2026To the communities we serve,
paragraphs: To the communities we serve,

In June, we announced the launch of recruitment for a renewed London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) Board of Directors. At that time, we shared our commitment to attracting skilled, experienced, and diverse candidates who could help guide the next chapter of LHSC's renewal and future success.

Today, I wanted to provide an update on the recruitment process, which has been met with an exceptional response from our community. We received more than 90 applications from individuals interested in serving on the renewed Board. The level of interest reflects a strong commitment to the future of health care in southwestern Ontario and to the continued success of LHSC.

I have been encouraged not only by the number of applications we received, but also by the breadth of experience and perspectives represented among the candidates. Applicants bring governance expertise, leadership experience, professional and technical knowledge, community involvement, and valuable lived experience. Together, they reflect a community that cares deeply about the future of LHSC and is eager to contribute to its success.

The selection committee, consisting of health system leaders, government partners, and a patient partner, is currently conducting a comprehensive review of all applications using a consistent evaluation process designed to ensure fairness and objectivity. Once that review is complete, the committee will meet to identify the candidates who will move forward to the interview stage.
Given the volume of applications received, the review process is expected to continue through late August and early September, with interviews anticipated later in September.

The response to this recruitment reflects the confidence many people have in the work underway at LHSC and their desire to help shape what comes next. As we continue strengthening our governance, accountability, and transparency, it is encouraging to see so many individuals willing to share their expertise in support of our organization and the communities we serve.

I want to sincerely thank every individual who submitted an application. Serving on a Board requires a significant commitment of time, thought, and energy. The willingness of so many people to step forward demonstrates the deep connection they feel to LHSC and the care we provide.

While not everyone who applied will ultimately join the Board, I hope every applicant knows how much we appreciate their willingness to serve. Applications will be saved for consideration in future recruitment. The exceptional response reflects a community that is engaged, invested, and committed to helping shape the future of one of Canada's largest academic health sciences centres.

As the recruitment process continues, we remain committed to providing updates and maintaining transparency about our progress. Thank you for your continued support of LHSC and the patients, families, and communities we serve.
David Musyj Supervisor London Health Sciences Centre 519-870-2999 david.musyj@LHSC.on.CA

As we continue strengthening our governance, accountability, and transparency, it is encouraging to see so many individuals willing to share their expertise in support of our organization and the communities we serve.

I want to sincerely thank every individual who submitted an application. Serving on a Board requires a significant commitment of time, thought, and energy. The willingness of so many people to step forward demonstrates the deep connection they feel to LHSC and the care we provide.

While not everyone who applied will ultimately join the Board, I hope every applicant knows how much we appreciate their willingness to serve. Applications will be saved for consideration in future recruitment. The exceptional response reflects a community that is engaged, invested, and committed to helping shape the future of one of Canada's largest academic health sciences centres.

As the recruitment process continues, we remain committed to providing updates and maintaining transparency about our progress. Thank you for your continued support of LHSC and the patients, families, and communities we serve.

stories.title: Expanding care across the region: Home hemodialysis training now available for renal patients at Brightshores Health System
stories.summary: August 6, 2026
paragraphs: From left: Keri Aitken Toby, Home Hemodialysis Nurse, with Marg and Bob Funston, in the hemodialysis room at the Funston's home. Photo credit: Brightshores Health System.

For the first time, patients in the Grey-Bruce area can access home hemodialysis training closer to home. This initiative, developed in coordination between the Regional Renal Program at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and Brightshores Health System, reduces the need for patients to travel to London for training and expands access to regional, patient-centred care.
Bob and Marg Funston are from Southampton, which is about 30 km from Owen Sound.

In 2019, Bob experienced a fall and broke his back. When he went to the hospital they found an aneurysm which led to complications and a kidney was unfortunately damaged, and it atrophied. Since then, the other kidney has started to fail and reached a point where Bob felt like he had no energy and, ON the advice of his nephrologist, decided to start dialysis.

"The kidney failure came on quite slowly so I had time to adjust and accept the fact that I would have to go on dialysis. Marg and I talked and wanted to go the route of doing treatments at home," Bob explains.
Neither Bob nor Marg knew much about dialysis but knew people who had to go in-centre three times a week and understood that they would have to adapt their lifestyle around treatment.
"We said, 'okay', at everything life has thrown at us. So, for this, knowing Bob needed to go on dialysis, we decided to make the best of it," shares Marg.

Bob had the permacath inserted for dialysis at Victoria Hospital, LHSC in London and had his first series of treatments there. "We would leave at 6:00 a.m. and get home around 6:00 p.m., going back and forth between Southampton and London three times a week. We were thrilled at the possibility of having the dialysis education in Owen Sound, saving us all those trips. It was a bonus that we met Keri in London initially and had a great connection," Bob says.
Bob and Marg say that Keri Aitken Toby, the home hemodialysis nurse that trains patients in home hemodialysis at Brightshores, was a great teacher and made the experience more relaxed.

"I am a teacher by background, and I was impressed with Keri's teaching approach," Marg says. "Bob and I have no medical background, so we had a lot of learning. We had lots of opportunities to practice what we learned and were provided a book with step-by-step directions which we read thoroughly many times. The book is valuable and something we refer to daily."
Bob has been doing hemodialysis at home with help from his wife Marg since the end of May 2026. They are grateful to have had the education provided so close to home.

"It's important to have something like this in rural Ontario since medical care is not as accessible as more populous areas. Keri was a wonderful teacher and we felt supported – and still do – through everything," Marg and Bob share.

Home hemodialysis (HHD) is an opportunity for eligible patients to have more flexibility and prolong independence. Patients who were eligible for home hemodialysis previously had to visit LHSC to complete their training.
For those who are eligible and choose to proceed with HHD, the training is three times a week for eight to ten weeks.

"It's a big commitment for patients to come down to London that frequently to do the training. And with the task of having to learn so much new information and spending a lot of time in a vehicle, that can be tiring," explains Dr. Andrea Cowan, Medical Director, Home Hemodialysis, LHSC.
Through the collaboration between LHSC and Brightshores, eligible patients are now able to access that training at the Owen Sound Hospital.

“By offering this specialized education locally, we can help patients build the confidence and skills to manage their treatment while reducing the need for travel,” said Colleen Ouwendyk, Brightshores, Director Cancer Centre and Ambulatory Services. “The program provides greater flexibility for patients and their caregivers—supporting access to expert education, ongoing support and specialized care closer to home.”
Keri Aitken Toby, HHD Nurse with Brightshores and a remote member of LHSC's HHD team, helps patients and their caregivers gain the knowledge and confidence needed to safely perform dialysis at home.
Aitken Toby has been a nurse for 27 years with much of her career in dialysis.

"I really enjoy teaching people about dialysis and helping them bring more quality to their life by helping them dialyze at home," says Aitken Toby. "I have also enjoyed my time in renal care because I get to know patients really well seeing them so frequently and get to help them through their kidney care journey."
Aitken Toby grew up in rural Ontario, so she is aware of the unique way of life, which helped with her adaptation to working remotely from the main regional renal centre in London.
She notes that the workflow requires continued collaboration and communication to ensure teams at both sites are on the same page to provide seamless and high-quality care for each patient.

"We're very fortunate to have excellent nursing and health discipline team members in the home hemodialysis program. This strength in the program means that patients have access to great staff support at LHSC and at Brightshores," Dr. Cowan says, "One of the big aims for home hemodialysis support is making sure we are doing as much as we can to bring care to patients instead of bringing patients to their care. This initiative is emblematic of that philosophy by making access to care more equitable and not limited by geography."

stories.title: LHSC enters 17th annual Canadian Blood Services Hospital Challenge
stories.summary: August 5, 2026
paragraphs: After achieving the most blood donations and winning the Canadian Blood Services (CBS) Hospital Challenge for two years in a row, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is back again this year with staff and community members who are eager to roll up their sleeves and support patients who rely on life-saving blood transfusions.
This year, the 17th annual CBS Hospital Challenge runs from August 1 until October 31.
This year our goal is to donate 150 units of blood to support all kinds of patients who rely on LHSC. (and keep the first-place trophy in London for a third year!)
We need your help to reach our goal and continue making a life-saving difference.
Blood transfusions aren’t just used in emergencies! Donated blood plays a critical role in everyday medical care at LHSC including surgeries, cancer treatment and chronic illnesses.

stories.title: Physician peer support program strengthens wellbeing
paragraphs: Image (left to right): Dr. Joy Mangel, hematologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead at London Health Sciences Centre, and Dr. Tamara Spaic, endocrinologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead at St. Joseph’s Health Care London.

Long hours, high demands and heavy responsibility can weigh down even the most resourceful physicians. That’s when a listening ear from a peer can make all the difference. London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Joseph's Health Care London’s (St. Joseph's) Peer Support Program brings that evidence to life, offering support one conversation at a time.

"It's really a human-to-human thing," says Dr. Tamara Spaic, endocrinologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead for St. Joseph's. “It’s about lending a listening ear and saying, yes, I understand what you are going through.”

The Peer Support Program is comprised of physician volunteers who make themselves available for informal colleague-to-colleague conversations. They often act as a first point of contact for wellbeing assistance and connection to available resources.

Dr. Joy Mangel, hematologist and LHSC’s Physician Wellbeing Lead, is leading the peer support program efforts, and she and Dr. Spaic have spent the past year growing and re-invigorating the program. Together, the two have recruited new volunteers, provided support to current peer supporters, and promoted the work and its many benefits across both hospitals.

The true value, Dr. Mangel says, lies in the shared experience of physicians. "You're talking to someone who understands what it's like to be in your shoes, to be on call and in clinic, teaching and managing a high patient volume. You don't have to provide the background - they already get it. It's also about having a place where you can share challenges, and a safe space where you can say, ‘I'm struggling.’"

The program initially began as an initiative through Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry to support faculty during the pandemic and has evolved into a hospital-led network of more than 40 volunteer peer supporters spanning every clinical department.

Dr. Mangel says potential wellbeing leads are usually identified by their department or division heads – physician leads in different clinical programs across the hospitals. Physicians who take on this role must have an interest in wellbeing, but do not need to have extensive prior experience.
“Wellbeing leads are provided with training in empathetic listening, recognizing crisis situations and knowing when and how to connect a colleague with additional support,” she notes.

Peer support is just one facet of a more comprehensive physician wellbeing program. When someone is in crisis or peer support isn’t the answer, colleagues are directed to the right place to find support. Drs. Spaic and Mangel also collaborate with the wellbeing programs at their respective hospitals and the wellness team at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry to ensure alignment with broader wellbeing initiatives.

For Dr. Mangel, the role has brought an unexpected sense of renewal. She says the meaningful work has changed how she relates to others in all areas of her life, making her feel more mindful, kind and attuned.

Dr. Spaic sees the program as something larger than any one conversation. It's building a structure and community so that every physician is supported, regardless of whether they have deep roots in the community or are a newcomer with fewer connections.
It has also caused her to pause and consider her own experience.

"This has kind of turned the tables," she says. "For the first 15 years of my practice, all I wanted to do was look after others. But now I'm starting to realize the value of someone looking out for me."

stories.content:
Image (left to right): Dr. Joy Mangel, hematologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead at London Health Sciences Centre, and Dr. Tamara Spaic, endocrinologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead at St. Joseph’s Health Care London.

Long hours, high demands and heavy responsibility can weigh down even the most resourceful physicians. That’s when a listening ear from a peer can make all the difference. London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Joseph's Health Care London’s (St. Joseph's) Peer Support Program brings that evidence to life, offering support one conversation at a time.

"It's really a human-to-human thing," says Dr. Tamara Spaic, endocrinologist and Physician Wellbeing Lead for St. Joseph's. “It’s about lending a listening ear and saying, yes, I understand what you are going through.”

The Peer Support Program is comprised of physician volunteers who make themselves available for informal colleague-to-colleague conversations. They often act as a first point of contact for wellbeing assistance and connection to available resources.

Dr. Joy Mangel, hematologist and LHSC’s Physician Wellbeing Lead, is leading the peer support program efforts, and she and Dr. Spaic have spent the past year growing and re-invigorating the program. Together, the two have recruited new volunteers, provided support to current peer supporters, and promoted the work and its many benefits across both hospitals.

The true value, Dr. Mangel says, lies in the shared experience of physicians. "You're talking to someone who understands what it's like to be in your shoes, to be on call and in clinic, teaching and managing a high patient volume. You don't have to provide the background - they already get it. It's also about having a place where you can share challenges, and a safe space where you can say, ‘I'm struggling.’"

The program initially began as an initiative through Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry to support faculty during the pandemic and has evolved into a hospital-led network of more than 40 volunteer peer supporters spanning every clinical department.

Dr. Mangel says potential wellbeing leads are usually identified by their department or division heads – physician leads in different clinical programs across the hospitals. Physicians who take on this role must have an interest in wellbeing, but do not need to have extensive prior experience.

“Wellbeing leads are provided with training in empathetic listening, recognizing crisis situations and knowing when and how to connect a colleague with additional support,” she notes.

Peer support is just one facet of a more comprehensive physician wellbeing program. When someone is in crisis or peer support isn’t the answer, colleagues are directed to the right place to find support. Drs. Spaic and Mangel also collaborate with the wellbeing programs at their respective hospitals and the wellness team at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry to ensure alignment with broader wellbeing initiatives.

For Dr. Mangel, the role has brought an unexpected sense of renewal. She says the meaningful work has changed how she relates to others in all areas of her life, making her feel more mindful, kind and attuned.

Dr. Spaic sees the program as something larger than any one conversation. It's building a structure and community so that every physician is supported, regardless of whether they have deep roots in the community or are a newcomer with fewer connections.

It has also caused her to pause and consider her own experience.

"This has kind of turned the tables," she says. "For the first 15 years of my practice, all I wanted to do was look after others. But now I'm starting to realize the value of someone looking out for me."

paragraphs: The Thames Valley District School Board is seeking interested applicants for appointment to its Election Compliance Audit Committee for the 2026 municipal election.

Compliance Audit Committees are required under the Municipal Elections Act , 1996 (MEA) to consider applications from eligible electors requesting audits of candidates’, contributors, and registered third party campaign finances in relation to the 2026 Municipal Election, and any by-elections during the 2026-2030 term pursuant to the MEA. Committees May be required to appoint auditors and determine if legal proceedings are required as a result of the auditors’ reports or reports from the clerk of the municipality. The powers and functions of the Committee are set out in Section 88 of the MEA and are in place to ensure that the provisions pertaining to campaign finances have not been contravened and to follow the necessary steps to ensure compliance.

Applicants with a background in accounting, auditing or law are encouraged to apply. The Thames Valley District School Board is committed to equity and inclusion in the recruitment of qualified individuals who reflect and support the diverse perspectives, experiences and needs of our students and school communities.

stories.title: Beyond the bedside: Research in the Paediatric Critical Care Unit
stories.summary: July 24, 2026 Paediatric critical care is a highly specialized field dedicated to the intensive treatment of critically ill children. Health-care professionals in this discipline manage patients with…
paragraphs: Stories July 24, 2026

Paediatric critical care is a highly specialized field dedicated to the intensive treatment of critically ill children. Health-care professionals in this discipline manage patients with life-threatening conditions and complex medical needs. The Paediatric Critical Care Unit (Pccu) at Children’s Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is a 12-bed facility that operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week and cares for approximately 800 children each year.

Supporting both patient care and the advancement of medical knowledge in the Pccu is a dedicated research team at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) that works closely with the clinical teams, patients, and their families. As a Clinical Research Coordinator, Maysaa Assaf oversees all aspects of research studies, from initial planning through to full implementation, to ensure strong protocol adherence and high-quality study conduct.

Children admitted to the unit who meet study-specific eligibility criteria are approached by the research team. Each day, the team reviews potential participants with the most responsible physicians (MRPs) and conduct chart reviews using electronic medical records. The team also checks in at the bedside to assess patient status and coordinate introductions between families and research personnel. The Pccu nurses further support the team’s research by collecting necessary study-specific assessments at the bedside.
During recruitment, the research team completes data collection, data entry, and patient follow-ups in alignment with protocol.

For most of the team’s research, data is captured by reviewing patients’ charts, completing real-time bedside assessments, and conducting parent surveys. The data is primarily captured in the research electronic data capturing system, REDCap.

The Pccu team is committed to delivering the highest standards of treatment, care, and safety for children at Children’s Hospital at LHSC. The research program continues to evolve, reflecting a wide range of clinical interests, including sedation and opioid management, infectious diseases, traumatic brain injury and neurocritical care, cardiac arrest, environmental health, and transport medicine.
In her role as Clinical Research Coordinator, Maysaa has the pleasure of working with a talented group of physicians.

Dr. Janice Tijssen is the medical director of the Pccu. Her research focuses on paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, transport medicine, and access to health care. One of her projects, the Prime Trial, evaluates the effectiveness of administering intramuscular epinephrine during resuscitation efforts in children experiencing cardiac arrest outside of a hospital. As a part of this research, Maysaa and the research team work with multiple paramedic services and their respective base hospitals across Ontario to ensure they are well equipped and trained for successful roll out of the trial.
Above: Paramedics from Middlesex London Paramedic Service (Mlps) run a simulated paediatric cardiac arrest scenario.

Dr. Douglas Fraser is a clinician-scientist specializing in paediatric critical care medicine. His research focuses on identifying key signaling pathways as well as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for acquired brain injury, severe sepsis, and COVID-19.

Dr. Fraser also serves as Director of the Translational Research Centre (TRC), a human tissue biobank that bridges clinical care and research by supporting the integration of patient-based studies with laboratory investigation. Much of the research conducted in the Pccu involves the collection of biological specimens, particularly blood samples. Maysaa is currently collaborating with Dr. Fraser’s team on an international Phase III clinical trial aimed at identifying effective treatments for long COVID.

Dr. Rishi Ganesan is clinician scientist whose work is dedicated to enhancing neurological outcomes for critically ill children in the Pccu. His work incorporates advanced neuromonitoring methods to deepen our understanding of delirium, as well as identify covert consciousness and assist in neuroprognostication. Maysaa assists with overseeing the projects, training and supporting the team, and actively recruiting for the studies in the Pccu. One new project, titled Precit-ABI for short, aims to support neuroprognostication of critically ill children with acquired brain injuries and understand covert consciousness by utilizing EEG, fNIRS, and fMRI tools.

Dr. Anna Gunz is the founding director of Children Environment Health Clinic (ChEHC) Ontario. Dr. Gunz’s research spans health monitoring of climate change, meaningful support for youth with eco-distress, and increasing community and health-care facilities’ understanding and action in planetary health. In her work with Dr. Gunz’s team, Maysaa assists with onboarding students and staff to support initiatives surrounding patient and family health and healing experiences through increased exposure to nature, both inside and outside of the hospital. She is currently working with the team on the Nature Prescription for Adolescents Health project, which focuses on prescribing nature toolkits for patients struggling with depression and mental health.

While serving as Research Coordinator in the Pccu presents unique challenges, it also provides Maysaa with opportunities to work alongside exceptional health-care professionals who, despite their extensive responsibilities, are eager to expand their knowledge and support research initiatives.
Maysaa also has the privilege of meeting many patients and families.

“These families, even during their most difficult times in the hospital, are wholehearted about participating in research,” Maysaa says. “They willingly contribute to enhancing care for future patients, fully aware that the research May not yield immediate benefits for their child.”

While executing research is not a straightforward process, Maysaa is honoured to play a role in the transformation of patient care. For her, the opportunity to connect clinical practice with research is invaluable.

stories.title: Nephew spends 10 years repatriating propellor from uncle’s Second World War plane
stories.summary: On this day 85 years ago, Andy Smart’s uncle Sgt. George Stevenson crashed his plane in Scotland during a training flight in the Second World War.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
On this day 85 years ago, Andy Smart’s uncle Sgt. George Stevenson crashed his plane in Scotland during a training flight in the Second World War. After a decade of searching, Smart not only found, but repatriated one of the wooden propellors from his uncle’s plane to the church he belonged to in Meaford, Ont.

“The plane was completely destroyed by fire with the exception of this propeller blade, which broke off. The propeller blade was taken from someone in the nearby village of Leadhills and put into a pub and hotel down there and hid for four years,” said Smart, who hails from Vanastra.

The wooden propellor served as an umbrella rack for years before Smart, who spent 10 years searching, finally tracked his uncle’s lost propellor down at a library in Scotland. He contacted the owners, who agreed to give him the propeller to display at the church his uncle attended every Sunday after moving to Meaford from Scotland in 1928.

“When he was killed, it was quite a blow to a lot of Meaford people who knew him, and also to the church, his fellow parishioners,” said Smart. Stevenson was the first pilot from Meaford to join the war effort, and the first to be killed overseas.

Bringing a piece of him “home” means the world to parishioners at Christ Church Anglican in Meaford. “While Meaford is a small town, it’s an international town. We have stories that go around the world, be that with the propeller, or be that with our glass here,” said the church’s Minister Father Brendon Bedford.

The glass Father Bedford spoke of are four memorial stained glass windows at the church, made up entirely of stained glass fragments recovered from European churches levelled during the Second World War. The church’s minister at the time, Fr.

Harold Appleyard, served as a military chaplain from 1942 to 1945. Seeing the destruction of centuries old churches everywhere he went, he was granted permission to sift through the ruins and collect stained glass fragments to create new stained glass windows at his church back in Canada.

The four memorial windows made from thousands of shards of stained glass collected from more than 130 European churches were unveiled shortly upon his return from war in 1946. “We have some of the oldest glass, by virtue of where it comes from, some of the oldest glass in North America.

Some pieces upwards of 700 to 800 years old,” said Fr. Bedford. A plaque, still with scorch marks from the fires that felled it, made from a destroyed church pew from the Second World War, adorns the church’s wall as well.

On it, the names of the six Meaford soldiers killed in the war. Atop that list, Sgt. George Stevenson, who, thanks to his nephew, parishioners at his former church will now have a tangible piece of for centuries to come.

“I’m the youngest nephew and I’m getting older. And by the time I’m gone, people in my family will still be able to come here to this church and see the propeller, read the stories, and see the stories about their Great Uncle George, or Great-Great Uncle George.

Because of what he did for all of us,” said Smart. A special memorial service unveiling George Stevenson’s propellor, and an 80th anniversary re-dedication of the church’s memorial windows, will take place on Aug. 15 at Christ Church Anglican in Meaford.

There will be about 40 members of Sgt. Stevenson’s family present, including his nephew Andy, who spent a decade bringing a small piece of him home to join a growing memorial at his uncle’s former church to Meaford’s war heroes.

“They have pictures, they have stories. But now they actually have a piece of what he sacrificed,” said Smart.

stories.title: Historic Model T Fords drive into London for 69th Annual International Tour
stories.summary: The streets of London, Ont. are echoing with the distinctive rumble of a bygone era as the 69th Annual Model T Ford Club International Tour, dubbed the Thames Valley Tour, has officially rolled into town.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
paragraphs: The streets of London, Ont. are echoing with the distinctive rumble of a bygone era as the 69th Annual Model T Ford Club International Tour, dubbed the Thames Valley Tour, has officially rolled into town. From July 19 to July 24, 2026, the city and the surrounding southwestern Ontario region are playing host to approximately 150 of the finest remaining examples of the first automobile to truly bring personal transportation to the masses.

Organized by the Ontario Region Model T Ford Club, which is also celebrating its 50th anniversary this year, the prestigious international event has drawn an estimated 350 to 400 enthusiasts from across Canada, the United States, and Australia.

The Ford Model T, produced between 1908 and 1927, is legendary for its role in transforming society. “This is the car that Henry Ford developed. So, everybody had a mode of transportation,” explained Brian Dowell, who brought a meticulously restored Model T from Saint Clair, MI., for the event.

Mark Schneider, tour co-chair, elaborated on its revolutionary impact, “This was the first vehicle they would have ever owned. They were literally showing up at the dealership in horses and buggies and leaving with the Model T.” The tour is not just a gathering of vintage cars; it’s a celebration of automotive heritage and the dedication of owners who preserve these icons.

Many vehicles on display have undergone extensive, painstaking restorations. Eric MacLeod’s sedan, one of two competing for the coveted Stynoski Award for the most meticulously restored Model T, has a remarkable history.

stories.title: Middlesex County seeking public representatives to serve on boards and committees for upcoming Council term
stories.summary: Middlesex County Council is seeking public representatives to serve on the following boards and committees for the upcoming 2026–2030 Council term: Middlesex County Accessibility Advisory Committee, Library Board, and Planning Advisory Committee.
paragraphs: Middlesex County Council is seeking public representatives to serve on the following boards and committees for the upcoming 2026–2030 Council term:

This is your chance to have a seat at the table and share community perspectives. County boards and committees play an important role in providing advice and recommendations to Council, helping to shape programs, services, and policies that reflect the needs and interests of our communities.
Learn more about each committee and read their Terms of Reference: Boards and Committees

Applicants must be residents of Middlesex County and have an interest in contributing their skills, knowledge, and perspectives to County decision‑making. Previous board experience is an asset but is not required.
The County is committed to building advisory boards that reflect all of our communities and encourages applications from individuals of all backgrounds, experiences, and abilities.
Term of appointment
Appointments will be for the 2026–2030 Council term.

Interested? To apply, submit an application form outlining your background, skills, and experience, and why you want to serve on a board or committee. If you’re applying to more than one board or committee, please complete a separate form for each position.
Visit the Committee and Board Recruitment page for the application form and more information.
Application Deadline: Friday, December 4, 2026
Accessibility accommodations are available upon request throughout the application and appointment process.
For more information, about Middlesex County boards and committees or the application process, please contact the Legislative Services Department at @email .

stories.title: Teen gets five years in youth facility for stabbing random woman to death 'to escape his old life'
stories.summary: The teen will get credit for time served and spend five more years in custody, and four years under supervision in the community.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
paragraphs: A teenager who stabbed a retired kindergarten teacher to death at random as she raked leaves in her Ontario suburban yard said he was determined to kill someone that day “to escape his old life” and to assume an alter ego based on a fictional serial killer, court heard.

The boy, 14 years old at the time of the murder in Pickering, east of Toronto, told psychiatrists after his arrest that when he was suspended from school for carrying a knife he made up his mind to kill, like the serial killers he was obsessed with, it was revealed in court Wednesday when the teen was sentenced for first-degree murder.

The boy said he wanted to be like Yoshikage Kira, a character in a best-selling Japanese manga graphic novel and anime cartoon who is portrayed as a meticulous killer trying to live quietly as a businessman despite periodically murdering women.

On Wednesday, Justice Lisa Wannamaker ruled that the killer should be given credit for the 13 months he has already spent in custody awaiting trial. While credit for pre-trial custody is routinely given in adult sentencing, in cases held under the Youth Criminal Justice Act credit is discretionary.

Wannamaker’s ruling means the boy will serve five more years in custody, instead of six, before being released under supervision in the community for another four years, before completing his sentencing.
Because of his young age, the identity of the killer is protected by law and cannot be published. In April, he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder.

Eleanor Doney was gardening outside her home in Pickering, just east of Toronto, ON May 29, 2025, when she was attacked by a 14-year-old boy dressed in a black shiny trench coat, a black mask, black gloves, overly large dress shoes and carrying a briefcase.

Court heard the get-up he wore was his usual form of dress — a black suit, black trench coat, and a briefcase every day since he was about 10 years old — and was a look he based on two fictional serial killers he admired: Kira, the anime killer, and Patrick Bateman, from the novel and movie American Psycho. Both characters are successful and materialistic businessmen leading a secret second life as a killer.

His interest in looking and acting like the murdering characters extended to talking like them and telling psychologists he wanted to be an accountant “because he wanted to wear a suit and count money.”
The boy said he stumbled upon Doney while out walking about to find a victim.

He told psychologists before his sentencing hearing that he walked past her but then returned because he did not see anyone else and decided she would be his victim. He said he remembers killing her but nothing else, including how many times he stabbed her. He said he felt calm and collected at the time and was not afraid.
“After killing her, he said his violent thoughts went away and he stopped thinking about them,” Wannamaker said in her sentencing decision that summarized her reasons.

The attack was recorded by a neighbour’s doorbell camera. The boy is seen stopping and briefly talking with Doney before pulling a knife from his briefcase and repeatedly stabbing her as she tried to retreat into her house. He then continued walking down the street. A community warning was issued until the boy was identified to police by school administrators and arrested that night at his home.

Since his arrest, psychologists examined and interviewed him as part of the criminal justice process. At the time of the stabbing, the judge was told, the boy’s autism spectrum disorder, learning disorders, and non-verbal reasoning deficits were undiagnosed.

Court heard he had a troubled home life. He was born in Canada to parents who had immigrated from Pakistan and lived in a multigenerational home where Urdu was the primary language; his father lived outside the province for work and only returned on short visits every month or so.

He had only superficial social connections and was fixated on violence and dark themes and had a history of inappropriate online activities, repeatedly researching real serial killers and videos about stalking, stabbing and psychopathy.
In interviews with doctors, he said he had fluctuating violent ideation, which he described as “an urge to kill,” in the weeks before the murder.

“While he acknowledged the seriousness of his misconduct and claimed that he regretted his actions, he had little insight regarding his impact, the impact of his behaviour on others, including his own family or the victim’s family,” Wannamaker said in her decision.

“He struggles with problem-solving. He is socially isolated and emotionally disconnected from others. There is a concern that he wishes to affiliate with individuals online who share antisocial attitudes and beliefs that are supportive of violence.”

After a recent fight with another resident at his youth facility, he told staff he “hasn’t felt this alive,” since he stabbed Doney. He still has a “strong preoccupation” with the anime character. Staff at the facility also said he was highly engaged in school and described him as their “best student.”
Reports told the judge the boy was willing and enthusiastic about programming and therapy at the facility.

“His delusional thought process and disorganized thinking remain present, and it is imperative that he be further assessed and followed over time. He needs psychiatric consultation, intensive individual psychotherapy, and caregiver family-focused services,” Wannamaker said. The best place for that was in a youth facility and not an adult prison, she said.
“He has slowly begun the growth that is necessary,” she said.

“I have been offered a plan that has been developed specifically for (him) and I find that there are reasonable grounds to believe that plan might reduce the risk of him repeating the offence or committing any other serious violent offence.”
She said that if she didn’t extend pre-trial credit the boy might be transferred to an adult facility after he turned 20 and it is unknown what type of programming would be available there.
“The greatest concern to this court is ensuring that he gets the rehabilitative and reintegration support needed,” she said.

Both the prosecution and the boy’s defence lawyer jointly asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence allowable under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, which is a 10-year sentence, split between six years in custody and four years of conditional supervision in the community.

Erin Dann, the boy’s lawyer, asked that Wannamaker deduct one year from her client’s custody portion as credit for his year in custody since his arrest. Crown prosecutor Tammi D’Eri asked that no credit be deducted from his sentence.

At his court hearing the day before, he stood in the prisoner’s box in a dark suit over a white shirt and expressed remorse for murdering Doney. He said that after months of reflection he now understood the impact of his actions and wants to work to become a better person; that he doesn’t want this “grave mistake” to define him.
Speaking to him directly, Wannamaker said she hopes he meant those words and “that you understand the consequences of your actions, at least minimally, at this time.

“Perhaps having seen a room full of Ms. Doney’s loved ones before you, expressing the tragedy that your actions have brought upon them and the unimaginable pain and grief that you have caused, has motivated you to change,” she told him.
Wannamaker said she was moved by the emotional victim impact statements filed by Doney’s family and friends.
“Anyone would be lucky to have an Eleanor Doney in their life,” she said, adding, “there is no sentence which will make Ms. Doney’s loved ones feel whole again.”

After sentencing and outside court, Judy Kirwin, Doney’s daughter, said the sentence given the boy who killed her mother highlights problems in Canada’s justice system. The light punishment doesn’t fit the crime, she said.

“Her horrific end cries out for justice,” she said. “Ironically, the name Eleanor means ‘shining light’ and this light is on the Canadian youth justice system. Are our youth being protected or is justice being served?”

If the boy had been an adult at the time of his crime or treated in court as an adult, his first-degree murder guilty plea would bring an automatic 25-year sentence. The Youth Criminal Justice Act substitutes six years in custody as the maximum prison time for young offenders. The Supreme Court of Canada recently made it harder for young offenders to be tried or sentenced as adults.

“The question I ask is, can this young man be rehabilitated after six years in custody and four years of conditional supervision in the community? It was alarming to hear in court that he still has a fascination with serial killers,” Kirwin said.

“We are failing our young people by dismissing the idea that they don’t know the difference between right and wrong. As a result, we are failing to fulfill the purpose of the justice system which is to keep our communities safe and secure.”
